Strange gamma-ray signal could be most direct evidence of dark matter yet

New Scientist August 20, 2026

An unusual gamma-ray signal could be the most direct evidence of dark matter yet. However, the signal could also be the result of a telescope anomaly or produced by something even stranger than dark matter.

Dark matter forms the bones of much of our universe, driving how galaxies cluster, for example. It also far outweighs all the visible matter, yet for decades researchers have puzzled over what exactly it is.

Part of the problem is that they cannot currently observe dark matter directly. Instead, they can only register its effect on its surroundings. A more direct line of investigation would be to detect particles produced when dark matter collides and annihilates with itself, which some theories suggest ought to happen. Now, Yun-Feng Liang at Guangxi University in China and his colleagues identified a gamma-ray signal that may be the result of this process.

Advertisement

Hints of exotic dark matter particles could be hiding in LHC data

They found the signal after analysing 15.5 years of data from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope (FGST), looking at the Virgo, Fornax, and Ophiuchus galaxy clusters specifically. The researchers chose these galaxy clusters because they are known to contain large halos of dark matter, says Liang. The gamma-ray signal the team found there was shaped like a spike or a line, analogous to a burst of light of only one colour, which some theories predict is the result of dark matter annihilating itself.

“Discovering a sharp gamma-ray line would be the ultimate ‘smoking gun’ evidence proving the existence of dark-matter particles and revealing their properties in particle physics,” says team member Yi-Zhong Fan at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Based on their statistical analysis of the data, the researchers estimated that there is less than a 1-in-10,000 chance that this signal is random cosmic noise or a purely coincidental pattern.

Yet, several questions remain before the team can declare a definitive discovery. Detecting dark-matter signatures in gamma rays has historically been difficult because the signals tend to be weak and can be confused with telescope errors. One promising gamma-ray signal from 2012, for example, proved to be exactly that. Zhao-Qiang Shen, also at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, who worked on the new study, says the team members performed a large number of tests to confirm the veracity of their signal, but some possibility of instrument error remains.

We can use ordinary sugar in the search for dark matter

Moreover, while the new signal is clear when looking at the three galaxy clusters, it seems to vanish closer to the centre of our galaxy, where dark matter is dense, so it should also be annihilating itself and creating gamma rays.

“The fact that the signal lights up in distant clusters but remains silent in our own cosmic backyard is deeply peculiar,” says Liang. “If this is truly from dark matter, it suggests the particles must interact in a much more sophisticated way than conventional theories predict.” Alternatively, the signal could be coming from some even more rare or novel phenomenon, such as ultra-fast particle winds from exotic magnetized neutron stars.

“I find the result intriguing, but I would be quite cautious about interpreting it as evidence for dark matter,” says Juri Smirnov at Liverpool University in the UK. He says that looking at only one galaxy cluster instead of all three together increases the chances that the signal is a product of noise or a random pattern. And he is also worried about how unconventional a dark-matter process would have to be to produce this gamma-ray spike far away from us but not close to the centre of our galaxy. “This puts the standard dark-matter interpretation under considerable tension,” he says.

The best map of dark matter has revealed never-before-seen structures

The team hopes that future telescope missions will add clarity to the situation, for instance the Very Large Area Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which was proposed several years ago and could collect more gamma rays with better resolution. By 2040, FGST will also have doubled its data set, which could further elucidate the nature of the odd gamma-ray spike, says Fan.

“If future telescopes confirm that this signal is genuine, it would represent a historic breakthrough. It would immediately reveal the mass of the elusive dark-matter particle and give physicists a concrete target to build the next generation of fundamental particle theories,” says Shen. “At the same time, it would force us to thoroughly rewrite our standard textbook models of dark matter.”

Physical Review Letters DOI: 10.1103/lq5r-sjp7

Will personalised mRNA vaccines transform cancer treatments?

New Scientist August 20, 2026

Every cancer is different. Because of that, researchers have for decades been working on personalised cancer vaccines designed to make the immune system recognise and attack cancers specific to each individual. The results have been mixed, but now a personalised cancer vaccine has produced positive results in a final-stage trial for the first time.

Moderna announced on 19 August that people who had undergone surgery to remove severe skin cancers, called melanomas, survived longer without the cancer returning or spreading to other parts of the body if they were given a personalised mRNA cancer vaccine in conjunction with another immunotherapy, compared with receiving that immunotherapy alone.

The hope is that this personalised vaccine will work for many other types of cancer. Trials are already underway for certain kinds of lung, kidney and bladder forms of the condition. The other big mRNA company, BioNTech, is also testing personalised cancer vaccines in human trials.

Advertisement

Cancer is increasing in young people and we still don’t know why

Cancers are caused by cells accumulating mutations to the point where they go rogue and start multiplying out of control. Mutations in proteins that protrude from the surface of cells also make cancer cells “look” a bit different to other cells. This allows our immune system to recognise and kill off many cancers without us ever knowing about it. But some cancers slip through the net – the idea of cancer vaccines is to teach the immune system to recognise them.

In the case of the Moderna vaccine, called intismeran autogene, a sample of a person’s cancer – a biopsy – is sequenced. It is then compared with their healthy blood cells to identify surface proteins on the cancerous cells that have distinctive mutations. Up to 34 are selected, and mRNAs coding for those proteins are made and put in the vaccine.

The cancer vaccine is injected into muscles, just like with the covid-19 mRNA vaccine. Cells in the muscles then temporarily produce the cancer proteins, triggering an immune response to them.

It is possible to use other kinds of vaccines, but mRNA has two huge advantages: speed and cost. Making protein-based vaccines requires using living cells, which is time-consuming and requires many safety checks. For people with cancer, the faster a vaccine can be created, the better.

mRNA vaccines are quick and easy to make, while virus-like nanoparticles produce a stronger immune response. Now, the two approaches are being combined to give us the best of both worlds

It is a so-called anti-PD-1 therapy consisting of an antibody called pembrolizumab (Keytruda). Many cancers evolve to evade immune attack by putting up a “don’t attack me” sign. Immune cells “read” this sign with the help of a protein on their surface called PD-1.

Blocking PD-1 makes the “don’t attack me” sign invisible to immune cells, so they attack regardless. However, anti-PD-1 treatments work only if the immune system is already trying to attack a cancer, hence the advantage of combining them with a cancer vaccine to provoke that attack.

Moderna hasn’t told us yet. The company has announced only that the results of the phase III trial “demonstrate statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements” in survival times.

The trial involved 1137 people who, after surgery to remove melanomas, were randomly assigned to get both the vaccine and pembrolizumab, or just pembrolizumab. What we do know is that in an earlier trial involving 157 people with melanoma over five years, the combination of the vaccine and pembrolizumab cut the risk of recurrence by 50 per cent and the risk of spread to other parts of the body by 60 per cent, compared with pembrolizumab alone.

Free newsletter

Analysts speaking to the Financial Times say it could be approved next year. But because it is an individualised treatment, scaling up production will be much more complex than with a standard vaccine.

It also isn’t clear yet what the pricing will be – even with the help of mRNA technology, it won’t be cheap. A January report by Reuters suggested it would cost around $200,000 per treatment. No wonder Moderna’s share price is soaring.

The hope is it will work for many cancers, but we will have to wait on more phase III trial results to be sure. That said, several other earlier-stage mRNA cancer vaccine trials have produced promising results. In fact, a study last year estimated that on the basis of these results, their potential health benefits could be worth around $75 billion a year in the US alone.

A revolutionary cancer treatment is now being applied to a wide range of autoimmune disorders. Columnist Michael Le Page finds it is proving to be even more effective than expected

Not like intismeran autogene. Some sources will tell you there are three approved vaccines for treating cancer: Provenge, BCG and T-VEC.

But Provenge is a treatment that involves removing immune cells from a person’s body, exposing them to a prostate cancer protein, then replacing them. BCG is the tuberculosis vaccine, which just happens to help treat some bladder cancers for reasons we still don’t understand. And T-VEC is a live herpes simplex virus engineered to kill cancer cells.

So only one of the three is a conventional vaccine, and its anti-cancer action is completely incidental.

These vaccines prevent infections by viruses that can cause cancers, rather than targeting cancers directly, which is an even better approach. The HPV vaccine has proved incredibly effective at preventing cervical cancer, for instance.

“Are these viruses going to keep expanding in ticks? Are we going to see more and more cases of human infections? These are questions that a lot of my colleagues and I are wondering about,” says Joseph Fauver at the University of Nebraska Medical Center.

Why Lyme disease and other tick-borne conditions are on the rise

Heartland virus was first reported in 2012 and Bourbon virus in 2015 after they were discovered in people who had become severely unwell or died after being bitten by ticks. Since then, they have been found to be transmitted by lone star ticks (Amblyomma americanum), named for the white, vaguely star-shaped spot on the female’s back.

Advertisement

Historically, lone star ticks were only found in south-eastern states of the US, but they have been pushing further north and west due to factors like climate change and reforestation of previously cleared areas.

Heartland virus or Bourbon virus, or both, have been found in lone star ticks in Missouri, Kansas, Illinois, Alabama, Georgia, New York, Pennsylvania and Virginia. Free newsletter

The team analysed more than 7000 lone star ticks collected by the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services from multiple locations across the state between 2022 and 2026. Both viruses were detected in ticks from Sarpy county, and Heartland virus was found in ticks from Richardson county. These are in the south-east of Nebraska, suggesting lone star ticks migrated from neighbouring Missouri and Kansas.

However, there is a “very real possibility” that human infections have occurred and gone undiagnosed, says Fauver. This is because the symptoms can be mistaken for those of other tick-borne illnesses or non-tick-related viruses, he says. Common symptoms include fever, fatigue, headache, loss of appetite, muscle or joint aches and nausea.

The most recent death, reported last October, was that of a 32-year-old Connecticut woman who had been exposed to ticks on a recent hiking trip. Bourbon virus is named after Bourbon county, Kansas, where the first known case of a human infection occurred in a man who noticed a tick on his shoulder after working outdoors on his property in 2014. “I think it’s a reasonable deduction that as lone star ticks expand their range, more and more people are at risk of getting exposed to Heartland virus and Bourbon virus,” says Fauver.

Mice overcame a Lyme disease infection after being given an antibiotic that is often used for pneumonia, and its effect on their gut microbiomes was negligible

Lone star ticks feed on animals like white-tailed deer and raccoons that have been found to have antibodies to Heartland virus and Bourbon virus, suggesting the viruses may continuously cycle between the ticks and these animals, says Fauver. “But there’s still a lot we don’t know.”

Lone star tick bites are also known for causing alpha-gal syndrome, which makes people allergic to red meat, and ehrlichiosis, characterised by fever, aches and headache. Lyme disease, which has similar symptoms, is caused by the black-legged tick (Ixodes scapularis). Ehrlichiosis and Lyme disease can be treated with antibiotics, whereas there are no antivirals or other treatments available for Heartland virus and Bourbon virus.

Advertisement

Free newsletter

The team did link depression to reduced grey matter volume or cortical surface area in the frontal cortex, the anterior cingulate and the insula. It is unclear why depression seems to affect these areas specifically. One possibility may be that areas like the insula have a high degree of neuroplasticity, which may make them more vulnerable to the stress of depression, says Bijsterbosch.

Bijsterbosch stresses that her team measured depression at only a single time point, while the 2015 researchers tracked the condition across multiple episodes. Many factors can be involved, including inflammation and sticky protein plaques and tangles in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s disease, he says.

If future research robustly links brain shrinkage to depression, transcranial magnetic stimulation – using magnetic fields to stimulate specific areas of the brain – has been linked to modest increases in volume, so it could be explored as a treatment, says Bijsterbosch.

“We hope that getting a clearer picture of the brain basis of depression will inform future work to understand individual differences and ultimately guide improvements in personalised treatment,” she says.

The melting of the Greenland ice sheet is causing more extreme heat in Europe, contributing to the major heatwaves experienced there so far this year.

The surge of cold meltwater into the North Atlantic is altering ocean temperatures and shifting the jet stream to favour heatwaves in western Europe and the Mediterranean, a study undergoing peer review has found. This newly discovered “atmospheric bridge” played a major role in the unprecedented heatwaves this summer, according to Marilena Oltmanns at the UK’s National Oceanography Centre, who is one of the study’s authors.

Advertisement

Drought and heat push Europe’s power grid to breaking point

“Europe heats up faster. This is because of the jet stream shift,” she says. “In future years… it will be even more extreme. In the future we will think this [year’s heatwave] was not a heatwave; this was nice.”

The steady rise in global temperature has increased heatwaves. But it’s still debated whether changes in prevailing weather patterns are also contributing.

In the past 30 years, high-pressure ridges – large areas of elevated air pressure that look like a ridge or upside-down U on weather maps – have been forming more frequently over Europe, the study finds, leading to sunny skies and extreme heat. These ridges are caused by waviness in the jet stream, the band of strong winds that circles the northern hemisphere. When the more or less straight-flowing jet stream meanders northward around western Europe, it allows warm air from the central Atlantic and Sahara desert to pour into the ridge that’s been created.

Years with extensive high-pressure ridges over Europe have resulted in heatwaves like the one that killed 70,000 people in 2003.

Free newsletter

The researchers say the formation of the ridges can be traced back to Greenland through a cascade of climate events. In the summer before years of extensive ridging, an average of 81 billion tonnes more meltwater rushes off the ice sheet, they found. The cold meltwater lowers sea surface temperatures as it spreads through the North Atlantic in the autumn and winter. Its freshness inhibits mixing with saltier, warmer deep layers, further cooling the surface.

These pulses of meltwater cooling come on top of the “cold blob,” a long-term decline in ocean temperatures in the North Atlantic that some scientists blame on the weakening of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) system of currents. Together, they create a sharp temperature front between the cold waters and the warmer surface waters further south in the Atlantic.

As warm air masses rise to the south of the front and cold masses descend to the north of it, they begin to swirl and generate cyclones. This makes the jet stream wavier. It tends to meander southward of these cyclones, then back northward over western Europe, creating the persistent, high-pressure ridges and heatwaves there.

The critical current could remain stable beyond 5°C of warming, but only if the warming happens very slowly

Most worryingly, climate models don’t fully capture this process, according to Oltmanns.

“This is a big problem,” she says. “It’s going to be even more intense in terms of heatwaves and droughts, in particular in the Mediterranean region, so the weather extremes are likely underestimated.”

A study in July found that the jet stream has shifted southward in the Atlantic in recent decades, similar to the pattern shown in the study. But it concluded that this was due to natural fluctuations in the climate and would eventually reverse.

Meltwater from Greenland could be forcing the jet stream to meander, according to John Methven at the University of Reading, UK, who was one of the authors of the July study. But the weakening of the AMOC or changes in atmospheric circulation over the North Atlantic could also be causing this shift.

“That’s the weak link as far as I’m concerned, the link between the cold blob and whatever’s melting in Greenland is not established, and there might be other things going on,” he says.

If North Atlantic cooling continues to affect the jet stream, it could cause not just heatwaves but also other extreme weather, according to Oltmanns. The research linked it to an unprecedented derecho, a stream of thunderstorms and strong winds, in the Mediterranean in 2022. Winds reached more than 60 metres per second, and fist-sized hail killed 12 people.

“We [will] have more droughts at some locations, flooding events at others, and the variability on top of this increases,” she says.

How long could we possibly live? A new estimate is mind-boggling

New Scientist August 21, 2026

A few years ago, I wrote a memorable and quite controversial story about Jeanne Calment, who was then – and remains now – the official holder of the world longevity record. She was born in 1875 and died in 1997, aged 122 years and 164 days. At least that’s the official version of events. According to some doubters, the woman who died as Jeanne Calment was actually her daughter Yvonne, who fraudulently assumed her mother’s identity when Jeanne died in 1934. Yvonne was 23 years Jeanne’s junior. Still a good innings, but not a record-breaking one.

The matter remains unresolved, and so, for now, Calment remains one of the most important data points in biogerontology. When we ask, “how long can a person live?”, the answer is “at least 122 years and 164 days” – assuming Jeanne Calment really did live that long.

Whether a person could live longer has long troubled scientists. It’s an important question in biogerontology because, if we want to achieve life extension, we need to know what we’re aiming for. But it’s surprisingly hard to answer. Calment is an outlier: nobody else has reached 120, which is one reason for the suspicion. The second-longest-lived person was Kane Tanaka, who racked up 119 years and 107 days, and the oldest person today has just turned 117. Aside from a few mavericks, however, everyone agrees that there is a natural limit.

Advertisement

But where is it? There are two main ways of tackling this question. One is by studying demographic data on verified supercentenarians. One such frequently cited analysis produced an estimate of roughly 115, but did not rule out somebody living to 125. Another concluded that Calment’s record is likely to be broken fairly soon.

Another approach is by computer modelling. One such model analysed short-term fluctuations in red and white blood cell counts in adults aged 85 and over, which the researchers converted into a measure of their resilience to terminal age-related disease. At some point, resilience breaks down completely, marking the point of no return. The researchers concluded that this varies from person to person, usually kicking in at about 120. But even for the most resilient individuals there is a hard upper limit of 150.

There’s a big difference between 125 and 150, and we’ll get onto this. But one thing these studies don’t take into account is future advances in medicine. In the 1920s, scientists believed that it was impossible to live past 105, according to biogerontologist Richard Faragher at the University of Brighton, UK. But over the following century, medical breakthroughs steadily added years to people’s life expectancies, helping (along with better nutrition and sanitation) to nudge the longevity record upwards.

What happens if that trend continues? To find out, a team at the Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology and the Artificial Intelligence Research Institute, both in Moscow, Russia, ran a thought experiment. Imagine, they said, that we manage to cure all the theoretically curable causes of ageing. The only unfixable one is damage to the DNA in our cells, which accumulates remorselessly as we age. In that scenario, the upper limit of a human life soars to 194 years.

I’ll stick my neck out and say it ain’t going to happen in my lifetime, and also point out that the causes of ageing are not yet fully understood. Even so, it suggests there’s quite a lot of room for improvement.

But back to the real world. Why do upper age estimates vary so much? Re-enter Jeanne Calment. When I was reporting that story, I spoke to a longevity researcher called Saul Newman, then at the Australian National University in Canberra. He had just published a paper showing that a small number of errors or fraudulent entries in paper records such as birth certificates can significantly distort longevity data. He told me he suspected the Calments’ alleged identity fraud was just the tip of the iceberg.

Newman, now at the University of Oxford, has just published a book, Morbid: Debunking modern longevity science, revealing the shocking extent of those errors and frauds. In Greece, for example, around 70 per cent of centenarians were found to be dead, kept alive on paper so their relatives could keep on drawing their pensions. Even higher levels of pension fraud were discovered in Japan. People have historically inflated their age for many other reasons, to join (or dodge) military service, get married or get a job. Clerical errors are rife too, especially from the time when today’s centenarians and supercentenarians were born.

Free newsletter

These errors inevitably feed into estimates of the upper limit of human longevity. If the demographic data used as an input is riddled with inflated ages, the output is probably also inflated. Garbage in, garbage out. People used in modelling studies are also tagged with an age, which could well be wrong. When the journal Nature asked Newman where this leaves the debate about a maximum human lifespan, he answered: “in an absolute shambles.”

When I was researching the Calment story, I also came across a 2011 paper that found that, across the whole world, 98 per cent of claims of lifespans over 115 could not be verified. The same paper also found that, in countries with rigorous birth records going back more than 150 years, not one person has been proved to have lived past 115. That, I think, is the best estimate we’ve got. Five score years and fifteen. I’m halfway there.

Much of the country is in for a “spring-like” reprieve after a wild weekend of damaging winds, power outages, heavy rain and snow.

Most parts can expect calmer and drier conditions today, with warmer-than-average temperatures forecast for parts of the South Island.

MetService meteorologist Sophie Huntington told the Herald that settled conditions would return for most, with the exception of the West Coast of the South Island, where rain and showers would hang about.

“It’s looking very spring-like you could say, which is nice with some warmer temperatures forecast as well, that’ll be a good change for us all,” she said.

Emergency services and maintenance crews were run off their feet yesterday as severe gusts caused havoc around central New Zealand, cutting power to thousands of homes.

Huntington said a ridge of high pressure would bring more settled conditions, although “pretty strong westerlies” could linger in Fiordland, Southland and around Dunedin.

She picked the sheltered eastern regions of Bay of Plenty, Gisborne and Hawke’s Bay as some of the places to be today.

Auckland was also in for a “pretty nice day”, Huntington said, with mainly fine conditions and a high of 16C.

She suggested Wellington could even be “the spot to be”, with fine conditions forecast and a high of 14C.

Christchurch is forecast to reach 18C, while nearby Ashburton could hit 19C, compared with an average of about 13C to 14C at this time of year, Huntington said.

Further south, Dunedin could see “a bit of cloud in the morning and in the late evening, otherwise mainly fine”, she said.

A high of 17C was forecast, which Huntington added was “quite nice” compared with an average of about 12C at this time of year.

Some wetter weather is expected to return to Southland and Dunedin tomorrow, before “another front comes across” the South Island on Wednesday and begins slowly pushing north.

Huntington said a high-pressure system would initially sit to the west of New Zealand before moving east.

“As that moves off, we’ve got a low-pressure system developing in the Tasman out to the west coast, west of Fiordland, so that’s what’ll be bringing those unsettled conditions again.”

By Thursday, the change could take a wintry turn, with snow potentially lowering to 400 metres in Canterbury and Otago.

Huntington said the low-pressure system would “drag up the cooler air from the Southern Ocean”, bringing the potential for snow across central and southern parts of the South Island.

“The ski fields will be happy with a bit of a late snow for them.”

The North Island should hold on to the settled weather for longer, with Auckland potentially seeing a few showers on Wednesday but the main change was not expected until Friday afternoon.

Huntington said the changeable conditions were typical of spring, when weather systems were less slow-moving.

“It’s good, and then a bit of rain, and then good.”

‘An absolute waste’: Police officer remains in ICU after being hit by vehicle

New Zealand Herald August 23, 2026

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett speaks to media. A policeman was critically injured after being struck by a fleeing vehicle when laying road spikes near Palmerston North early on Saturday morning.

By RNZ Morning Report

A senior police officer says he stood at the bedside of a critically injured colleague in despair over the weekend listening to machines whirring and thought “what an absolute waste”.

In the early hours of Saturday morning, the young policeman was allegedly hit by a fleeing driver in Palmerston North as he lay road spikes.

It was not the only incident in the region, with another man critically injured after being hit by a car in Feilding just two hours earlier. The driver fled the scene, police said.

The injured policeman was flown to Wellington Hospital, where he remains in intensive care.

On Monday, Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett told Morning Report the officer was in a stable condition but remained on a ventilator.

“It’s a time [to] wait and see as time heals him.”

Bennett said the two people in the vehicle that allegedly hit the officer are 14 and 15 years old.

They are facing a “raft of charges”, including theft of a vehicle and reckless driving causing injury – an offence that carried “significant and serious penalty”, he said.

Bennett said despair came to mind when he thought about the injured men.

“I stood at the bedside of our officer yesterday with his family and as we watched and listened to the machines whirring and uh, you stand there and think ‘what an absolute waste’. This could be avoided. The behaviour of the drivers in both incidents is not acceptable and this is a tragic event for the two families involved but also for all of Manawatū.”

Bennett said police staff were “getting on with business and acting professional”.

However, there was a sadness hanging over the officer’s team and wider team “as we wait for some positive news about how he’s doing and whether his recovery is going to be successful”.

Bennett said the man hit by a vehicle in Fielding also remained in the intensive care unit (ICU) on a ventilator.

He said two separate inquiries were being carried out and would determine if the incidents were connected.

At this stage, it didn’t appear they were – with one incident involving a fleeing driver and the other involving “anti-social illegal road users”.

Bennett told Morning Report the region had a history of serious and violent interactions with boy racers and it wasn’t a challenge police would back away from.

He said police were keen to hear from anyone with information about the driver who fled the Feilding scene.

Which foods have become less affordable for New Zealanders?

New Zealand Herald August 23, 2026

Price rises have slowed, but the cost of food continues to increase. Photo / 123rf

By Susan Edmunds of RNZ

Some essential food items have increased in price twice as fast as wages have risen over the past 10 years.

New Zealand has gone through a long period of food-price inflation, particularly propelled through the post-Covid period, but while price rises have slowed, the cost of food continues to increase.

Stats NZ data shows many types of food have hit record prices, including fresh fish at $49.62 a kilogram on average, lamb chops at $24.23 a kilogram, fried chicken at $17.12 for five pieces, fish and chips at $11.07, a fresh or toasted sandwich at $6.86, a meat pie at $6.61, two litres of milk at $5.12 and white sliced bread at $2.38 a loaf.

Others were at a level that was already a record, including long-grain white rice and canned pineapples.

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod said food prices would tend to track up over time, so the fact they were at record prices was not entirely unexpected.

He said what was notable was how much some staples had increased compared to the rate at which wages had risen.

Over the past decade, wages had risen by about 52%. By contrast, butter prices were up 157% since 2016, eggs were up 125%, a loaf of sliced white bread was up 120%, fish and chips were up 78%, mild cheese was up 75%, beef mince was up 71%, lamb chops were up 72%, potatoes were up 73%, cabbage 75% and two litres of milk 57%.

“We have seen some pretty widespread increases in the cost of household essentials. That includes things like butter, milk and meat products, but those are also the same products that New Zealand produces,” Ranchhod said.

“We’ve seen strong demands, both onshore and offshore, and that’s one of the big factors that’s pushed up prices, not just here, but globally.”

He said shoppers had probably not seen the full extent of the increases yet.

“We think there are a couple of factors that are going to keep prices for a lot of those essential food items high for a while. In part, we’re still seeing strong demand for protein globally, so that is adding to the prices for a lot of dairy products, but also meat products.

“We’re also seeing some big increases in production costs, especially in the food sector, where we’ve had big increases in fuel costs that are adding to on-farm operating costs. It’s also rippling through transportation and packaging, and other parts of the supply chain.

“All of that eventually lands on the supermarket shelf. One thing we’re conscious of, though, is that the full impact of that won’t have been seen yet.

“We’ve still got pretty high fuel costs. While we did see some increases in prices in the June quarter, there’s probably still some signs that there is going to be further increases.”

Ranchhod said there were positive aspects to that, though.

“These prices are certainly adding to the pressure on a lot of households’ finances when they go through the checkout, but the other side of that is, if you are in these more rurally focused areas like Canterbury, Southland and Otago, those strong export earnings in the commodity sector are flowing through to higher incomes, spending and confidence more generally.

“Not just on the farm, but the regions more generally are seeing some pretty positive economic conditions.”

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said people should not expect food prices to fall.

“The rate of growth might slow, but it will still be growing. Slowing inflation rates don’t actually mean anything to somebody who’s paying still a ton of money for the basics.”

He said many foods increasing quickly or at record prices were the basics of life for many New Zealand homes.

“It’s making a sandwich, cooking a roast or whatever.”

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen said protein demand had pushed up prices across the world in recent times and that was showing through in the list of rapidly rising food costs.

“Demand from the US is still strong because of GLP-1s. You’re seeing that move across the world, where people are not eating nearly as much, but when they eat, it needs to be quite nutrient dense and protein dense, so they’ve got enough to rebuild muscles.

“That’s definitely keeping prices elevated and that comes through to New Zealand, because we’re in that global marketplace.”

He said even the price of plastic had increased, since oil prices rose, which would add to things like the cost of a bottle of milk.

An increase in vegetable oils had been felt in the international market and, while it was not showing up in supermarket prices in New Zealand yet, commercial producers of things like fish and chips might be feeling it.

Olsen said it was worth noting that food-price inflation had slowed to 1.9% in the latest update, which was the lowest since 2024.

Taranaki dairy farm lifts milk solids by 30,000kg with herd home

New Zealand Herald August 23, 2026

Since putting a herd home in, the farm's milk solids production has increased by 30,000 kilograms by allowing an extra month of milking. Photo / RNZ, Gianina Schwanecke

By Gianina Schwanecke of RNZ

Bordering the national park that surrounds Taranaki Maunga, Crystal Rivers Farm takes its name from the many waterways which radiate out along its paddocks.

It’s nestled in a part of the region prone to high rainfall, where big storms can bring more than 200mm of rain in just a few days.

As such, it’s a hard place to winter dairy cows without running the risk of runoff and paddock sediment making its way into the waterways.

It’s why Paul Kuriger made the decision to spend a little more money when buying into the 194ha farm and investing in a herd home.

A herd home is a type of covered shelter used on dairy farms where cows have the freedom to move around and rest in a large open area with a roof.

“We didn’t want to contribute sediment throughout the winter and runoff into the streams,” Kuriger said.

“We’re always looking at winter grazing, and winter grazing bills were always going up and up and up.

“So we thought at the time, we would take an extra $500,000 out, spend that capital on putting a barn on so it could have greater uses than just grazing off-farm, as it could be used for calving as well.”

The 4400sq m barn can fit up to 400 cows.

But with only 360 cows in the herd, that’s about 12sq m per cow on a soft bed of wood chips and cows enjoying about 11kg of dry matter – hay or silage – each day.

Kuriger told RNZ’s Country Life it had been a great investment and allowed him to increase milk production by an extra 30,000kg of milk solids each year.

That’s because it allows the farm to keep milking for an extra month, with the cows taking shelter and being fed from inside the barn between May and October.

The cows average 11 to 15 full days in the barn over winter, but Kuriger prefers they have the freedom to come and go from the shelter to the paddock.

“I’ve had the cows in here when we’ve had eight inches [20cm] of snow on the ground outside, and I’ve even opened the gate at the other end of the barn, and all I’ve had is a cheeky heifer walk out and then spin around and run back inside.”

Kuriger said it had also helped reduce feed wastage as it prevents hay and silage being pushed into the ground and not utilised.

It means they can save the pasture for when it’s needed.

“With the utilisation of the feed in the barn, you’re finding in some senses you’re actually feeding less because the cows do so well.

“They’re contented. They’re quite happy in here. They’re not battling the elements.”

He said the animal welfare benefits had been huge.

In the spring, two weeks before calving starts, he’ll move the cows to the shed where they stay until they’ve calved – offering the best possible start for the newborns.

“[We have] very few calf losses because it’s just they’re born into a temperature of probably 24, 25 degrees when all the cows are in the barn.

“So those calves are up and running straight away.”

The wood chip base provides another benefit – it’s eventually taken out and spread across up to a third of the paddocks on farm as a fertiliser.

All of the farm’s waterways have been fully fenced off, and about 36ha are covered in native bush, which also helps to ensure the waters of the farm run crystal clear.

At an existing wetland, Kuriger pointed out how the stock setbacks had been pushed further out, allowing him to infill the border with more native plants.

He told Country Life these helped to filter water from big rainfall events before it made its way into the stream.

“Before it actually enters the inner half stream, which is right beside it, the water [will] turn a bit brown, and then it will clear itself up a day or so after the event, and the sediment will sit in the pond in the base of the pond, and it keeps returning clear water back to the stream.

“With the bush filtering it, it’s a great advantage, and it’s a great asset for the farm.”

Kuriger said it was about regenerating the bush “as best as possible” and looking after it for future generations.

Former principal accused of not passing on complaints to school’s board

New Zealand Herald August 23, 2026

Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Waitaha in Christchurch. Photo / Google Maps

By Sam Sherwood of RNZ

A former principal at a Christchurch school has been accused of not passing on complaints to the school’s board.

RNZ earlier revealed that the former principal of Māori immersion school Te Kura Kaupapa Māori o Waitaha, Melissa Waitoa-Paki, resigned in June amid allegations she failed to protect the safety of children and manage conflicts of interest.

Last week RNZ obtained a series of documents from the school under the Official Information Act (OIA).

The documents include a March email from a police officer to the chair of the board and lawyers representing the school regarding a formal complaint about a staff member’s behaviour. RNZ understands the staff member is Waitoa-Paki.

The email is heavily redacted; however, RNZ understands the email also includes allegations that Waitoa-Paki did not pass on complaints to the board of the school.

Last Tuesday, RNZ asked the Ministry of Education if it was advised of allegations.

In response, the ministry’s director of education for Canterbury and Chatham Islands Coralanne Child said they “weren’t notified that the former principal failed to pass complaints on to the school board”.

“If the board was working through an employment process with the former principal, that was a matter for the board, not the ministry, as we are not the employer.”

Child said the ministry later became aware of concerns that Waitoa-Paki had not passed on complaints to the board “through its work supporting the school, rather than through any formal reporting process”.

Asked what concerns the ministry had about the claims, Child said school boards played “an important governance role and need access to relevant information to make informed decisions and meet their obligations”.

“The school has a new presiding member, and the board is being supported by the ministry and external advisers. Our focus is on helping the school to provide a safe and effective learning environment for students and staff and minimising disruption to teaching and learning.

“Employment matters involving a principal are the responsibility of the board as the employer. We expect concerns or complaints to be raised through the school’s processes so they can be considered and responded to by the appropriate people.”

Child earlier confirmed that the ministry gave “careful consideration to a statutory intervention”.

“However, through its ongoing engagement with the board, the ministry considered that the board had put appropriate supports and governance arrangements were in place, including support provided by the ministry and external advisers.”

RNZ has attempted to approach Waitoa-Paki for comment.

In response to questions from RNZ, the board said it was not able to comment about “whether or not any allegations were ever made relating to the conduct of any specific current or former employee, in order to protect their privacy”.

“The current Ohu Whakahaere of Te Kura Whakapūmau was elected in November 2025 and remains committed to its governance responsibilities, supporting the educational achievement, wellbeing, and holistic development of tamariki in accordance with the values and aspirations of the kura community.

“Te Ohu Whakahaere continues to work collaboratively with relevant agencies, including the Ministry of Education and the Teaching Council and remains committed to fostering a safe, nurturing, and high-quality learning environment where Tamariki can thrive as learners, confident in their identity, language, and culture.”

National is considering other mechanisms to help tourism destinations facing cost pressures after ruling out a widely supported accommodation levy.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast he had no regrets about ruling out the bed tax after raising it as a possibility just two weeks ago.

“I want to reassure the regions and the mayors, we understand the issues around infrastructure pressures and the cost of tourism. We will think about other mechanisms to be able to deal with that.”

Asked if that meant using Act’s bed tax alternative - a “local tourism dividend” giving councils $1 for every guest night in their area - Luxon said there were “lots of other ways to do it” and he did not want to predetermine the outcome.

The party was taking advice and looking at how other countries approached the issue.

Luxon and finance spokesperson Nicola Willis announced yesterday their party’s promise of “no new taxes” would be upheld in any coalition agreement - which meant scrapping both the bed tax and bank tax.

Luxon’s U-turn on a bank tax and bed tax came at his official Botany electorate campaign launch, where the party pledged it would allow no new taxes if re-elected.

Two weeks ago the Prime Minister had raised the possibility of an accommodation levy, which had been previously discussed with Auckland Council, while noting Willis had also spoken about possible changes to bank tax settings.

But he said yesterday that a bed tax would hurt “everyday Kiwis who are just going away for a weekend in Auckland or Queenstown”, while Willis said the party had been unable to find a way to raise taxes on banks without increasing costs to Kiwis.

Luxon also said it was highly unlikely National would enforce next year’s legislated fuel excise tax increase.

The bed tax backdown has disappointed mayors in tourism hotspots, who had previously pushed for a nationwide accommodation levy to help fund public infrastructure in key tourist destinations.

The levy was backed by mayors from Auckland, Rotorua, Ruapehu, Wellington, Marlborough, Christchurch, Timaru and Queenstown, among others.

Meanwhile Nicola Willis is refusing to rule out increases to ACC levies if the party returns to Government after the election.

Speaking to Herald NOW’s Ryan Bridge Today, Willis said she would not rule out such an increase but National strived to keep the levy low, pointing out there was a formula to assess the increase in the levy.

The party has pledged to add no new taxes if re-elected, but Willis said they had been “very open” that the petrol levy would be increased in future.

Congestion charges were also not ruled out but would be up to councils.

Labour finance spokeswoman Barbara Edmonds said her party would keep the ACC levy cap if the books were still manageable.

Edmonds told Ryan Bridge TODAY that Labour would also not go ahead with the 12c petrol price increase planned by the Government for January next year.

RNZ-Reid Research poll: Opportunity in kingmaker position, Luxon and Hipkins approval slumps

New Zealand Herald August 23, 2026

The Opportunity Party, led by Quilae Wong, has tipped over the 5% threshold for the first time in this poll. Photo / Sylvie Whinray

By Giles Dexter of RNZ

The Opportunity Party is in the kingmaker position, with the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll showing neither the coalition nor the opposition would have the numbers to form a government without its help.

The party has tipped over the 5% threshold for the first time in this poll, changing the seats in the House calculations, and the make-up of Parliament altogether.

If replicated on polling day, the right bloc would have 59 seats and the left bloc 55 – both needing Opportunity’s 6 to get over the line.

Labour has been unable to capitalise on National’s recent woes, and has taken a dent as the government parties ramp up the tax attacks.

The party is still in the lead, on 32.2%.

However, its drop of 1.8 points since July has put Labour on its lowest result in this series since the election.

National has emerged from its aborted coup with a slight bump in support, but remains stuck in the twenties, now on 29.1%, up 0.4 points.

The other parties are all riding steady.

Winston Peters’ widely-condemned comments towards a Green MP and Paul Henry’s star power have not shifted the dial for New Zealand First or Act.

New Zealand First is on 11.9%, up 0.4 points, the Green Party is on 10.2%, down 0.1 points, and Act is on 7.7%, also down 0.1 points.

Te Pāti Māori is on 3%, up 0.7 points, but the party has confirmed it wants people’s candidate votes, not their party votes.

Opportunity is on 5.3%, up 0.6 points from the previous poll, and above the 5% mark for the first time.

Undecided or non-voters made up 4.6% of respondents.

If the results were replicated at the election, Labour would have 39 seats, the Greens 12, and Te Pāti Māori 4, making 55 seats for the left bloc in total.

National would have 35 seats, New Zealand First 15, and Act 9, or 59 in total for the right bloc.

Opportunity’s 6 seats would mean it holds the balance of power, deciding whether the left or right bloc forms the next government.

Those projections are based on party vote and assume no overhang seats. If National won more than 35 electorates, or if Te Pāti Māori picked up more than 4, it would create an overhang.

Both Christopher Luxon and Chris Hipkins have taken hits to their personal popularity, with the Prime Minister recording his lowest approval rating to date.

In the preferred prime minister stakes, Hipkins remained in the lead on 21.3%, but that is a 2.6 point drop on the previous poll.

Luxon is on 19.9%, a drop of 0.1 points.

Peters is in third on 11.1%, another who has taken a hit, down 2.1 points.

Chlöe Swarbrick is fourth on 7.4%, and David Seymour rounds out the top five on 6.2%.

Approval ratings for both Luxon and Hipkins have slumped, with Hipkins in the negatives for the first time.

Luxon continues his downward trend, with 30.3% of respondents saying he is performing well as prime minister, compared to 53.2% who think he is performing poorly. This gives him a net approval rating of -22.9.

Hipkins, meanwhile, is on -3.8, his first negative result since leading the party, with 34.4% saying he is performing well, and 38.2% saying he is performing poorly.

That malaise is reflected in voters’ opinions on how the country is tracking.

The results showed 30.8% of respondents thought the country was heading in the right direction, while 51.8% said it was going in the wrong direction.

This produced a net score of -21, down from -11.8 in the previous poll in July.

Another 15.2% said it was neither, while 2.2% did not know.

This poll of 1000 people was conducted by Reid Research, using quota sampling and weighting to ensure representative cross section by age, gender and geography. The poll was conducted through online interviews between 14-21 August 2026 and has a maximum margin of error of +/- 3.1% at a 95% confidence level.

Central Otago gold mine supporters say backing was always there

New Zealand Herald August 23, 2026

Supporters of Central Otago’s proposed Bendigo-Ophir gold mine say local backing is becoming louder – but not necessarily larger.

Santana Minerals has pointed to a growing number of vineyards, suppliers and contractors publicly associating themselves with the project after years of heated debate.

The company recently backed a supporters’ initiative selling Santana caps to raise money for the Cromwell and Tarras volunteer fire brigades, while mine supporter stickers have appeared on vehicles around the country.

Supporters spoken to by the Herald said backing for the project had been present for some time.

Shane Norton, who runs Radio Central and is reopening the Omakau pub after it had been closed for nearly three years, said he believed the mine represented an opportunity for the region.

“It’s the future of Central, really.”

Norton, who previously lived in the Thames Valley, pointed to the history of gold mining in Waihi and Otago and the development it had helped fund.

“I think the gold from Santana and the other mines that will happen will help Central Lakes, which we desperately need if you look at all the infrastructure issues around Queenstown.”

Through his work, Norton said he spoke to people from a broad cross-section of the community and had not personally encountered anyone opposed to the mine.

“A lot of people sort of like to keep to themselves because they open up and they get shot down, but if you look at the Santana Mine supporters page, nearly 15,000 people now, people have had enough of the naysayers and they just want to get on with it.”

He did not believe the increased visibility of supporters necessarily represented people changing their minds.

“I think the support’s always been there.”

Elevate Central business group chairman Dewald de Beer said he was seeing more businesses publicly support Bendigo-Ophir, but similarly believed much of the underlying support was not new.

He said he had not often encountered business leaders opposed to the project and believed some had previously been reluctant to express their views.

“I think it’s probably just the fact that people can now actually – they don’t feel victimised almost by showing support.”

De Beer said businesses saw economic growth as important for creating opportunities in the region, but that did not mean development should occur regardless of its consequences.

He said Santana still needed to listen closely to those living near the proposed mine, who would potentially experience its effects most directly.

His own support was conditional on the project being developed responsibly.

“We need to hold them accountable to that; that’s the thing.”

Cromwell contractor Ruben Connelly said the potential benefits were more immediate.

Connelly’s company Precise Fencing employs six people and has previously carried out work connected with exploration at the site.

“It’s a big one for us, that long-term steady flow of work for our company.

“It’s not guaranteed work, but it gives you that security that you can look to grow and invest in your business knowing that you’ve got that potential workflow coming in.”

Connelly said Precise Fencing had been involved at the site since 2018, initially working with Matakanui Gold before Santana took over the project.

The company’s work included removing and replacing boundary fences to allow drill rigs through, and it had completed more recent projects for Santana.

However, Connelly said Precise Fencing would still have to compete for any future work.

He said he had supported the project from early on: “I just feel that the positives far outweigh the negatives.”

Custom Fabricators Ltd owner Scott Canham was similarly enthusiastic about the potential flow-on effects for Cromwell businesses.

Canham expected an “absolute abundance” of opportunity in Cromwell if the mine went ahead, and a benefit for businesses beyond those directly supplying the project.

“It’s going to get a lot more foot traffic coming through.”

Contact our South Island newsroom

Like Connelly, Canham already had links to Santana. He said he had been involved with the company since it arrived in Cromwell, initially through another company that worked alongside it.

“I want to be a part of the growth, I want to be a part of the support, I want to be a part of everything moving forward – and them moving forward will help my business move forward as well.”

Canham said he had always supported the project and, like Norton, said he had not personally encountered local opposition.

“I haven’t met someone so far that has had a bad thing to say about Santana.”

He has also been distributing “Dig Baby Dig” supporter stickers, including around New Zealand and overseas.

Santana has described the increasing willingness of businesses to publicly associate themselves with Bendigo-Ophir as an important change in the debate surrounding the project.

Chief executive Damian Spring said more businesses were becoming comfortable publicly expressing views they had previously held privately.

The company says the proposed mine would produce about 120,000 ounces of gold annually at peak production over a 14-year mine life and create hundreds of jobs.

The project remains one of the highest-profile proposals being considered under the Government’s Fast-track Approvals process.

Santana plans four open pits, including one up to 1km long, 800m wide and 200m deep, alongside a processing plant and tailings storage facility.

An economic impact report commissioned for the fast-track process projected the mine would contribute about $360 million to GDP annually on average and employ about 350 workers directly.

The proposal has faced significant opposition over its potential effects on water, landscapes, the environment and nearby communities.

Sustainable Tarras, which has been campaigning against the project, has previously warned that the mine could create long-term risks for Central Otago despite its potential short-term employment benefits.

The group’s Stop Central Otago Gold Mine campaign has raised more than $53,000 from more than 400 donors, with donations surging following the death of prominent mine opponent Sir Sam Neill in July.

Santana has spent about $17.7m pursuing Fast-track approval for the project.

Processing of its application was due to resume on August 17 after a pause, with the company expected to provide final workshopped consent conditions to the expert panel later this month.

Sustainable Tarras did not respond when approached for comment.

Ben Tomsett is a multimedia journalist based in Dunedin. He Joined the Herald in 2023.

Two people have been taken to hospital with injuries after a family harm incident in South Auckland.

Emergency services were called to Papatoetoe around 10pm yesterday.

Two people in a moderate condition were transported to Middlemore Hospital, Hato Hone St John said.

A police spokesperson said one person was taken into custody and inquiries are ongoing after the family harm-related incident.

Hours earlier, four people were arrested after a brawl in the central city, which left one person seriously injured.

Emergency services went to the intersection of Queen St and Wellesley St East about 6.40pm after reports of a group of people fighting.

Two of those involved were injured and taken to Auckland City Hospital, while the other two were taken into police custody.

Charges are pending, police said.

By RNZ

The Auckland and Queenstown Lakes District mayors are both disappointed with National’s announcement on Sunday ruling out a bed tax, with Auckland mayor Wayne Brown hitting out at National “walking away” from its commitment to the Auckland Regional Deal.

On Sunday, the National Party ruled out the idea of a bed tax, promising that there will be “no new taxes” if it’s re-elected.

It comes a fortnight after Prime Minister Christopher Luxon spoke publicly about the possibility of three new taxes under National – a bed tax, a bank tax and a fuel excise increase.

Brown said that Sunday’s announcement raised serious questions about the Government’s commitment to the regional deal.

“The deal is meaningless if the Government cannot honour even a relatively modest commitment to explore an agreed proposal.

“Ruling out the bed-night levy without offering any meaningful alternative to support the industry is deeply disappointing.”

The regional deal, signed in April this year, included the Government committing to considering the accommodation levy policy in 2027.

Brown said the bed-night levy was a user charge, not a general tax.

“Taxes are unavoidable, you can avoid this by just not staying in a hotel.

“It would result in no additional rates or taxes on Aucklanders, while enabling Auckland to attract more events, support local businesses and grow the regional economy.”

Brown said the regional deal was an agreement between the Crown and the council.

“It should not be something one party can simply disregard.”

Brown said he looked forward to discussing the issue with ministers responsible for the regional deal – Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop and Local Government Minister Simon Watts – at the next quarterly review of progress in September.

Queenstown Lakes District mayor John Glover told RNZ it appeared to be a “complete u-turn” on policy, after the Government agreed to consider the accommodation levy for visitors in both the already-signed Auckland Regional Deal, and the deal for his region, which was almost signed a week and a half ago – but had to be rescheduled due to National’s crisis talks on the same day.

“It feels like policy-making in a state of panic. I appreciate there’s a campaign message about no new taxes, but the Government particularly says it doesn’t want to tax Kiwis for a weekend away.

“Well, what we just need to be clear about is that Kiwis are already being heavily taxed across the country, because every ratepayer that’s in a tourism town is already having to pay for the cost of tourism, so to say they don’t want Kiwis to be taxed is a bit of a rabbit hole to be going down,” he said.

Glover said not being able to implement a bed tax would be “significant” for his region, where infrastructure was strained by the number of visitors each year – doubling the population during peaks.

“Things like car parks or waste collection, you know we’ve got some really expensive roads that go to the likes of the Routeburn Track or Skippers Canyon, there might be five ratepayers live down there, but tens of thousands of visitors go there every year.

“You would think we deserve governments that support tourism in this country, and they need to give council the tools to do that.”

Rotorua mayor Tania Tapsell said she was “surprised” with the announcement, considering that the bed tax formed part of the Auckland Regional Deal.

“We’re definitely sad to hear that because there’s been so much hard work behind the scenes.

“Councils without any alternative will have to continue to use ratepayer funds to invest in tourism offering.”

Tapsell said she and other mayors had also been pushing hard for a fairer distribution of the International Visitors’ Levy back to the regions, like Rotorua.

Atlético’s Alvarez booed by own fans in home draw

Ferran Torres came off the bench to score a late double ⁠on his debut as Paris Saint-Germain rallied from two goals down to draw ⁠2-2 with ⁠hosts Rennes in their Ligue 1 season opener on Sunday. Sebastian Szymanski and Esteban Lepaul gave ⁠the home side a 2-0 lead at half-time but PSG piled on the pressure in ⁠the second period and were rewarded with a point.

Rennes led ​inside nine minutes as ‌Szymanski’s shot went ‌in off the post to provide the perfect start ‌to the season for the hosts. Przemyslaw Frankowski found space ‌on the right wing and his low cross into the box was turned into the ​net by Lepaul.

The Terror: Devil in Silver review – this psychiatric hospital horror is scary on so many levels

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 21:05:42 GMT

Expect gory set pieces and jump scares galore in the return of the supernatural anthology series, with Dan Stevens among the many poor souls terrorised by an evil spirit haunting their ward

Things that go bump in the night? Bad. Things that go bump in the night in a dilapidated psychiatric hospital? Infinitely worse. That, basically, is the premise of Devil in Silver, the latest volume of anthology series The Terror, which began in 2018 with a supernaturally charged tale of a polar expedition to find out what happened to Sir John Franklin’s voyage. Crikey, it does not end well. The next was set during the second world war and was about shapeshifters from Japanese folklore terrorising a Japanese-American community in southern California. A hiatus followed, but now The Terror is back with a double dose of horror: a malevolent spirit moving in and out of the bodies of the patients of New Hyde psychiatric hospital, and the more tangible but no less frightening diabolism of the US mental healthcare system.

Pepper (Dan Stevens, still of Downton Abbey fame despite his many varied roles since) is in New Hyde because the three policemen who arrested him after they caught a few punches he was aiming at his girlfriend’s controlling ex threw him in there rather than completing the paperwork the station would have required. There he meets the lost and suffering souls who have ended up in what amounts, due to underfunding and understaffing, to a holding pen rather than a rehabilitative or care facility. Dorry (Judith Light) is the longest-serving resident – put there decades ago by her husband because of her endless crying fits, though her later memories reveal a greater darkness. Kofi (Chinaza Uche) – or Coffee, as he is called by the rest of his companions until it is too late – was a structural engineer in Ghana but now depends on medication to keep himself steady. Loochie (played by non-binary actor b) ended up in the system after a violent incident with a sibling, but at least one member of staff believes her charge is able to cope in the real world and, as the hospital’s evil spirit gathers strength and wrath, gets the chance to prove it.

Pepper comes to understand from his fellow patients – and some of the staff, none of whom is an out-and-out villain and many of whom are almost as trapped by circumstance as their patients are – that the key to whatever is haunting the hospital lies behind a locked silver door. Beyond it is a single occupancy room that contains the comatose body of a man who has, in one state or other, been at New Hyde even longer than Dorry. Arnold received a transorbital lobotomy after killing a doctor a year after he was sent to the ward.

Jump scares, gory set pieces, flickering lights, endless corridors and an extremely unsettling turn from John Benjamin Hickey as the hospital’s founder Dr Walter take care of the required horror element of the show in a fairly rote manner. We have seen it all before, often more punchily done (though the ending does redeem the lack of innovation before). Ditto the idea of monster as metaphor for both mental instability and the systems that are supposedly in place to steady it.

You could say that Devil in Silver does not shy away from the latter point. If you were feeling less generous, you could say it labours it. Dorry embodies the effects of misogyny and patriarchalism on the medical profession. The question of racial prejudice permeates the fates of all the patients of colour. None of the patients/prisoners comes from the kind of money that might have protected them – or at least got them placed in a facility that does not require the services of a nurse like Scotch Tape (Hampton Fluker), so called because of his talents for keeping mod cons running with little more than a roll of the stuff and a prayer.

It works best as a straightforward drama. The real-life horrors of old-fashioned treatments (as we see when Dorry’s backstory starts to play out), and of contemporary care standards for the forgotten and marginalised masses, are bleaker than any imaginary beastie prowling through psyches and corridors. The ease with which Pepper gets trapped in the system – drugged on arrival, he sleeps through discharge time – the guilt he wrestles with over his abandonment of his young son and how an essentially good man can find a way to redemption: these are all more terrifying and more mesmerising to contemplate than any bogeyman under the bed.

The Terror: Devil in Silver aired on Sky Atlantic and is on Now

Reform says it would put foreign-born UK citizens lower on social housing list

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 21:00:42 GMT

UK-born married couples under 35 with children would get priority under proposals to be outlined by Farage’s party

British citizens who were born abroad would be made to wait longer for social housing under proposals to be announced by Reform UK on Monday.

Nigel Farage’s party will announce the policy at a press conference in London. Under the policy, people born in the UK and young married couples with children would be given priority for social housing.

The party has previously said it would ban foreign nationals from social housing, meaning the new policy specifically prioritises Britons born in the UK over those born overseas.

Richard Tice, the party’s deputy leader, said in a statement: “There are now 1.3 million people waiting for social housing in Britain. The vast majority of them do not have jobs. In terms of the social houses we have, less than half of households are in work and over half a million social homes are currently occupied by foreign nationals.

“Meanwhile, young British men and women, who are working hard, can’t afford to move out of their family home, and when they do often find themself sharing a house with strangers, with no realistic prospect of forming a family or getting on.

“It is time for us to prioritise young British workers, and that is what our policy is about.”

The party said some foreign-born Britons would be exempted from the new rules, including those born while their British parents were temporarily overseas. Officials said, however, the new rules would require legislation to avoid breaking existing laws.

Under the terms of a previous announcement by Farage, foreign nationals would be barred from social housing, with those already in homes given three months to find private accommodation or face deportation.

The new policy would give priority access to British-born people in employment and married couples under 35 with children.

The party said veterans would also be given preferential treatment – though soldiers, veterans and their families are already given priority under existing government policy.

Experts have said that prioritising people based on nationality, age and family status could punish some of the most vulnerable in society.

Sarah Elliott, the chief executive of the charity Shelter, said: “Designed to stoke division, these plans will only serve to disrupt the lives of thousands of families, tear communities apart, and put even more people at risk of homelessness.

“Putting nationality and employment ahead of housing need, and moving away from a system designed to prioritise people who are homeless or at urgent risk of homelessness, could leave even more families trapped in awful temporary accommodation for years on end. Not to mention putting those escaping domestic abuse and violence at serious risk of harm.”

A Labour spokesperson said: “Illegal migrants, asylum seekers and migrants on student or work visas are not eligible for social housing. This policy would go after long-term UK residents that have contributed to our country but are not British citizens, including NHS staff.”

Reform has also said it would build 50,000 socially affordable homes a year, a significant uplift on the 18,000 the government has promised to build on average each year for a decade.

Labour’s plans are being financed by a £39bn affordable housing scheme, 60% of which is due to be allocated to social homes, which are the most heavily subsidised.

Reform said its plans would be funded, with no extra borrowing or taxation required to pay for the additional homes. It did not give further details on where the money would come from.

Families release pictures of police officers killed in A66 crash in which five others died

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 19:55:13 GMT

Emotional tributes paid to PCs Matthew Blades and Tom Clough whose vehicle was in a head-on collision with car travelling wrong way

Cleveland police have published photographs of PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough who died when a car travelling the wrong way on the A66 crashed head-on into their police vehicle.

Two 17-year-old boys were among the seven people who were killed in the incident on Teesside.

Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and 23-year-olds Michael Robert Cahill and Jacob Matusiak died when their Volkswagen Passat, believed to be using cloned plates, collided with a marked armed response vehicle early on Saturday near Middlesbrough.

Blades, 37, and Clough, 38, of Cleveland police, who were also killed in the collision, had been driving in the correct direction. Tributes have been paid to the officers, with their chief constable, Victoria Fuller, describing them as “brave officers protecting our communities”.

Clough’s family described him as “our hero with a fantastic sense of humour” and someone who “jumped into action whenever needed, and [was] willing to help anyone for any reason”.

In a statement issued via Cleveland police, the family said Clough had “proudly fought for his country to make the world a better place. Always on public duty throughout his short life.

“We as a family and Tom’s partner would like to express our sincere gratitude for the overwhelming support and condolences from friends, colleagues and the wider community.”

Blades’ wife said the pain of losing him is “beyond words” and the family’s lives “will never be the same”.

In a statement issued through the force, she said: “No words will ever feel like the right words to honour our Matt – my beloved husband, my best friend, and the most devoted father to our two young boys.

“He was an adored son and brother, a perfect son-in-law, and the most fun uncle. He was loved beyond words by all his family and friends, and his loss has left a space that can never be filled.

“He gave his life in the line of duty, protecting and serving others with courage, dedication and selflessness.

“The pain of losing him is beyond words, and our lives will never be the same. Neither will the love he gave us ever fade.

“Our children will grow up knowing what an incredible father he was and will always be, and I will carry his love, his memory and everything we shared with me always.

“He may have left this world committed to the duty he believed in, but his greatest legacy will always be the love he gave to his family.”

Blades’ wife, who has not been named, also expressed “deepest gratitude and heartfelt thanks” to the police and emergency services and concluded: “Forever loved. Forever missed. Forever our superhero.”

A local football club, Seaton Carew FC, said Blades had recently joined as coach and was preparing for the season with the new under-sevens Seahawks team. “He was looking forward to being part of the team and, most importantly, to coaching his own son, who is going to be playing for the Seahawks this season,” the club said on social media.

“Matty and his oldest son are much-loved members of our club and our U10 Lions football family. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Matty’s wife, his two boys, and all of his family and friends at this incredibly difficult and heartbreaking time.”

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has opened an investigation into the circumstances leading to the crash at 3.39am in South Bank after a mandatory referral from Cleveland police.

On Sunday the IOPC said initial inquiries showed the Passat had been pursued by police for just under seven minutes before it turned on to the A66 against the flow of traffic.

At that point the pursuit was aborted, the IOPC said. “Approximately 10 seconds later, the Passat collided with another police vehicle which was not involved in the pursuit but in the area to assist in a search for the Passat believed to be using cloned plates that had activated an ANPR camera.”

The IOPC director of engagement, Derrick Campbell, said: “Our thoughts continue to be with the family and friends and all those affected by yesterday’s collision. We recognise the devastating impact the incident has had on those in the force, and the wider policing community, and offer our condolences.”

On Sunday, Anna Turley, the Home Office minister and local Redcar MP, said it was “devastating” to think about the grief of the families of everyone who lost their lives on Saturday morning. The whole community was “reeling”, she said.

“All of us in the community here are sending our heartfelt thoughts and sympathies to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives so tragically.”

“I do want to place on record my tribute to PC Blades and PC Clough. The bravery that we see from our police officers every day, every night is incredible. No one should not come home to their families at the end of their shift.”

She also said it was important to thank the emergency service workers who had attended the scene during “a really horrific incident”.

Security camera footage from local houses appeared to show the police pursuit moments before the fatal crash on the A66.

Andy Burnham said he was “devastated” to hear two police officers had lost their lives on duty, as well as five members of the public. The prime minister said: “My thoughts are with the families and loved ones of everyone involved, and with everyone at Cleveland police. Thank you to the emergency services responding in incredibly difficult circumstances. I would urge people to avoid speculation at this time.”

Fuller said she and her deputy had on Saturday visited the families of the two officers to offer condolences and support.

“This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland,” she said. “This loss is being felt across our communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies. These were brave officers, protecting our communities and serving our residents, who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift.”

Lauren Somerville, the chair of Cleveland police federation, said the grief among officers was “all-consuming, overwhelming”. She said: “Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland police family are feeling.”

The Cleveland police and crime commissioner, Matt Storey, described the force as a “really tight-knit family” and said the deaths “will have a big impact on them”.

The young men in the car were named by Cleveland police on Sunday afternoon. The force said family liaison officers were working with the families.

This article was amended on 23 August 2026. An earlier version gave the age of Cole Robert Worthy as 16, based on initial information provided by Cleveland police. After publication, Cleveland police corrected this to 17.
