‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade war

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 19:32:59 GMT

PM Mark Carney says ‘we got attacked’ as tariffs come into force on items from hockey sticks to tongue depressors

The lesson from Canada’s collapsed trade talks with the US: negotiation may be futile

Donald Trump has hit back at Canada after a breakdown in negotiations plunged the two countries into a trade war.

In his first public comments since negotiations collapsed on Friday in Washington, the US president wrote on social media: “Canada wants the benefits of being a State, without being one!!!”

“They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” he added. “No more!!!”

His comments came after the US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.6bn) worth of Canadian goods, while Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, has vowed to match them “dollar for dollar”.

The US tariffs came into force on Saturday, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Trade experts have predicted that the tariffs could result in some job losses, but the biggest impact is expected to be political, triggering fresh tension between the neighbours.

Both sides blamed the other for the breakdown in talks on Friday. Carney told Canadian journalists that the country was “at war” over trade with the US, after Trump “miscalculated” by escalating his tariff attack.

“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” the Canadian prime minister told reporters in Ottawa. “We cannot accept what they’ve offered and we will not give what they’ve asked.”

Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, has said the US was compelled to act after a year of retaliatory measures by Canada. He told Fox & Friends Weekend: “We’ve said enough and so we’ve taken countermeasures. Our interest is in protecting American workers and protecting American supply chains.”

Dan Kelly, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, estimated that 40% of small Canadian exporters will be directly hit by the US tariffs, and that nearly one-third expect their revenues will drop by 50% or more as a result.

The escalation was also met with anger by Democrat lawmakers and governors from US states that border Canada including Minnesota, New York and Washington.

New York governor Kathy Hochul posted on X: “Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That’s Trump’s economic policy in a nutshell.”

Minnesota senator Amy Klobuchar, said the new tariffs meant “higher costs for small businesses, farmers, and all Minnesota families.”

She wrote on X: “Canada is Minnesota’s #1 trading partner. Minnesotans are paying for Trump’s chaos.”

Carney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England, was elected as Canada’s prime minister last year after campaigning to lead a fightback against Trump, who has suggested he wants to make Canada a 51st state with “economic force”.

Carney’s “dollar for dollar” tariffs are expected to take effect from 8 September, with new levies on steel, dairy, appliances and electronics. The escalation has also called into question the future of the North American trade pact between the US, Canada and Mexico, known as USMCA.

The pact, which was signed by Trump during his first term, governs about $2tn annually in goods and services between the three countries. Trump refused to renew the USMCA this summer after Canada and Mexico formally requested for it to be renewed for another 16 years.

When asked how the US-Canadian collapse in trade talks would affect the USMCA, Carney said it was “certainly not good news”.

Increasingly aggressive rhetoric and trade policy from the Trump administration has damaged US-Canadian relations, with tourism also suffering – there was a 21% drop in Canadians entering New York state in 2025 and 3mn fewer visits compared with the previous year.

Furthermore, a petition to expel the US ambassador to Canada, Pete Hoekstra, from the country has gathered around 248,000 signatures since late July, according to the Associated Press.

This year a poll by Globe and Mail newspaper found that only 9% of Canadians agreed that the US was a “trustworthy ally”, and that 51% of those polled had cancelled American trips in reaction to comments by Trump.

Frustrated Lewis Hamilton claims Ferrari strategy cost him F1 Dutch GP podium

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 19:15:57 GMT

Briton says team too slow to pit Charles Leclerc

‘It’s something that we need to discuss offline’

Lewis Hamilton has told his Ferrari team that they must up their game if he is to remain in the Formula One world championship fight after the British driver was angry with strategy calls at the Dutch Grand Prix, comparing them unfavourably with the decisive way his former team ­Mercedes had acted.

The race was won by McLaren’s Lando Norris from Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and George Russell. Hamilton was fourth but believed he might have had a shot of a podium had Ferrari moved Charles Leclerc aside sooner when Hamilton, on a different tyre strategy, was quicker than his teammate.

“Great way of wasting time, good job,” was his unusually blunt admonishment when Ferrari finally pitted Leclerc. In contrast Russell had been given swift instruction to move over for Antonelli in the final stages of the race when the Italian was similarly on much faster rubber.

“I think what’s clear is I’m looking ahead and seeing Mercedes execute like that,” Hamilton said. “They’ve got the car, they’re fighting for the championship, in the lead and they did it straight away. Here, I’m sitting back, losing seconds. It’s something that we need to discuss offline.”

Despite Antonelli finishing second he has extended his lead over Russell and Hamilton, who are now 59 points behind the Italian, and Hamilton was adamant that his team could not afford to drop any points.

“Today was definitely frustrating for me,” he added. “I’m here to win and I really believe that this team can win. To win championships you have to pick up every point. The last few races have been difficult with penalties and today I lost several seconds behind Charles which I think ultimately would have made the difference at the end.

“My goal is to try and lead this team to the championship and we’ve got some work to do for sure.”

Mercedes’ quick intervention with team orders was questioned, not least by Russell at the time given he is also vying for the title, but the British driver accepted it had been the right call.

“We’ve always said as a team, when we’re on different strategies, we’re never going to fight, that’s always just been our sort of rules,” he said. “Kimi was ahead of me anyway, so he deserved to finish ahead. When you’re in the race, you want to fight for every single position but with the pace, with a new tyre, he would have overtaken anyway. So it’s the right decision.”

Toto Wolff maintained it had been a straightforward on the pit wall. “Team orders are always harsh from one drivers’ perspective but it is what we always discussed,” the Mercedes team principal said. “We are not losing time with each other if there are competitors breathing down our neck. Today wasn’t a difficult call.”

Megasquirt: Fully Loaded review – how to combat existential angst? A comedy rave at an ungodly hour

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 19:00:40 GMT

Underbelly, Cowgate, EdinburghAshley Blair and Drew Reilly send up gen Z anomie with hardcore ditties about awkward dinners, megachurches and centaur boyfriends

‘How to feel whole in an empty world?” There are many possible answers to that question, and Megasquirt’s late-night comedy rave workshops a good few of them. But there’s probably no better way than putting on a banging show and performing it to an adoring audience of your peers – and that’s what Brooklyn imports Ashley Blair and Drew Reilly do in Fully Loaded, turning the Underbelly at some ungodly hour into a pulsating queer(ish) celebration-cum-sendup of gen Z anomie. “Everything is empty / Life is a hole / You gotta fill it up,” they sing, looking like refugees from Warhol’s Factory but delivering comedy that couldn’t be more now.

The show starts as if we’re being seconded to a generational revolution, but it’s soon clear that this pair, both Second City alumni, are threats to nothing but your funny bone. Their premise is that life is void of meaning. We flash back to meet them as alienated schoolkids and one terrific sketch, a silly symphony of clinking cutlery and ASMR tuts and sighs, imagines two parents at dinner, struggling to repress their mutual loathing. If this is our hosts’ generational inheritance, why not look for a better way of being? Like a romance with an inverted Centaur Boyfriend, the title of one daft ditty, or like forming a megachurch to start replenishing the spiritual chasm.

There are first-base satirical sideswipes in that latter sketch, against Christian homophobia and the church’s obsession with sin. But Blair and Reilly’s satire is usually garnished with, or eclipsed by, silliness, as they belt out their songs about being bullied in bakeries, and “gooning in the DJ booth”. So much the funnier that these songs are tightly constructed, lyrically adroit and delivered with hardcore hyperpop attack.

Only occasionally does the standard slip: the skit about straight female writers fetishising gay male sex is on point, but soon devolves into so-so smut. That’s not going to fill anyone’s gaping hole – but there’s lots here that will, as Megasquirt minister to our existential angst with whip-smart, high-energy comedy.

Liverpool’s Szoboszlai spot on with late, late leveller to salvage point at Newcastle

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 17:43:20 GMT

Before kick-off a banner was raised in the Gallowgate End inscribed with a quotation from the late Kevin Keegan. “I want people to dream about their football,” it read. “We should all be dreamers at heart.”

Out on the pitch it swiftly became apparent that both Matthias Jaissle, Keegan’s latest successor in the Newcastle dugout, and Liverpool’s new manager Andoni Iraola are on individual missions to create forms of organised chaos capable of subjecting the best opponents to torrid nightmares.

Despite a few, ultimately forlorn, attempts to introduce semblances of control on the parts of the visiting playmaker Florian Wirtz and Newcastle’s elegant central midfielder Lewis Miley, this was sheer, unadulterated, mutual mayhem of the sort to make Iraola’s more purist Anfield predecessor Arne Slot wince.

Along the way to a draw secured, perhaps slightly fortuitously, by Dominik Szoboszlai’s 99th-minute penalty for Liverpool, the returning former Newcastle striker Alexander Isak left minimal imprint on a match that had been supposed to be all about him. Instead Isak was upstaged by Jaissle’s forward William Osula.

No sooner had the heartfelt tributes to Keegan, a player and manager adored by both clubs, been completed it very quickly became apparent that Jérémy Jacquet and Virgil van Dijk had no answers to Osula as the young Dane turned and accelerated towards goal following Ryan Gravenberch’s inexplicable surrender of possession.

The stage was set for this most unpredictable of strikers to spot Anthony Elanga, then in the process of leaving Milos Kerkez for dust down the right, slide a pass in the winger’s direction and watch as, a steadying touch later, Elanga’s shot flashed beyond Alisson’s reach.

Only five minutes had passed, Jaissle’s tenure as Newcastle’s manager was off to perfect start and already Iraola looked distinctly stressed.

His defence did not convince, with Kerkez finding few answers to Elanga. Like Jaissle, Iraola is a high priest of pressing but Liverpool’s best hope here seemed to be to retain possession, impose their technical superiority and out-pass Newcastle.

Significantly their best moments coincided largely with those albeit sporadic occasions when Wirtz –who would be withdrawn midway through the second half – managed to get on the ball and began unnerving a Newcastle side supposedly in the throes of a dramatic transition.

It is only three weeks since Jaissle succeeded Eddie Howe but the former Al-Ahli manager has certainly succeeded in not merely re-energising a mentally jaded team but sharpening a swarm pressing game that had become more than a little half hearted and untidy. “The manager is top,” said Elanga. “Playing for him is fun.”

Given that Jaissle has inherited a team shorn of last season’s luminaries – Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães – this achievement was all the more impressive. The 38-year-old German trusted 18-year-old Sean Steur, recently arrived from Ajax, alongside Miley in the key holding roles in his 4-2-3-1 system and for long periods they held their own.

Behind them, Malick Thiaw and Sven Botman excelled in central defence while Amar Dedic shone at right-back following his £30m move from Benfica.

There are ways to leave a football club but the route Isak chose – mounting a one-man strike before forcing a record £125m move to Liverpool last summer – ensured he was greeted by chants of “rat, rat, rat,” as he alighted from the visiting team bus.

If Isak seemed quite unconcerned – he grinned broadly in the face of some further sustained hostility before kick-off – the Sweden striker added to Iraola’s problems by miscuing his sole chance of an alarmingly anonymous afternoon. Instead it was a forward facing an uncertain future at Anfield who kept Liverpool in it. When Jaissle’s midfield inexplicably stood off him Cody Gakpo’s first time shot from outside the area defied Lukas Hornicek.

With Osula now limping, on came Joe Willock for Newcastle leaving the impressive Yoane Wissa – arguably man of the match – to shift from the No 10 to No 9 role. Willock is reportedly close to joining Besiktas but delighted in immediately offering a reminder of his enduring worth on Tyneside.

When Wissa, rather wonderfully, dodged three supposed markers his ensuing pass to Willock was superbly calibrated and the latter returned the compliment by curling a shot past Alisson and in off a post. Tellingly, Willock was mobbed by every outfield teammate with Nick Woltemade and his fellow home substitutes racing the length of the pitch to congratulate him.

The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s foreign policy: work in progress

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 17:30:38 GMT

The prime minister has focused on domestic affairs since coming to office. But at a time of global disruption, he will need to define Britain’s place in the world

A run of volatility in domestic British politics in recent years has tracked a period of global turbulence, and yet foreign policy over the same period has been an area of relative stability. What little is known about Andy Burnham’s approach to international relations expresses more continuity with Sir Keir Starmer’s administration than deviation. In negotiations with the EU, the red lines that prohibit membership of the single market or customs union still stand. Where Washington is concerned, Mr Burnham shows no interest in performances of bonhomie with Donald Trump, but his predecessor had already swapped that approach for a cooler pragmatic tone by the end of his tenure.

The new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has opened a good dialogue with Marco Rubio, his US counterpart. Such is the density of integration in defence and security matters that incoming UK prime ministers, regardless of ideology, have little choice but to invest time in cultivating a bond with whoever sits in the White House. Anyone hoping for a spectacular transatlantic rupture and sudden clinch with Brussels will be disappointed.

Some patterns of consistency date back beyond the recent transfer of power within the Labour party to the previous Conservative administrations. Support for Ukraine in the face of Russian aggression was one of the few creditable positions taken by Boris Johnson, and that line has held through four transfers of power in Downing Street.

The process of rebuilding functional relations with European neighbours predated the 2024 general election. Rishi Sunak negotiated the Windsor framework for Northern Ireland. He also ditched a bill that threatened chaos for businesses by vaporising retained EU laws without a timetable to replace them.

The business secretary who executed that U-turn in defiance of the Tories’ fanatical Eurosceptic tendency was Kemi Badenoch. It was not a choice she highlighted in her subsequent bid to become Conservative leader. By then the party, relieved of the burden of governing responsibility, was in no mood to consider the merits of pragmatism where Europe was concerned.

Having withdrawn to an ideological comfort zone, the Tories still cannot pretend that Brexit has been a success. Sir Keir became gradually more confident in attributing Britain’s economic woes to the terms of departure from the EU. But the shift was largely rhetorical because he was locked into a manifesto commitment that precluded a substantial change of direction. Mr Burnham has accepted the same constraint as a condition of his hand-me-down electoral mandate.

Having accepted the parameters of Boris Johnson’s hard Brexit and acknowledged Britain’s security dependency on Washington, the prime minister doesn’t have much room to innovate in foreign policy. Nor has he shown much interest, focusing instead on domestic issues that are much more salient to voters than geopolitics.

That is a rational priority for a new leader hoping to win over sceptical voters. But with no sign of global volatility abating, an international crisis will force itself on to Mr Burnham’s agenda soon enough. Global strife, especially when it whips up economic headwinds, quickly manifests itself as pressure to act in domestic politics. The prime minister has proved adept at connecting with an audience close to home. That advantage will be degraded if he cannot also connect his domestic agenda to a coherent strategy for engagement with the wider world.

The Guardian view on the new Hungary: de-Orbánising at pace

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 17:29:38 GMT

As a Brussels deadline looms with over €10bn at stake, Péter Magyar’s first three months have been transformative in addressing a corrupt legacy

Some elections are more important than others. Since taking office in May, Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, has embarked upon the country’s most far-reaching and dramatic programme of transformation since the fall of communism in 1989. Mr Magyar’s predecessor, Viktor Orbán, established a soft autocracy which thrived on corruption and, over 16 years, exerted its grip on most areas of Hungarian life, from religion to culture and the media. It is being dismantled at extraordinary pace.

Last week, a newly appointed president took office following the sacking of Tamás Sulyok, accused by Mr Magyar of having rubber-stamped the erosion of the rule of law in the country. In stark contrast, András Baka is a former president of Hungary’s supreme court, a role he was removed from by the Orbán regime in an action judged unlawful by the European court of human rights.

On Hungary’s national day last Thursday, news bulletins returned to the main state television channel, having been shut down for six weeks. In July, viewers had encountered a blank screen along with the message: “Public media should not lie. We are sorry for doing it for so long.” Ending naked bias on state TV was one of Mr Magyar’s key pledges, in a campaign that saw him buck an electoral system weighted in favour of Mr Orbán and win a landslide.

The tempo has been equally relentless when it comes to attacking networks of corruption and clientelism built up over a decade and a half. Well over €100bn in public funds, including billions of euros of EU money, is believed to have been siphoned off during the Orbán years. Investigators have been empowered to go after it via a new National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Mr Magyar has also confirmed Hungarian participation in the European public prosecutor’s office, enabling the EU to better protect itself from financial crime in the country.

It will take time for Hungary to feel like a normal pluralist European democracy again. For now, Mr Magyar is functioning as a one-man political whirlwind, heading what amounts to a national unity government elected by voters across the political spectrum. Concerns have been raised over constitutional manoeuvring to ensure many MPs in Mr Orbán’s Fidesz party cannot stand again, and Mr Baka has warned against appearing to take revenge on the former prime minister’s supporters. But a root-and-branch approach to de-Orbánising Hungary was what was needed, and continues to be rewarded by record levels of popularity in polls.

The next major threshold is likely to be crossed in the autumn. Brussels has given Hungary’s new government until the end of this month to demonstrate that enough is being done on corruption to warrant the release of over €10bn in frozen funds. If, as seems likely, the vast majority of the funds are disbursed, it will seal the ongoing rapprochement between the EU and its former rogue member state.

In May, Mr Magyar relocated the prime minister’s office away from a controversially cordoned-off former Carmelite monastery used by Mr Orbán, opening the building up to the public. “I was not elected simply to change the government, but to change the regime,” he had told interviewers soon after taking power. Three months on, the symbolism is being supplemented by a peaceful political revolution.

The lesson from Canada’s collapsed trade talks with the US: negotiation may be futile

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 17:24:46 GMT

Breakdown shows Washington now prioritises its own interests over any semblance of shared economic ground

‘No more!!!’: Trump lashes out after US-Canada talks devolve into trade war

The calamitous collapse of trade negotiations between Canada and the United States is a warning to nations worldwide that pursuing any kind of dialogue with the current US administration is doomed at the outset, according to observers who say this recent episode indicates seeking a fair deal is futile.

Andrea Lawlor, an associate professor of political science at McMaster University in Ontario, said: “No matter the closeness of the historical relationship, the American administration has signalled that it now prioritises its interests above those of some sort of global economic coordination or harmony.

“It feels like these talks ‘failed’. However, I’m not sure there was really a success to be had.”

The two countries are now in a deepening trade war after weeks of urgent talks fell apart shortly before the 12am EST (5am BST) deadline on Saturday, when the US imposed 50% tariffs on $20bn (£14.6bn) worth of Canadian goods.

A defiant Mark Carney said on Saturday that he had rejected the deal because of last-minute US demands that would have undermined Canada’s sovereignty. The Canadian prime minister said: “They asked too much and they offered too little … you’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked.” He promised to match US tariffs “dollar for dollar”.

Donald Trump had initially announced the tariffs on 20 July, saying Canada had unfairly discriminated against American businesses.

The core example provided by the White House is Canada’s bans on the sale of US alcohol in eight of its 10 provinces and all three territories. The removal of US spirits, wine and beer from shelves came into effect after Trump’s first round of tariffs, slapped on Canada in early 2025.

The breakdown of talks came as a shock. Trump had claimed on Tuesday that a three-day extension would be applied to the tariff deadline, as an agreement was all but signed. On Wednesday, he told reporters that a “very fair deal for both” sides had been ironed out.

But as details of the agreement began to leak to Canadian media, there was growing alarm that Carney and his negotiators were conceding too much in exchange for lower tariffs on steel, aluminium and cars.

The premier of Manitoba, Wab Kinew, and his Nova Scotia counterpart, Tim Houston, confirmed this week that Carney had asked the provinces to return US alcohol to shelves in order to seal the trade deal.

Kinew told reporters he believed Canada “should fight” Trump instead, and that “you can’t get a good deal with a bad person”. He encouraged Canadians to avoid buying US alcohol, even if the premiers agreed to put it back on shelves.

Fears of capitulating to Trump also emerged in a high-level briefing call held by Canada’s ambassador to the US, Mark Wiseman, with the Canada-US trade council.

Sources told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that Canada’s former chief trade negotiator Steve Verheul had warned in the call that concessions now would only lead to further demands from the Americans down the road.

JD Vance the US vice-president, was also recorded at a private event, seemingly mocking Carney for standing down on “a lot of issues” as the trade negotiations were occurring.

Instead, Carney took the dramatic decision to bring his negotiators home to Ottawa, with no further meetings planned – and to launch a barrage of criticism against Trump, who in turn accused Canada of wanting “the benefits of being a state, without being one”.

Goods covered by the swingeing US import taxes include everything from anoraks to Christmas ornaments.

Lawlor suggested Canada would soon be back at the negotiating table, given the likely economic impact of the tariffs. But she said any negotiation with the Trump administration should be understood as prone to disintegrate at a moment’s notice.

She said: “We are very much in a state of constant flux, where even where negotiations do produce agreements, these should not be viewed as eternally binding.”

To end homelessness, look to the root causes

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 16:57:32 GMT

Readers respond to Andy Burnham’s pledge to get all rough sleepers off the streets by Christmas

As a vulnerable teenage girl carrying my life in a rucksack, I have been the person Andy Burnham describes people walking past in his article (I won’t abandon anyone to sleep rough on our streets. That’s my £442m promise, 19 August). That experience taught me that homelessness is far more complex than rough sleeping alone, and that ending it takes more than getting people off the streets.

Getting everyone in for Christmas is an important ambition. But lasting success means preventing people from reaching crisis point and giving those who do the practical support and opportunities they need. I was lucky. Public sector work gave me structure, stability, and someone willing to believe in my potential.

Housing must sit alongside education, healthcare, employment and social mobility, giving people not just somewhere to live, but a genuine route to stability, independence and opportunity.

This is why charities and initiatives such as Homewards, with a collaborative, prevention-first approach, are so important. Solving homelessness takes joined-up support, earlier intervention, and a belief that people need routes into housing, work, health, safety and belonging. As Mr Burnham rightly says, homelessness is a problem to solve, not step around. Prevention must be at the heart of that solution. Dr Sabrina Cohen-HattonChief fire officer, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service

The prime minister’s pledge to end rough sleeping is admirable, and he’s right about the importance of catching people “long before they hit the pavement”. But to succeed, the he must confront the Home Office’s role in creating homelessness. Last year, around 21,000 households in England needed homelessness help after eviction from Home Office accommodation.

Research by the Refugee Council and others has highlighted how delayed documentation, inadequate support and too little time to find accommodation leave refugees facing homelessness and destitution within weeks of a being given leave to stay in the UK.

Current plans making refugee status more precarious, putting refugees in thousands of pounds of debt and further restricting asylum support will only worsen this. Until the Home Office stops pushing refugees on to the streets, ending rough sleeping will be out of reach. Imran HussainRefugee Council

As a psychiatrist, I have seen an increasing number of patients with severe mental health difficulties ending up homeless, and the local council concluding that it doesn’t have a duty to house them as they have made themselves “intentionally homeless” by failing to stick to the rules.

This is usually because the patient has used drugs on the premises and they are evicted from their temporary accommodation. They are then expected to demonstrate three months of abstinence while being street homeless before they can try again for accommodation – with no understanding that housing will aid their ability to get off drugs.

While I have some sympathy for the local authority’s position, we need to have a system that thinks housing first, with recognition the reducing drug use takes time and requires wraparound support from mental health and drug services.

Until that happens, I fear Andy Burnham’s new initiative will result in accommodation being found, but the patient quickly falling foul of the rules, and the local authorities washing their hands of them again. Dr Charles DixonExeter

Is this why close encounters with intelligent aliens have so far eluded us?

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 16:57:24 GMT

Readers offer their explanations for the absence of hard evidence for extraterrestrial civilisations, in response to an article by Adam Kirsch

When thinking about why we have not encountered intelligent aliens yet, as Adam Kirsch does (The long read, 11 August), it seems to me that one factor gets neglected: fossil fuels. Alien life could develop intelligence on myriad planets, but to develop advanced technology that would enable them to get off‑world, they need to go through an equivalent of the Industrial Revolution, and that needed first coal, then oil and gas.

There could be many intelligent alien races out there, but on planets without an easily accessible fossil fuel equivalent, they’d never get past a 17th-century level of development.

Even if we can eventually detect life on planets outside our solar system, we’d never know these civilisations existed, as their signature from afar would be indistinguishable from that of a planet with just plant-like life and a fire ecology.

It is entirely probable, as a result, that almost all alien races, if they exist, are living in an eternal equivalent of Game of Thrones’s Westeros, not Iain M Banks’s Culture, doomed never to be detected from afar. Ian SimmonsWestcliff-on-Sea, Essex

Adam Kirsch’s article misses one possibility: that any advanced civilisation might simply be keeping its distance. Humans have long imagined such watchers. The Kayapó people of Brazil, for example, tell of Bep Kororoti, a visitor who shared knowledge and helped their ancestors build a stable and sustainable society.

It’s easy to imagine a similar conversation among distant observers today. A younger voice might look at our atomic weapons and shake its head, predicting that we’ll finish ourselves off. An older voice might reply that humans have a habit of rebuilding, and that societies like the Kayapó show we can live with balance when we choose. Their verdict might be to wait a while, and see whether we can keep our civilisation going, before attempting contact. Given our history, who could blame them?Miland JoshiBirmingham

Given the age of the universe, estimated at 13.8bn years, it is quite possible that many forms of life and civilisations have arisen, flourished, declined and disappeared (just as humanity seems likely to). The notion that two such phenomena might occur at the same time and thus permit mutual communication would be a mind-boggling cosmic coincidence. So one response to Fermi’s question “Where is everybody?” might be “they all left before we got here” or “they haven’t arrived yet, and we’ll be gone by the time they do”. David WalkerSheffield

Maybe aliens have arrived, but were too small for us to notice? Perhaps they fell down a drain, were eaten by seagulls, or ended up in an ants’ nest?Sheila PrestonShoreham-by-Sea, West Sussex

The far right is steering the EU’s response on migration

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 16:57:13 GMT

Positions once associated with the radical right have travelled well beyond it, says Giuseppe Martinico

I agree with much of Alberto Alemanno’s analysis (How the far right is tightening its grip over the EU – from the inside, 18 August), but I wonder whether framing this primarily as the far right tightening its grip on the EU risks missing an even more troubling development.

What we are witnessing is not simply the success of the far right. It is a broader cultural shift within the European political mainstream. Migration is perhaps the clearest example. The convergence between governments as politically different as those of Denmark and Italy suggests that positions once associated with the radical right have travelled well beyond it. Parts of the centre-left and centre-right have progressively abandoned a rights-based understanding of migration. More fundamentally, migrants increasingly disappear from the European political conversation as persons – as bearers of rights whose dignity should constitute a limit to what political majorities may legitimately do.

This cultural transformation has been facilitated by an increasingly weak European Commission. The second Ursula von der Leyen commission was born under the auspices of a strong presidency, but that political authority seems to have progressively evaporated. The response to the Ceuta crisis is revealing. Neither the commission’s president, Von der Leyen, nor its European commissioner for internal affairs and migration, Magnus Brunner, has provided the kind of strong political signal that might counterbalance the competitive hardening of national positions.

The problem, therefore, may be deeper than the collapse of the traditional firewall around the far right. The firewall becomes almost irrelevant once much of the mainstream has internalised the assumptions that it was originally supposed to contain.

The real question is no longer simply whether mainstream parties cooperate with the far right, but how much of the far right’s understanding of migration, rights and belonging has already become mainstream European common sense. Giuseppe MartinicoProfessor of comparative public law, Dirpolis Institute, Sant’Anna School of Advanced Studies, Pisa, Italy

“We are aware of an incident, which is reported to have taken place in Derby last night, and are currently investigating,” read the ECB statement. “We will provide a further update when possible.”

According to reports, Carse was released without charge.

The incident comes after a spate of bad publicity off the field for England and just five days after Joe Root, the returning England captain, spoke of his desire for his players to be “really good role models, good human beings”.

England’s winter tour of Australia was rocked by various off-field incidents, including the infamous boozy week in Noosa during a mid-Ashes break and the hushed-up account of Harry Brook being punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington last November, the night before leading England out in a one-day international against New Zealand. Then this summer, Stokes and Gus Atkinson were suspended for the second Test against New Zealand after breaking the team’s newly imposed midnight curfew following the first Test win – an incident that was the catalyst for Stokes’s shock retirement from international cricket.

Stokes himself has said cricket has a drinking culture. This month, he told the For the Love of Cricket Podcast: “We are in 2026 now, where the game has gone more professional over the years, and one thing that has stayed within cricket is its relationship with alcohol – from club cricket it works its way up.”

Carse was England’s leading wicket-taker during the Ashes series but injury has kept him on the sidelines this season. He was picked in the super-sized squad for the Headingley Test against Pakistan but released to play for Durham. He is in the squad for the second Test at Lord’s.

Hull punished United defence in victory but Carrick’s attack is bigger area of concern

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 15:07:39 GMT

Manchester United again struggled against a back five as the promoted hosts exploited a set-piece weakness

Hull scored nine league goals from set plays last season, the joint-fewest in the Championship. Yet two in 21 minutes earned them a victory over Manchester United on Saturday.

It was a disastrous start to the campaign for the visitors. While Michael Carrick said before the game it would not be easy, he would not have expected victory being so straightforward for Hull. It was a match United simply had to win given the gulf in resources and expectation. Opta rated their chance of victory at 68.9% before kick-off.

United’s inability to deal with Oli McBurnie as the target man was painful to watch. Their slack defending on the set pieces from which Hull scored will also draw focus. Their attacking should be the greatest concern, though.

A glance at expected goal numbers can paint a false impression. Hull generated 1.01 expected goals to United’s 1.83, so did the visitors deserve to win? The issue is the breakdown of chances that contributed to the total. United had 21 shots, 16 of which were worth less than 0.1 expected goals.

This was a theme last season, albeit less obvious when they performed well under Carrick. United’s open-play shots were worth an average of 0.104 expected goals in 2025-26, the third worst rate among teams that finished in the top half of the Premier League. Against Hull, this figure was just 0.087.

Not until the 78th minute did a notable opportunity fall to a player they would hope to have one, as Bryan Mbeumo received a through ball from Matheus Cunha. Before that, their highest-value chances fell to Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui. The former has experience as a winger, and started in the attacking midfield trio in United’s 4-2-3-1 formation, but the duo have just 16 top-flight goals between them. They are not reliable chance converters.

Marcus Rashford is far stronger. He should take Dorgu’s berth in the long term, assuming he remains with the club. His natural attacking instincts may have aided in the creation of better chances in the first half. Regardless, it was alarming how hard United found it to fashion valuable opportunities against a club that conceded the second-most expected goals in the 2025-26 Championship.

Hull’s manager, Sergej Jakirovic, used a back five. He deployed three centre-backs on 10 occasions last season, notably in victories in the playoff semi-final second leg against Millwall and the final against Middlesbrough.

It worked against United, with the extra bodies at the back able to crowd out attackers. Opta’s shot map showed Hull conceded eight efforts in the “danger zone” – the centre of the penalty area that covers the width of the six-yard box out to the 18-yard line. Five of the eight were headers, which are harder to convert, leaving little else of note. Space in the most valuable real estate came at a premium at the MKM Stadium and United were unable to penetrate it.

This structure has caused United problems before. They have now won only one of their last six league matches against teams that started with a back three or five. Leeds won 2-1 at Old Trafford in April with a 3-4-3 formation and used the same system to draw 1-1 two weeks ago in a pre-season friendly. Milan employed the same framework when beating United 4-2 in their final warm-up game.

“We got beat, we’re hurt and it’s not a nice feeling. It doesn’t mean it’s going to change the whole direction of how we’re going as a team or as a football club,” Carrick said. As sensible a long-term approach as that may be, United’s attack needs work.

Spying device detectors may give domestic abuse victims false sense of security, study finds

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 15:00:37 GMT

Many tools fail to help victims find hidden cameras, microphones and trackers, leaving them at risk of ongoing surveillance

Commercial detectors intended to help domestic abuse victims find hidden spying devices may actually give them a false sense of security, a study has found.

The consumer detection tools claim to identify hidden cameras, microphones or trackers through methods such as signal-strength readings, infrared lens detection and scanning for wifi or Bluetooth devices.

However, researchers at University College London’s computer science department found that many detectors fail to adequately help users identify hidden surveillance devices, giving them a false sense of security.

“There’s quite a great disparity in the capabilities of the [spying] devices themselves and the tools that are available for detecting them,” said the lead author, Akhil Polamarasetty.

The researchers said that if the detectors failed to find surveillance devices it meant victims continued to be spied on in their homes unaware.

The researchers identified approximately 1,000 covert surveillance products and 500 detection tools sold in the UK through mainstream online platforms, such as Amazon, AliExpress and eBay.

Hidden surveillance devices included small cameras or microphones concealed inside everyday household items such as USB chargers, plush toys and clocks.

Often marketed as home security or pet tracking tools, the researchers and campaigners said the devices could be misused for spying and abuse.

“These devices are so small, it doesn’t actually make sense for them to be used for home security purposes,” said Polamarasetty. “[They’re] essentially designed for spying on people.”

The researchers asked 34 study participants to search for hidden surveillance devices on their own inside a simulated living room, and then to do the same again using detection tools. The latter showed only a marginal improvement: participants missed 67% of the hidden devices when searching on their own, compared with a 59% miss rate when using a detector.

During the experiment, many participants reported difficulties in interpreting a detector’s readings. Other tools gave out false positives, causing anxiety in the participants, or missed surveillance objects entirely.

“Most of the detectors on the market are not designed with the typical consumer in mind,” said Polamarasetty. “Many people do not necessarily understand the limitations of such detectors and risk misinterpreting the results.”

He said many of the detection products were not built with at-risk users in mind, often emitting loud sounds that could alert the person spying on them. “They’re absolutely not safe to be used when you’re living with the perpetrator. The devices are not discreet enough.”

The researchers made several recommendations for manufacturers of detection devices, including making user guidance clearer and communicating inconclusive readings.

However, the authors noted these recommendations alone could not prevent tech-facilitated abuse, and the only real solution was to stop the sale of hidden spy devices.

The co-author Dr Leonie Tanczer said: “Most technology is dual-use, and companies have a responsibility to think about how their products can be misused – at the design stage, rather than after the harms emerge.

She added: “A camera in things like a showerhead or a plug – I just cannot really see a legitimate reason for that without the intention to monitor someone without their consent.”

The UK domestic abuse charity Refuge said it had seen a “notable rise” in victims reporting finding hidden microphones or cameras inside their homes. Its policy manager, Bo Bottomley, said: “What is especially worrying is how accessible and affordable these devices are, allowing more perpetrators to weaponise them as a form of control.

“We urge the government to review how these products are designed, safety tested, marketed and sold, and to take swift regulatory action to mitigate the risk they pose to survivors,” Bottomley said.

Amazon declined to comment. A spokesperson from eBay said the platform “prohibits the sale of many products that are used to transmit or receive signals or for covert surveillance, and all sellers are required to comply with our policies and applicable UK law.

“After investigation, we’ve removed two of the three listings shared and we are committed to maintaining a safe and trusted marketplace for our buyers and sellers.”

A spokesperson for the Home Office said: “We will not tolerate covert filming or the harassment of victims.

“The government has committed to updating controlling and coercive behaviour guidance to reflect clearer recognition of technology-facilitated abuse and we’re making it an offence to take intimate images without consent, including by installing equipment such as cameras to enable people to do so.”

The kindness of strangers: I was a young, solo tourist when a taxi driver became aggressive – then two men stepped in

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 15:00:37 GMT

They relayed to me that the driver wanted more money. I went to grab my wallet, but they told me to put it away

Read more in the kindness of strangers series

I travelled alone a lot when I was younger and often got myself into stupid situations. You think you’re immortal when you’re in your 20s.

One such occasion happened when I was 25 and travelling solo in Egypt, not long after the turn of the century. I had taken an overnight bus from Cairo to Dahab, which dropped me and my fellow passengers off in the middle of nowhere. I had to get a shared taxi into town at about 3am – one where everyone sat up the back in a ute tray – then find somewhere to stay.

I was the only tourist in the taxi and definitely the only woman. When we reached Dahab, things quickly went south. I didn’t speak Arabic, so I couldn’t understand what the driver was saying, but it was quite obvious he was becoming increasingly aggressive toward me.

As things got more and more heated, two Egyptian men who were also in the back of the ute stepped in. The taxi driver was gesturing to me and the other guys shouted back at him. They relayed to me that the driver wanted more money. I went to grab my wallet, but they told me to put it away. They paid him off themselves and the driver left. Suddenly I was alone with these two men, in the middle of the night, wondering if I’d gotten myself into an even hairier situation than the one I’d just exited.

The men asked where I was staying and I replied that I hadn’t booked accommodation. So they took me to a hostel, ensured the owner only charged me the locals’ rate, then disappeared without asking anything in return.

I woke up the next day determined to find – and thank – those two men. It took me three days of searching the city high and low, but I eventually found them, working in an internet cafe. It turned out they were medical students funding their studies by installing internet all over Egypt. I was a student nurse, so we had a lot in common.

They invited me to their home town, where I stayed for a few days and met their wonderful friends, families and future wives. Every time I went out, they escorted me to make sure I was OK. We stayed in contact for years afterwards.

You often meet the worst people when travelling alone as a young woman. I have been robbed everywhere, in every language under the sun. But those men were not motivated by anything selfish in helping me. I think they’d have done that for anyone, simply because it was the right thing to do.

They started as strangers, but I now regard them as two of the best people I’ve ever met.

From making your day to changing your life, we want to hear about chance encounters that have stuck with you.

Iran-linked hackers blamed for cyber-attack that shut down UK power plant

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 14:46:56 GMT

Incident marks apparent escalation by Tehran in its in retaliation against UK over allowing US to use British bases

Hackers linked to Iran have been blamed for a cyber-attack that caused a British power plant to be temporarily shut down.

The incident involved a small-scale energy generator, according to the UK government, which said that at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system.

However, it marks an apparent escalation in the threat posed by Iran after the UK said it had given permission for the US to launch “defensive” operations against Tehran from British bases.

The power plant was shut down for four days as a result of the attack last month, according to the Sunday Telegraph, which first reported it.

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “This story refers to an incident impacting a small-scale energy generator, and at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system. The UK has a highly resilient energy system. We work closely with the energy sector to protect infrastructure and ensure the highest security standards.”

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which deals with attacks on critical infrastructure, is understood not to have received any reported outages from regulated operators of power stations.

The Conservatives said the incident reflected a “new kind of warfare”, which meant Britain needed to prioritise “cheap, reliable energy”. “The world is getting more dangerous, which is why we need to prioritise our energy security,” said Claire Coutinho, the Conservative spokesperson on energy.

“Leaving ourselves reliant on imports of gas and electricity and failing to build enough reliable gas or nuclear plants for backup at home, all leaves us more vulnerable.”

Hostile states such as Russia, China and Iran are increasingly targeting systems behind the UK’s key services, according to a warning this year from Richard Horne, the NCSC’s chief executive.

The government said last month the UK was “ready to defend itself” after Iran’s military warned any bases being used by the US were “legitimate targets”.

The UK has allowed the US to launch so-called defensive operations from British bases hosting American planes since the start of its war on Iran but has refused to help in offensive operations. That policy has not been altered by the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, who was notified last week that a decision had been made to extend the agreement with the US.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said last month that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.

Iran has been accused for years of carrying out cyber-attacks on various countries, including in relation to a massive power outage in Turkey in 2015 and several possible breaches of Israeli government websites in 2022.

US government security agencies issued a warning earlier this year of cyber-attacks on critical infrastructure by hackers linked to the IRGC.

The US has alleged that an Iran-affiliated group known as “CyberAv3ngers” carried out a campaign against it in 2023 that compromised at least 75 devices in multiple infrastructure sectors.

Le Court, who won a stage and finished ninth overall in the Tour de France Femmes earlier this month, based her success on a solo victory in Friday’s uphill finish to the Great Orme, overlooking Llandudno. It was the most significant race victory of the Mauritian rider’s career.

“This win is really special,” she said. “This is my first general classification win and it is a first GC win for me in a team.

“People had questioned if I am a GC rider or not, and it is good to know that the mental state is still quite high and I’m glad I could achieve that for me and the team,” the AG Insurance Soudal rider said.

The 30-year-old has had a chequered past in the British race, but this year proved the strongest of the overall contenders.

“I had a bad experience last year and I just wanted to redeem myself after that,” she said of her 2025 Tour of Britain, when she won the first stage, only to crash out of the race on day two.

“In 2015 I came here and I was dead last, so I didn’t have a good experience of the Tour of Britain in the past. Wiebes, who is quickly becoming more than simply a fast finisher, admitted that the overall classification was not her ambition but added: “When I crossed the finish line on stage three and was still third on GC, I knew we could fight for second.”

Even with under 5km remaining the trio still led by half a minute but they were finally reeled in with barely a kilometre to race, as Wiebes once again moved ahead of her peers to claim another success.

‘I love it. It’s hope’: the mysterious self-willed wildflower meadow that seeded itself

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 14:00:34 GMT

Farmer Derek Sayer let a boggy field run wild and just one annual hay-cut has led to remarkable biodiversity

Tucked away on a country lane, a small field bursts with yellow and pink flowers. Quail and whitethroats call from the thick hedges and the plants, including common centaury, yellow rattle and marsh and common spotted orchids, bounce with hoverflies and butterflies.

More than 150 plant species have been recorded on Sayer’s Old Meadow, in north Norfolk, England, which is remarkable when there was just one – oilseed rape – growing there 21 years ago.

This transformation has happened without sowing any commercial wildflower mixes or making any other expensive interventions such as deep ploughing or top-soil removal, often undertaken when arable land is “restored” to nature-rich meadow. Instead, the four-acre field was simply cut for hay once every summer, with an abundance of wildflowers naturally – and rather mysteriously – finding their way into the field.

These findings, published in a scientific paper in Restoration Ecology, could transform the approach to recreating flower-rich meadows. Conservationists and landowners are pushing to revive old meadows because 98% in England and Wales have been destroyed over the last century.

“Everyone is planting and seeding wildflowers, but sometimes we’re not patient enough,” said Carl Sayer, a professor of limnology and freshwater ecology at University College London and lead author of the paper. “You don’t always have to reach for that expensive commercial wildflower seed mix. We’ve forgotten that nature has known what to do for quite a long while.”

The fact that Sayer shares his surname with the meadow is no coincidence: it is owned by his father, farmer Derek Sayer, 86, and has been part of a tiny traditional farm for generations. The land was ploughed and fertilised and sprayed with pesticides as was conventional in postwar farming, but Derek Sayer stopped cultivating it in 2005 because the small field was always “hit and miss” at producing good yields.

Springs feeding the Glaven chalk stream rise in the meadow and parts of the field were always boggy. The land was “abandoned” for five years and became a forest of thistles before Carl Sayer began studying its growing diversity, beginning an annual hay-cut in 2011.

Fifteen years on, thistles and other arable annual weeds have almost completely disappeared – without any human intervention – to be replaced with a flower-rich perennial sward, which is growing more biodiverse every year.

For Sayer’s father, watching farmland run wild with “weeds” was challenging but he gradually became more interested in his son’s experiment. “He started off saying: ‘What are you doing, Carl? What a load of rubbish.’ Now he’s like: ‘How many orchids are there this year?’” said Sayer.

When Derek Sayer arrived to look at the field during the Guardian’s tour, he still cast a fierce countryman’s gaze over it, checking for “weeds” such as ragwort. “It looked a bit strange at first but I quite like it now,” he said.

Each August, a neighbouring farmer cuts and removes the hay, which he feeds to his cattle, grateful for the biodiverse hay crop. “Much more diversity is a tonic to cattle because it’s full of medicinals,” said Carl Sayer. “The monoculture of a rye-grass field may not give them everything they need. The old farmers had it right.”

Cutting it each year prevents the meadow becoming an oak woodland. The sward is full of baby oaks and sallow, and a patch of the field which hasn’t been cut regularly is now filled with hummocks of sallow as high as a house: still wildlife-rich habitat but not as rare or much-needed as flower-rich meadows.

Removing the grass growth each year with the hay-cut also reduces the nutrients, enabling more delicate wildflowers to flourish. Several years ago, yellow rattle found its way into the meadow. This is known as “the meadow maker” because it parasitises grass and creates space for other wildflowers, although Sayer said the meadow was thriving without it.

after newsletter promotion

“Everyone will tell you this approach [not sowing wildflowers] doesn’t work unless you’re close to a seed source. But no one has done a long-term study like this,” he said.

The surrounding land is intensively farmed and the nearest populations of some of the rare flowers now found in the meadow are at least 3 miles (4.8km) away. One possibility is that seeds have been brought in on the hooves or coats of wild deer that roam the countryside.

“Everyone’s accused me of bringing it in on my upturned trousers but I don’t wear upturned trousers,” joked Sayer, who was wearing shorts.

Sayer’s Old Meadow looks noticeably different from what some conservationists disparagingly call generic “McMeadows” created from popular wildflower mixes which are dominated by white oxeye daisies and purple knapweed. The advantage of “self-willed” meadows is that they are filled with locally-appropriate plants which are likely to be more genetically diverse than those found in commercial seed mixes. This type of meadow creation was also much cheaper, said Sayer.

Since last year, barn owls have taken up residence in a field-edge nest box and hunt over the field. The Sayers allow local people to walk in it and an informal path now runs down one side. “Everyone in the village loves it, people walk through it and respect it. It’s working to make people happy as well,” said Sayer. “It’s the thing I’m most proud of in my life. I love it. It’s hope – we can recover things. We just need to do less in the recovery process.”

Is there a pending AI ‘debt bomb’ crisis? No. This isn’t Enron 2.0

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 14:00:34 GMT

Fears of a datacenter buildout debt crisis are exaggerated. The risks are different than in the past and they are recoverable

Some experts are warning of a looming “debt bomb” crisis because big datacenter builders such as Meta, Oracle, xAI and CoreWeave are not only raising billions to construct these facilities but are also not recognizing these long-term debt obligations on their balance sheets.

Should we be concerned? No. I know because I’ve seen this movie before.

It works like this: Meta wants to build a datacenter to accommodate its growing AI and cloud computing needs. It forms a separate entity that’s not consolidated in its financials, which builds the datacenter. To fund this, the entity raises money from investors, banks and other financial firms (including some from Meta) that own the majority of the entity. There is a contract by which Meta has exclusive and full use of the datacenter once built. This way Meta gets its datacenter but most of the debt incurred to build it is not shown as a liability on its books.

The worry comes from the enormous sums of money being plowed into these entities. The Financial Times reported in December 2025 that tech companies had shifted more than $120bn of AI datacenter spending off their balance sheets through special-purpose vehicles and similar financing structures. Goldman Sachs estimates that hyperscalers could spend $5.3tn on AI and datacenters through 2030 and expects private markets to play an increasingly important role in financing that buildout.

Skeptics are worried that these tech guys are pulling the wool over the public’s eyes and not properly disclosing the long-term impact of all this debt. They point to Enron, the energy firm that spectacularly failed in 2001, causing tens of billions of dollars of losses to its shareholders and contributing to a historic market meltdown.

Fine. Scrutinize them. Read the footnotes. Argue about consolidation. But don’t call them Enron. Enron caused the Enron crash. It’s highly unlikely that fraud at that level is being perpetuated now by these companies.

When I first started out in accounting back in the mid-1980s, my biggest client was a publicly held biotechnology firm called Centocor, which, at the time, was developing drugs using a technology based on monoclonal-antibody treatment for various purposes including sepsis. To raise money, Centocor also did off-balance-sheet financing. The company formed limited partnerships in which it held a minority interest but the entity issued debt and took in investments from limited partners in order to fund the development of various drugs, which Centocor then had the exclusive right to use.

In the 1980s and early 1990s, hundreds of millions of dollars were plowed into these partnerships. This was common practice in the biotechnology during that time.

Did some of the drugs fail in clinical testing? Yes. But did this cause a stock market panic? No. Like with today’s datacenters, the risks were spread. During that time – before the Internet, SEC disclosures and 24/7 media scrutiny – the public little knew of these vehicles. The good news is that the accounting has evolved, although the economic idea has stayed the same – no debt was shown on Centocor’s balance sheet. Ultimately, this financing vehicle became more expensive and less popular because it was easier and more affordable to raise money other ways.

The off-balance-sheet financing strategies today that are being used by big tech firms have different risks than what the biotech companies were doing when I was younger. Today, the disclosures required by companies doing this are significant. The scrutiny is intense. The investing public is smarter. Today’s risks are different and arguably more recoverable.

In the 90s Centocor, Genentech, Amgen, Biogen and other companies like them were raising millions in partnerships that were developing products with a high probability of failure during clinical testing.

Today’s investors are financing land, buildings, electrical infrastructure and computing equipment. A datacenter can disappoint financially, but it doesn’t disappear because a clinical trial fails. It’s why Jeff Bezos calls AI an “industrial bubble”. Industrial bubbles leave things behind. Railways. Fiber-optic cable. Factories. And this time, datacenters.

If this is a glut, it’s a strange one: developers increased North American capacity by 36% last year and vacancy still fell to a record 1.4%. According to CBRE’s North America Data Center Trends H2 2025 report, demand is outpacing supply in nearly every major market. Unlike the drug companies hoping for success, there’s a legitimate market need today for datacenters. AI isn’t going away. Microsoft estimates that only 17.8% of the world’s working-age population currently uses generative AI. If that’s anywhere near correct, we’re still much closer to the beginning of adoption than the end.

Some of these investments will fail. Some lenders will lose money. Some datacenters will be worth less than their owners paid for them. But that’s exactly why these financing structures exist: to spread enormous capital requirements and risk among investors willing to take it. The obligations are disclosed, the assets are real and demand for computing capacity remains strong. That’s why I’m not losing sleep over big tech’s off-balance-sheet debt. I see financial engineering, yes. I don’t see a debt bomb.

“I felt it was a top performance. I enjoyed it at times for the intensity with the lads willing to run for each other,” Morrison said. “We did the basics really well – we won tackles, and when we lost the ball, we ran back and when the opportunities were given to us, we took advantage.

Burnley, without injured star striker Zian Flemming amid intense speculation of a move, failed to match their lofty billing in a disappointing second-half display. Albion continued their 100% start to the season, gaining their third straight win in all competitions and second in the league to lie second in the early table, behind Millwall on goal difference.

In a fast and furious start, there were two goals in the first 18 minutes. Styles put into his own net in the eighth minute from Jacob Bruun Larsen’s cross. Albion complained that Hannibal Mejbri fouled Felix Horn Myhre in the buildup 70 yards away, with several passages of play unfolding before the goal. Styles had to make contact to prevent Oliver Sonne getting the chance but the ball hit his left heel and it flew into the net.

Whitwell equalised on 18 minutes when he slotted home low to Max Weiss’s left from 12 yards for the 20-year-old’s first league goal for Albion. Burnley appeared wrongfooted by Jimmy-Jay Morgan’s flick-on from Price’s cross, before Bashir Humphreys failed to clear. But it was Burnley who went closest to scoring again when Bruun Larsen sidefooted against the foot of the post from Marcus Edwards’s searching cross.

It was a different story after the break. Inspired by Price, Albion produced a dominant second-half performance, with the perfect start. Price put them ahead for the first time, in the 46th minute, curling the ball beyond Weiss, who had strayed five yards off his line, into the far corner. The goal came from a loose ball when Morgan tried to help back Styles’s cross and Hannibal challenged.

Burnley made a triple change in the 57th minute with the arrival of Ugo Raghouber, Zeki Amdouni, and Dastan Satpayev. Amdouni tried to test Max O’Leary with a rising, curling effort from 20 yards but it flew straight at the Albion keeper.

Instead it was Albion who struck next to effectively seal it, after Humphreys upended Whitwell for a clear penalty. Price made no mistake from the spot, firing low to Weiss’s right with the keeper going the wrong way.

Afterwards, Morrison said: “We enjoy competing against the so-called bigger teams and we competed really well today. We don’t want to get carried away. We have to keep our feet on the ground, keep working hard and stay humble.”

The PM is promising to fix our everyday annoyances – and I have a list to get him started

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 13:00:33 GMT

Andy Burnham hopes we’ll forget the big stuff if he sorts out our minor frustrations and low-level gripes. Pothole politics hasn’t won me over yet, but I know some changes that could

This is a vulnerable confession, but I spend way too much time on the social media of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani. Whether he is seemingly effortlessly speaking Mandarin, hanging out with kids or charmingly accepting that he should wear a cycle helmet, the man with the million-watt smile is my antidepressant. (Even more vulnerable confession: I believe, irrationally, he is looking after my elder son, who lives there.)

This means that I know all about Mamdani’s fight against what Business Insider recently deemed the “annoyance economy” – daily frustrations that make you poorer or drive you slowly, miserably mad. These include the absurd complexity of cancelling subscriptions; hidden fees; getting charged more for something you looked up last week, because of cookies; never being able to find a public toilet; and potholes. He has taken to responding when he gets tagged in people’s “Mamdani, fix this” posts to the point where Britons online are even jokily asking him to take on their problems.

He may not need to, because Andy Burnham has started doing something similar with his “everyday fixes” for irritations and unfair expense: bringing forward the ban on auto-renewed subscriptions; tackling betting and vape shops and misleading “sale” prices; and capping bus fares in England.

It’s surely human nature to start by sweating the small stuff – faced with a to-do list, most of us tick off the quick wins first – and would you rather tackle climate breakdown or potholes? More cynically, it also plays well for politicians online. These fixes are visual and easily communicated. As Eric Phillips, who was press secretary for the former New York mayor Bill de Blasio, says: “Theatre is part of the job.” But does Burnham really think fluttering his eyelashes and telling me it will be easier to cancel a Paramount+ subscription I took out in 2021 and then forgot about means I’ll roll over and let him tickle my belly, forgetting all about his unconscionable attitude to North Sea drilling?

I suppose it’s not impossible. It’s nice to feel as if someone in power understands the low‑level irritations that sap our joy, energy and resources – and will do something about them. And, just possibly, winning public confidence by sorting minor gripes could build goodwill to tackle the big, hard, slow, unpopular stuff.

I’m not won over by British pothole politics yet – Burnham doesn’t have Mamdani’s magic. So, having seen the consumer champion Martin Lewis suggest that the government fix “100 small things that piss people off”, I’ve compiled a list of silly little ways to get me on side.

Obviously, start with the scourge of delivery companies claiming you were out when you were in all day, staring out like a lonely dog, waiting for your package. Please also eliminate the headbanging futility of updating “delivery preferences” only for them to be ignored. I could reconcile myself to the surveillance state, I reckon, if the surveillance included a database of everyone’s whereabouts and preferences, so you never had to argue with a bot or retrieve your contact lenses from your mortal enemy at No 114. Perhaps the surveillance state could also remind me where I’ve put my keys?

Then there is the “digital annoyance economy”, by which I mean shopping sites that, when you click on an item and then click back, return you to the top of the page, so you have to scroll back down through all the items you’ve already seen: this outrage needs to be stamped out. And if I buy something and the seller signs me up to marketing guff unless I opt out, I want to be able to press a big red button (on my phone, around my neck?) that places the company in administration and bars the entire board from holding corporate office in perpetuity. Please impose the same punishment for having a non-functioning “unsubscribe” option on emails.

The CEO of every manufacturer of plastic-film lids needs to demonstrate they can open them effortlessly, using their non-dominant hand, before they can sell them. See also sticky tape – make them prove it unrolls without ripping or the end disappearing. Washing machines should have a built-in tissue sensor; bread should be bio-engineered to fall butter side up and we need free scissor and nail clipper distributors on every street corner. Also, issue everyone with a single, universal sock.

Once you’ve fixed all that, @andy. burnham, you might just get my vote.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 11:50:12 GMT

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said holding elections in Ukraine during wartime would risk splitting the country at a time when Russia is amassing ballistic missiles and considering whether to mobilise an extra 300,000 soldiers.

The Ukrainian president, responding for the first time to a demand made by the sacked former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, sharply criticised an idea that he said was impractical given Russia appeared to have no interest in a ceasefire.

“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move in the selection of elections,” Zelenskyy said in a briefing to selected journalists that was held on Saturday, but details of which were reported on Sunday.

“I believe that during such a war, elections in general are big risks. Elections right now are a tsunami for the state that will split Ukraine,” he said, adding that his plan was to end the war and preserve Ukraine as an independent state.

Elections have been suspended in Ukraine since martial law was imposed at the start of the full-scale invasion by Russia. Zelenskyy’s five-year term ended in May 2024 but there had until recently been little desire in Ukraine to hold a contest while the war continued.

That shifted when Fedorov, a popular minister who had been dismissed by Zelenskyy a month earlier, called for a fresh contest. It was the most open challenge to Zelenskyy’s authority from inside Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion.

Zelenskyy said, according to a transcript from the briefing, that if Ukraine’s allies were to establish “specific conditions” under which elections could be safely, legitimately and democratically held in Ukraine, he would support them.

It would require “the participation of the military, in frontline territories, abroad, where millions of our citizens have gone, fleeing the war” and a poll would have to take place safely “without strikes and shelling”, he said.

Fedorov, he said, had moved from his post because had had overreached, trying to cover functions belonging to the military. He had been offered four alternative jobs in the government but declined all four, the president added. “I really had and still have a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” Zelenskyy said. “We have been through a lot together. But I believe that he himself goes, or is pushed, into the wrong things.”

Russia had a stockpile of 600-630 high-speed ballistic missiles, its most potent type of weapon, and was trying to build a little more than 100 more a month in the run-up to winter, Zelenskyy said. Its maximum production capacity was 1,300 a year, he added.

Ballistic missiles have been used to bomb Ukrainian infrastructure and warehouses and to attack the capital, causing increased civilian casualties. There is a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapon that can effectively counter them.

“I wanted to secure 300 Patriot missiles for the winter package. The request from our air force is 360,” Zelenskyy said. He acknowledged this was difficult given that only about 600 of the most capable PAC-3 interceptor missiles were made a year. He said he had reached an agreement with France on at least one SAMP/T air-defence system ​this year, and with ‌Germany on the supply of ​about 600 PAC-2 and PAC-3 ​interceptors in 2027--28.

Burnham to face pressure at Labour conference to recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 11:26:40 GMT

Grassroots groups to urge PM to break with Starmer policy and impose full arms embargo on Israel

Grassroots Labour groups are gearing up for a conference showdown with Andy Burnham over Gaza, as the party’s members seek to force the prime minister to recognise Israel’s actions as a genocide and impose a full arms embargo.

Momentum, Labour & Palestine, the Campaign for Labour Party Democracy and Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) plan to ramp up pressure on Burnham before his first Labour conference as prime minister next month.

The groups are circulating a model motion for Labour members to submit to conference, demanding the government accepts the findings of a UN commission of inquiry that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, and to impose “comprehensive sanctions”, including a full arms embargo.

The motion also demands that ministers impose comprehensive sanctions and ban trade that “aids or assists” Israel’s military actions in Gaza or its unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territories, including trade with Israeli settlements.

Burnham’s refusal to use the term genocide has caused frustration among many Labour MPs, not just those on the left of the party. Several MPs told the Guardian they welcomed Burnham’s apology, but wanted him to go further and explicitly “acknowledge Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide”.

The prime minister has apologised for the party’s handling of Gaza under Starmer’s leadership, saying Labour had “not got it right”.

Weeks before he became prime minister, Burnham told the Guardian: “We’ve got to do more to put pressure on the Israeli government … let’s be honest, the UK was too slow to call for a ceasefire. And we must now do more to strengthen our approach.” But he stopped short of describing what was happening on the ground in Gaza as a genocide, saying that while there was “increasing evidence” of war crimes, it was for the international courts to make that ruling.

The UK government has signalled that further measures against Israel could be coming. Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, said ministers would set out a “comprehensive set of measures” after Israel moved ahead with its controversial E1 settlement plans in the occupied West Bank.

In the run-up to the 2025 party conference, Labour sought to rule out motions on Palestine being debated at the conference, which triggered accusations that the party was trying to stifle debate. About 30 motions about Palestine from local parties were struck off last September.

But conference went against the then leadership and backed an emergency motion proposed by the Unison union that the Labour government should “employ all means reasonably available to it to prevent the commission of genocide in Gaza” and “fully suspend the arms trade with Israel and the UK-Israel trade and partnership agreement”.

The Labour groups are seeking to force the issue back on the conference floor this year, presenting it as an early test of Burnham’s promise not to “stifle debate” within Labour. Momentum is launching a petition aimed at current and former Labour members and voters, urging the prime minister to stick to the position backed by delegates last year.
