Stores are selling Halloween stuff in August. Time has lost all meaning

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 11:00:33 GMT

Capitalism and the climate crisis are conspiring to destroy the concept of seasons. I’ll take solace in my pumpkin spice

Happy spooky season, everyone! Get those jack-o’-lanterns out, because Halloween is just around the corner!

Just kidding, no, it’s not.

It’s August, for God’s sake. Every day, I wake up to 90F weather – my skin moist with sweat and my eyelids stuck together. I can’t drink coffee on my porch without being consumed by an army of voracious mosquitoes that seem to find my blood to be the most delicious of all.

And it’s not just Los Angeles that’s withering under a summer of discontent. The east coast heatwaves are piling up, sending millions of young people to the absolute last place they want to be: an air-conditioned movie theater. But you want to tell me it’s fine to be putting out Halloween decorations? If I don’t store my giant bag of fun-size Twix in a standup freezer, the whole damn thing will melt into chocolate soup. (Don’t even get me started on recent claims you should eat soup when it’s hot outside. It’d rather slurp up my own sweat from a bowl.)

Why am I fuming about this? Even though I love Halloween, I’m mad because our glorious big-box overlords have declared, via careful inventory selection, that Halloween season has begun. In August. I find all of that unacceptable. It feels like a violation of the natural order, a realignment of one of the few glorious constants left in the world. I yearn to go back to the tidy order of holidays, where no two ever cross paths. At most, Halloween celebrations should start in late September. Not a month after Independence Day. I fear those days are done, that our world has irrevocably changed and I need to start getting ready to give in to the new normal.

I first became aware of Halloween’s creep into the summer during a recent sundries run at Target. There are costumes, life-size skeletons, treats and various decorations on offer in-store. I’ve seen massive candy bags positioned to move at CVS. There’s even a smattering of greeting cards, which I find doubly frustrating, as I’ve never in my life considered buying someone a card for Halloween, a holiday that most adults spend binge drinking or squeezing into provocative outfits. What does a Halloween greeting card even say? “I Boo-lieve You Should Get an Uber Home”? “Have a Spooktacular One-Night Stand With Your Marginally Attractive Co-Worker”?

On that Target outing, my friend Halle (an admitted Halloween pervert) bought a miniature cauldron from the growing, metastasizing spooky section. I asked what she expected to do with such a trivial piece of merchandise. “Maybe I can put my keys or some change in here.” For two months? Then what? Do you say Back to the closet with you and wait another nine months before getting your coin cauldron out again?

I know there are people with boxes and boxes of festive decorations who swap them out season after season. Christmas ends, but Easter is just around the corner. Once that’s done, you chuck the bunny rabbits and start bedazzling your home with American flags to prep for the Fourth of July. Now I’m seeing the insidious truth: we aren’t far off from that Fourth-to-Halloween corridor shrinking even further. I see a world in which witches, demons and vampires slowly start bleeding into our patriotic revelries. It’ll get to the point where some of us might start thinking Frankenstein’s monster fought at the battle of Yorktown.

One day, we’ll all just celebrate whichever holidays we want, whenever we feel like it. As the climate crisis renders the idea of distinct seasons and unique weather conditions a relic of a bygone era, why wouldn’t we just all live our own little celebratory truths? Even if my local store isn’t carrying Halloween decorations, I could feasibly buy them year-round on Amazon – my mailbox jammed up with boxes of plastic fangs, fake blood and green grease paint. If it never gets cold again, then Halloween can be whenever. Though I suppose the lifestyle I’m describing already has a name and it’s “being goth”.

It could be that our society is naturally evolving to be unbound by passé limitations such as “calendars” and “nature”. Instead of using holidays to mark the phases of the harvest or cycles of the moon (boring), they can be dictated by big data (chill and modern). Surely retailers around the country have statistics that point to consumers having a hankering for Halloween by August. Otherwise, why would Target be hawking rubber bats or decorative ghosts right now? We’re giving ourselves over to analytics in almost every other sector of our lives. Why not holidays?

If the data says we want Halloween in the heat, then data shall be respected and worshipped. Who am I to argue with hard numbers? If the sun’s always shining, the grass is consistently brown and the acrid bite of wildfire smoke is clogging our lungs, the average human being might not be able to differentiate between the phases of our natural world. The only way for me to not continue to rage against this phenomenon is to surrender to capitalism completely. Instead of putting my finger out and seeing which way the wind blows, I just have to pop into Target to know what season it is.

The cognitive dissonance I might feel carrying my friend’s cauldron to my car in August is something my son might never feel. Time passes under the pall of climate control and fluorescent lighting. Our lives are measured by the movement of currency undulating and cresting like waves in the ocean. As this existentially crippling revelation washes over me, I take comfort in one thing:

Soon, sooner than you think, it will be pumpkin spice season.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

Walking the Peak District, I discovered a wonderful rejection of the right’s monotone vision of England

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 11:00:32 GMT

The landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers. We can make this the new normal – and we should

A fortnight or so ago, my two teenage kids and I set out on a three-night visit to the Peak District where temperatures were hovering at a comparatively tepid 28C. We stayed at a youth hostel – more of which in a moment – and began the trip with the 20-minute ascent of Mam Tor, a modest peak that pulls in both dedicated ramblers who then yomp along the ridge beyond, and newbies who mostly want to get to the top and immerse themselves in the jaw-dropping view.

The next bit might sound self-parodically Guardian-esque, but what the hell: in its own way, the most striking sight was the diversity of the scores of people rambling up, down and along. Women in their 20s wearing hijabs picnicked on giant rocks, while multiracial gaggles of young men attempted to race to the top; solo and shirtless white fitness freaks and retirement-age dog walkers took their places alongside them. With plenty of justification, country walking has long been typified as one of the most monoculturally white pursuits there is. But here – presumably because of the relatively close proximity of Manchester and Sheffield – things looked different.

The scenes didn’t quite suggest Britain in microcosm, but they weren’t far off. I began to wonder, in fact, whether I was witnessing the (extremely) belated next emancipatory phase of a story that began with the mass trespass at the nearby Kinder Scout in 1932, led by the Jewish anti-fascist Benny Rothman: the protest in which hundreds of men and women defied the law to walk on privately owned Derbyshire hills and moorland. Five of them received prison sentences, but the way was thereby opened to the creation of the UK’s first national parks.

The latter-day people and organisations working to make walking more inclusive – in response to national statistics that remain depressing, and often in the face of straight-up prejudice – surely deserve as much praise as Rothman and his comrades. Black Girls Hike was founded in 2019 by the brilliant Mancunian Rhiane Fatinikun, aimed at creating “a safe space for Black women to explore the outdoors … challenging the status quo”. Soon after, the Coventry-based rambler Haroon Mota started Muslim Hikers, and began group walks just over a year later. In the same city, Cherelle Harding created Steppers UK, intended to “normalise black and brown faces in outdoor spaces and create a community of outdoor enthusiasts”.

All this reflects aspects of our culture and politics that can be fascinating and inspiring – and, on the other side of some modern political and cultural divides, very unsettling. If he were to visit the Peak District, Nigel Farage would presumably get no further than his chosen pub. But his vision of bucolic England is symbolised by the outfit he tends to wear when he wants to accuse the supposed metropolitan elite of neglecting the countryside, usually by turning up at one of those faux – or not so faux – fox hunts. We all know the drill: flat cap, Barbour jacket, wellies, fag and pint. The cosplay is replete with meaning, and not just in its embodiment of what a cultural-studies specialist might call white rurality. Look, for example, at the terrible twist Farage and his political allies got their collective knickers in over the National Trust’s drive to be open about some of its properties’ links to colonialism and slavery, and the same organisation’s campaigning to protect the environment.

Further to the right, somewhere in the heart of every nativist lurk darkly romanticised visions of the British landscape – think of what is meant by that toxic phrase “blood and soil”. Last year, news broke about two wooded stretches of land in mid-Wales being bought by the Woodlander Initiative, a scheme led by the far-right activist Simon Birkett. He has links to Patriotic Alternative, reckoned to be the UK’s largest fascist organisation. The people involved were never going to be interested in urban land: to the fascist mind, the countryside, as opposed to the cosmopolitan and decadent stereotypical city (think about the far right’s constant demonisation of London), represents notions of racial purity and noble simplicity. From some far-right activists, there was sympathetic talk in response about “indigenous heartlands – places for our people”.

The upshot of all this is obvious: the UK’s rural expanses can be as toxified and contested as any other aspect of our national life, and without wanting to sound too dour – walking is meant to be fun, after all – we need to actively promote the idea that the countryside belongs to all of us. To do so is to deprive the assortment of opportunists and hate-mongers who span the hard and far right of any idea that the British landscape and its romance and mythology might be theirs to monopolise.

There is another, much more benign and everyday obstacle to maximising access to green spaces. In many places, hotels and hospitality increasingly embody a different kind of exclusivity: the upgrading of pubs and hotels to boutique, gastro-centric establishments with sky-high prices. Those charged on such platforms as Airbnb are part of the same problem. So if your ambitions extend further than a day trip and such luxury is beyond your budget, where can you stay?

Part of the answer lies with the Youth Hostels Association (YHA) of England and Wales (the equivalent north of the border is Hostelling Scotland) and its network of places to eat, sleep and socialise. But the pandemic caused the YHA an income loss of £40m in the first year alone, and in March last year, it said that its energy costs had quadrupled. In 2023, it had about 150 hostels; to date, it has announced the sale or closure of 29. Eight are now run as hostels thanks to a YHA franchising scheme, and there are similar hopes for at least one of my threatened favourites: Bellever on Dartmoor, one of the most idyllic places I have ever spent the night.

But here is the crucial point: the YHA runs a programme that provides fully or “partly funded stays at youth hostels for young people and families facing significant challenges” (including young carers, and those involved in refugee and migrant groups), and a scheme called No Child Left Behind that helps to ensure that financial hardship does not stop kids going on residential school trips. It is an organisation that should be expanding, not shrinking.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Having come down off Mam Tor, I drove the half hour back to where we were staying: Hartington Hall, a 17th-century manor house owned and run by the YHA. As we were having dinner, I noticed a plaque fixed to the wall, presumably dating from the distant days (the YHA was founded in 1930) when guests were obliged to muck in with the chores rather than sample the £14 burger-and-beer meal deal. “This youth hostel,” it said, “is one of many, both in this country and abroad, where young people, regardless of race or creed, may spend the night. The buildings are diverse in character but they have a common purpose: to help all, especially young people of limited means, to a greater knowledge, love and care for the countryside.”

How, then, to preserve as many hostels as possible, bring in more young people and make those words real? An injection of cash from big-spending philanthropists? A modest tourist tax on hotels and short-let accommodation? Or the kind of relative loose change that could presumably be found by the departments for Food and Rural Affairs, Education, Culture, Media and Sport, or all three? Some parts of the British landscape are starting to undergo what seems to be an overdue and very welcome social change, but it needs the kind of support that comes in the form of bunk-beds and brickwork. In a country whose divisions are constantly inflamed and hyped up by demagogic chancers, that challenge is a lot more urgent than it might seem.

John Harris is a Guardian columnist

Dining across the divide: ‘I thought he was going to be quite “stop the boats, bring up the drawbridge”’

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 11:00:30 GMT

A Green party member and a Labour-voting Brexiter didn’t agree on the EU, but what about renewable energy and the NHS?

Want to meet someone from across the divide? Click here to find out how

Occupation Press officer at a university

Voting record Historically, under Jeremy Corbyn, Labour; is a Green member now but was planning to vote Labour in the mayoral election

Amuse bouche Long-distance cycle touring is Joe’s big thing: he has been all over Europe solo, staying with families, trying to speak the languages, embedding himself with local people

Occupation Retired – used to be a journalist, moved to Liverpool to edit a shipping newspaper and ended up owning it

Voting record Keith normally votes Labour. There was one occasion when he voted Conservative, for Margaret Thatcher

Amuse bouche Keith once went to Rio de Janeiro for the day. He was producing a magazine for British Airways Cargo and they wanted to promote the route to São Paulo

Joe I’d formed a view of what his character might be but he was really warm and friendly. It was like two old friends. It was just so comfortable.

Keith The first thing he said was, “Are you as nervous as I am?” I said I wasn’t nervous at all. I’m used to talking to people and it didn’t bother me.

Joe I had the prosciutto and melon, then chicken in breadcrumbs.

Keith I started with calamari, then gnocchi with prawns.

Joe He was very set on the idea that the EU is anti-democratic. The arguments I had about the damage that leaving the EU has done to the British economy – how it has destroyed exports and left us isolated – he agreed with. But none of it mattered to him. He was a Brexiter from quite a leftwing perspective. I thought he was going to be quite “stop the boats, bring up the drawbridge”, but he wasn’t like that at all.

Keith I voted for Brexit for independence, not for the economy, although the economy could have been handled better by the prime ministers since. You had Theresa May – who was, I believe, a remainer at heart – trying to cobble together some sort of deal that looked like Brexit but wasn’t. Both she and Boris Johnson should share the blame because they let it drag on for so long. You should never be governed by people you can’t vote out of office.

Joe He said Nigel Farage sometimes says things that he agrees with – principally stuff about the European superstate. When he was talking about that, you couldn’t put a cigarette paper between him and Farage. But at the same time, he’s really anti-Trump, and really anti the rightwing position on migrants.

Keith There are 4,000 different edicts in the EU that we should have got rid of. I don’t feel we’ve taken advantage economically of the opportunities. Joe sort of saw that, but he believes too many small companies have lost business. I did point out that traders should have looked elsewhere for business. We were the sixth largest trading nation in the world before and we still are.

Joe On the NHS, I don’t think we were miles apart. I’ve worked in the NHS in the past; the right wing dresses up overspending as back office stuff and equality and diversity, but all of that is a tiny drop in the ocean compared with PFI.

Keith He saw how the NHS is paying hundreds of millions in interest on PFI payments. PFI has been a bit of a disaster, but I’d be very open to other ways of bringing in private money.

Joe Drilling in the North Sea won’t make us more resilient as a country because it has all got to be sold on the international markets anyway. Is there any point doing damage to the environment when it won’t benefit British consumers? We could be spending that money and energy building renewable capacity.

Keith I’m all for going to renewables, I’m all for cutting pollution. I agree with all that, but I just don’t think we need to do it as quickly as people like Ed Miliband want us to. It’s impoverishing the country, we’re losing industry.

Joe As I was driving away, I did think I should have taken his email address, so we could have kept in touch.

Keith The only problem I was left with was that I’m never going to see him or hear from him again. He’s a long way away to go out for a casual drink.

Additional reporting: Kitty Drake

When my husband died in a surfing accident, life as I knew it was destroyed. Ten years on, this is what I’ve learned about grief

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 11:00:30 GMT

One crashing wave on one single day changed everything for our family. How would I keep going?

Before they enter the water, surfers will study the ocean. They consider wind and tide conditions. They analyse currents and patterns, break points and swells. They try to read the waves. I have travelled across oceans and a day to sit here on Tamarama beach in Sydney on a high-tide weekday morning in 2024. A notebook and pen lie beside me on the sand as I, too, attempt to read the waves, to find meaning in their unfathomable churn.

These past 10 years, this beach has loomed large in my mind. Even when absent, it’s as if my face has been turned to these waves and I have been buffeted, sometimes staggering, sometimes falling, always bracing for the next set to roll in. For I have learned that all it takes is one ocean, one day, to come along and knock you off your feet.

It’s an ordinary Wednesday afternoon in Sydney, the first week of July, when two plainclothes police officers knock at our front door. I am not home to greet them. I am a few streets away, buried in my studio, wrestling with the tangled threads of a novel, when I receive a call from my husband’s PA.

“I’ve had a call from a Bondi detective,” she tells me. “They were asking for your address. I can’t reach Matt.”

I grab my laptop but leave everything else in place and try Matt’s number as I half-run, half-walk up the steep hill to our house. No answer. I call our childminder. “Weird question but has anyone come to the house?”

“Yes,” she says. Her voice is different, strained.

“Police?”

“Yes.”

The red front door to our tiny sandstone cottage is shut tight. Through the glass pane I see two figures in dark clothing standing in our living room. I fumble for my keys. The door opens and I cross the threshold.

“Hannah Richell?” they ask. I guess I nod, and they introduce themselves as police detectives. One of them, I think, has tears in her eyes.

I glance between them, my panic rising, until the more composed of the two comes right out with it. “I’m sorry to tell you your husband has been in a surfing accident.”

“Is he OK?” I’m already running through childcare options to make a hospital dash.

“I’m afraid he died.”

I’m still in my coat and boots. My laptop bag hangs from my shoulder. I look down at the old wooden chest that stands in the front room, doubling as a coffee table, and notice an unfamiliar box of tissues sitting on its surface – a box of tissues I have not bought or placed there. A small part of my brain, one not yet numbed by shock and disbelief, registers that the police must have brought it. I look at the tissues, then back to the police. My bag slides from my shoulder to the floor.

On the way to the morgue, I gaze out of the window. He is dead, I keep telling myself. You are going to view his body. But I don’t truly believe it. I will see the body and I will feel only relief, because of course it won’t be him. There is no way it can be him, my warm, vivid, drily funny, thoroughly alive husband. It will be another man, belonging to another family, who are at this very moment unaware of the tragedy that awaits them. I will leave the morgue dizzy with relief and return to the life I should be living.

But it is him.

And it isn’t.

The body in the blue gown lying on the gurney belongs to my husband, but it isn’t my husband as I knew him. What lies before me is a stiff wax model of the man I love.

Matt. But not Matt.

It is the longest, shortest, most loving, most painful hour of my life. One hour alone, to kiss and caress him. To stroke his stubbled cheek and hold his hand and lay my head upon his chest and weep. Kissing his temples, I see the cuts on his face and a diamond crosshatch line of stitches across the back of his head from the autopsy. The sight of those stitches makes me reel. They have cut open his beautiful skull. The one I absent-mindedly caressed while reading on the sofa, the prickle of his shaved head under my fingers. The one my three-year-old daughter would stroke while high on his shoulders and proclaim “spiky” with a giggle. I try not to think about what else they have had to do to him.

From our inauspicious beginning, when Matt joined the London publishing company to steal the promotion I had coveted, to a deep bond forged through travel, marriage and babies, I sit in this closed, quiet morgue and remember words written in my diary as our first new year together had raced towards us. “Don’t let him hurt me,” I had written, imploring an unseen, unknown power. I suppose I knew, even then, that a love like this could break my heart.

Wendy, a counsellor from the forensic science team, enters the room and sits quietly with me. “You’re very affectionate with him,” she says.

“I thought his eyes were opening,” I tell her, knowing how crazy I sound for still wishing that they might.

“That can happen,” she admits. “Muscles can relax.”

“He smells different.”

“They will have washed him,” she says.

Though not as carefully as they’d intended, perhaps, for when I try to hold his stiff hand, grains of Tamarama sand fall from his palm into mine. They feel like a last gift: a piece of the country he loved so deeply. Precious. I want to scoop the sand up and take it home with me, carry the grains around in a locket, but they slip through my fingers and fall to the floor, disappearing with the sound of my crying and the last kiss I leave on his lips.

I text Adam, the friend who was with Matt when he died. “Hi, this is Hannah, Matt’s wife. Yesterday must have been terrible. Are you OK?” We tread carefully, cautiously polite, until Adam offers to come to our home and talk me through what happened. He is a virtual stranger at my front door, but the moment he steps over the threshold, I am with him. The connection feels instant and real. We sit for a couple of minutes on the sofa in our front room, but the kids are noisy in the background and the house feels claustrophobic and all wrong. “I need to get out of here. Can we get some air?”

Adam looks relieved.

We walk to the park and sit on the grass. It is strange but, out here, in the sunshine and clean air, I feel calmer. Adam’s presence is comforting, like a blanket, muffling me from the horror of the last few days. Slowly, he begins to tell me about the accident. He talks of their joy paddling out from Bronte beach, two work friends choosing to talk shop on their surfboards rather than over lunch in an overpriced restaurant. “Surely this must be the definition of success?” Adam had said.

“Yep,” Matt had replied, and when Adam says it, he delivers it just as Matt would have. In that one word I can see Matt in his wetsuit, straddling his board, salt water in his stubble and a wide grin plastered across his face as he gazes towards the horizon.

Adam tells me of the suddenly shifting tide conditions and of seeing Matt’s board come loose. He describes the rip, pulling Matt dangerously close to the rocky Tamarama headland. I sense his internal struggle as he relives the tragedy, and I sit quietly, listening.

Adam’s explanation comes to its end. The swallows are dancing around us, twisting and looping over the grass. I lean back and close my eyes. For the very first time since I arrived home to find the police in my house, I feel my heartbeat begin to slow in my chest. It’s shock – madness – but for a moment it’s as if he is here with us. Three people, not two, Matt’s presence hovering lightly between us.

“Have you talked to Wendy?” Adam asks.

“Wendy at the morgue?”

“She offers counselling. You might want to call her.”

My mum appears at the far edge of the park with the kids. They have a soccer ball. I point them out and Adam sprints away to kick the ball back to my son. They play like any others in the park around them – a man and a boy kicking a ball back and forth across the grass – but watching them, I feel a deep pain radiate through my body for all that our children have lost.

Grief is a sinkhole, opening up where real life once stood. A cavernous black void swallowing everything I hold dear. Life as we know it has been destroyed in a single day by one crashing wave. The world feels tilted. How to process the enormity of what has happened when everything shifts and moves around me?

I visit Wendy for a counselling session. We sit opposite each other in a small windowless room, a box of tissues on a side table at the ready. I am getting used to their subtle placement. I never seem to be far away from a box of tissues these days.

Wendy exhales and smiles her greeting. “Hello,” she says. There’s a stillness in the air between us as we regard each other and the threshold we sit upon. Her opening question is to ask how I feel about coming to see her. I think about this carefully, trying to identify the fizzing adrenaline rush inside of me. “Excited,” I reply, then worry she will think me unhinged.

“And why is that?” she asks, her face unchanging.

“Because this was the last place I saw Matt. It feels like I am returning to him … although I know I’m not,” I add, certain she must think me mad. “I guess I’m excited to talk about him. Glad to be doing something.”

I feel that painful ache in my throat, of everything broken held so tightly. “I can’t bear this pain. I need to know how long it will feel like this. I miss him.” That’s all it takes for me to dissolve into tears.

There is no judgment from Wendy. No rules. Nothing off limits in our roaming conversations. As I discover in the coming months, sitting in this room with this woman, there is never any judgment, only compassion and a kind ear. Wendy gives me a safe place to explore everything Matt is and was to me, a space where I can crack open the dark chrysalis of grief. I think about her job title. Forensic counsellor. I like that. She allows me to examine the substance of my grief. Not just the macro experience of loss but all the tiny micro details I need to pore over. And afterwards, when I step out through the sliding doors of that building, I feel a lightness in my body that wasn’t there on walking in.

Days and months pass in lonely, blunt-edged monotony, a low, breathless panic beating in my chest. I try to return to my novel, but my brain is treacle. I don’t know if it’s single-parent exhaustion or grief, or if there is something physically wrong with me, but the focus required to plot fiction feels beyond me. I have no capacity for creativity or imagination. “No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear,” writes CS Lewis. I am so full of fear. For the future, for my children, that they’ll grow up holding only the faintest outline of their father.

A friend tells me about “memory jars”, how they can help grieving children access happy memories and start conversations about their lost parent. We sit down with pens and paper, and begin to talk about the things we love and remember about Matt.

My daughter remembers swooping and giggling with her dad on the round saucer swing in the park. My son recalls curling into the crook of Matt’s arm when he read him a bedtime story. I remember the special light that shone in Matt’s eyes whenever he stepped from the waves after an ocean swim. We all remember the unique kind of grumpy he could get when he was hungry. I write each memory down on a slip of paper before placing it into the jar.

“Singing Frozen songs at the top of his voice in the car.”

“He made the best yorkshire puddings.”

“He loved us … and we loved him,” my daughter says.

The kids, needing sudden escape from the emotion, race outside. I can hear them squealing and laughing in the courtyard, on the edge of meltdown. It is heartbreaking to reduce the love of your life and the father of your children to fragments of memories scrawled on to pieces of paper, but it feels important. They remind us that he existed and the love was real. I turn the jar under the light, scraps of folded paper trapped in glass. How can it ever be enough?

It’s an early spring day when I take the kids to the beach, a gentle bay with a dappled park, a shark net and tapering cliffs that curve to embrace the thin crescent of sand. It has been chosen carefully. No surf. No swell. No obvious signs of danger. We lay our towels on the sand, unpack fruit and water, buckets and spades, before the kids make a break for freedom.

“Wait! Sunscreen! Hats!”

My son returns grudgingly and allows me to apply the necessary sunscreen, then turns and scampers along the shoreline, lost to the sensory experience of the gently lapping water. I see him stop, then run back. “I’ll put your suncream on, Mummy.” He looks worried, and I hate this new responsibility he bears.

Friends arrive. We drink coffee and watch the children dig tunnels in the sand. Go for a swim, Han. It’ll do you good. I hear it just the way Matt used to say it – teasing, goading, slightly exasperated at my reluctance to hurl myself into the cold waves he loved. I study the water, gently undulating, turquoise. I haven’t been into the ocean since his accident, but the water looks enticing, hardly foreboding.

Fine, I think. Have it your way.

I wade out quickly, eager to get through the chill and minimise the onslaught of emotion before diving under, my body tightening at the sensation of being enveloped. Not thinking. Just doing. Losing myself in movement.

A little way out, I stop and float on my back. Blue below me and blue above me. My skin has cooled enough to feel the water like an embrace. I let go and for a moment it’s as if I am not being held by the water but by Matt. I feel him, right there with me, the warmth and pressure of him, and it is the strangest, most unearthly feeling.

Settled there, I find the perfect, fleeting glimpse of him from another time, another beach. Shaved head, broad shoulders tapering to a slim waist, feet planted in the sand and arms folded. He is sun-speckled and his beard – longer in the holidays – is salt-crusted and scratchy. I notice how, even in this memory, his eyes don’t leave the sea. Whenever I think of Matt by the ocean, it is always like this. Turned away from me, his gaze fixed on the waves he was so drawn to.

More and more, I find myself thinking about Matt’s last moments. Not so much the actual sequence of events now, but the experience of them. The sensation. The decision, turning to paddle, feeling the wave lifting his board. The surge of the water. The snap of his leg rope, the surfboard going in one direction as the rip took him in the other. The wash of water. The scrape of rocks.

I think he must have had hope; he was a hopeful man. The hope of pulling himself out. The hope of survival, until that last wave, rushing at him, pushing him forwards. The cliff rising up. A churn of salt and sunlight – a final letting go to blackness.

I hope it was peaceful.

I hope he didn’t know he was about to die.

I hope he knew we were with him, holding his hand in that moment, loving him. Always.

It is Wendy who tells me, nearly two years later, that an inquest will be held. She explains it is not about pointing fingers or finding fault, but to see if things could be done differently in the future. She adds, gently, that as Matt’s death was so high‑profile and in such a popular beauty spot, it is deemed to be “in the public interest”. Such a jarring phrase for something that feels so intensely private, but I nod. The last thing I could bear is for another family to endure a loss like ours and to know there was a chance it could have been prevented.

For two days, over and over, the fast and treacherous chain of events leading to Matt’s death is relayed. The facts are given, all carefully gathered and noted by the coroner, until the last witness steps down from the box and the coroner closes the proceedings and withdraws to consider all the evidence.

In the more peaceful days that follow, I retreat to the coast. I find myself thinking more and more about acceptance. The formal procedure seems to have lifted something in my being. I feel calmer and more balanced. I know he is gone. I know my life is transformed.

But can there ever be a final stage to grief? I’m not sure there can. The pendulum keeps swinging back and forth, though with less sickening ferocity. And the pain still rises frequently, as consistently as the tides, the absence of Matt a deep ache. What feels different is how I hold myself, the pain more often tucked away inside, less obvious to others. The grief is a weight I hold almost sacred now, my body developing the muscle to carry it.

I realise that I have been looking at the concept of acceptance all wrong. It is not about rightness. There will never be anything right about Matt’s death. No, acceptance is allowing it to be, whatever it is. A letting go of the need for things to be different. Acceptance is seeing a new path open up before you. Not the one you thought you’d be taking. Acceptance is seeing this new path winding ahead of you and finding the strength to put first one foot on it, then the other.

I ready the house for sale, our belongings for the move ahead. Sifting through our life’s possessions is not an easy process, but it is the last hours in the house that are most painful. Wandering alone for the very last time, I revisit the empty rooms, my footsteps echoing strangely through the space. I look out at the Japanese maple we planted, new purple-green leaves shimmering in the morning light. I let my hand trail up the polished wooden banister, take the creaking steps to the first floor. It’s all so familiar – so touched by us. I know it almost as well as my own skin.

I sit on the floor in my son’s room by the window and let the tears fall. I think of all the moments that have made up our lives here. Big and small. Joyful and painful. Through the windowpane I can see the spire of the church across the road. I remember noticing it the first time Matt and I looked around the house. I think of the number of times we tiptoed into this room to check on our sleeping boy. To retrieve a fallen toy. To tuck his small body beneath a sheet. Time breaks my heart. I wonder what of ourselves we will leave behind. A lost note, fallen down the back of the mantelpiece? A stray marble caught between the cracks of the floorboards? Or perhaps just the lingering of feeling – of lives bound by love and loss – of the simplicity of our everyday, echoing in these empty rooms.

Our story here has ended.

I thank the house. I lock the door. I leave.

Golden hour is settling over Tamarama, the sun sliding low on to the hill behind the beach. I’ve been here a while, traversing a decade of grief, honouring and assessing the shifting weight of our loss. With time and patience, I have returned to writing, found solace in books and reading. Slowly, I have relearned the world, restitched my heart.

Down at the tideline, I step into the shallows, the water washing the sand from my skin. It’s cold, but my feet are planted. Steady. I can breathe, my chest no longer tight and pained. These waves will not topple me today.

I know now that grief will never leave me. It will always be a part of me, just like the love it stems from. The shift comes in wanting to embrace it – to own it. And in the embrace, in pulling it close and examining it, the grief has shifted from something ugly and unthinkable to something softer, more akin to love than pain. So when I hear a song on the radio that reminds me of Matt, I can smile now and offer up my silent thank you.

The waves still come, yet we carry on, living lives illuminated by wonder and grief, the duet of both. I think of those on the path, a little behind me. Am I brave enough to share my writing in comfort and solidarity?

The surfers are still out, straddling their boards as the waves barrel in, occasionally chasing one down to the shore. I know everything has its time and that one day I, too, shall be called upon to take my place in the lineup, but as I stand here in this golden hour, facing the horizon, thinking about this ocean and that day, and all the days that came before, and all the impossible, joyous, wretched, beautiful ones lived since, I feel only gratitude to be here, holding this love and this pain.

You will survive your greatest loss.

You will be altered, but you will survive.

Listen to the breathings of your heart. They will show you the way.

This is an edited extract from An Ocean and a Day by Hannah Richell, published by Bedford Square at £16.99 in the UK and by HarperCollins in Australia. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Jumpy bond markets make it clear: Trump risks driving US into debt crisis

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 10:53:53 GMT

Treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s attempt to calm bond markets is a sign of weakness not strength

“Look, there’s nothing magic about that $40tn number,” the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, told CNBC insouciantly last week, as the country’s debt mountain surpassed another bleak record.

Yet Bessent’s decision to intervene in government bond markets in an effort to combat soaring yields belied his studied calm in TV interviews – and reignited fears the US may be on the road to a debt crisis.

Half a lifetime ago, in 1992, Bessent cut his teeth in markets shorting the pound alongside George Soros in the chaos that led up to Black Wednesday, when the UK plunged out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.

Today he is on the other side of the tussle between policymakers and markets. When the US Treasury intervened to help prop up the Japanese yen earlier this month – crucially by selling euros, not the US dollar – it was widely read as a sign of weakness.

Japan is a mega holder of US treasuries, and it looked as though the Trump administration was fretting that Tokyo might be preparing to dump a chunk of them to buy yen – potentially pushing up the yield, or interest rate.

The US Treasury’s announcement that Japan would in future be able to use a little-known facility called the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility, effectively to borrow against its treasury holdings without having to sell them, was read as another sign of concern.

As the economist Barry Eichengreen wrote in the FT at the time: “The bottom line is that Washington, fearing the consequences for US financial markets, is reluctant to see foreign central banks use their dollar reserves. This is telling us that the dollar is not the attractive reserve currency it once was.”

In last week’s fresh intervention Bessent promised to double the rate at which the Treasury woul buy up the longest-dated bonds – hoping to massage the yield downwards.

It was the clearest sign yet of anxiety in Washington about a sell-off that has pushed up yields on 30-year government bonds to levels last seen before the global financial crisis in 2008.

There are several, overlapping reasons for the bond market sell-off. One is inflation. Treasuries, which pay a fixed amount each year, are in part a bet on the future value of money – with higher inflation eroding the real value of those payments.

With the Iran conflict slipping towards a forever war, keeping oil prices elevated, and amid concerns about the new Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh’s willingness to raise interest rates, investors are fretting more about future inflation.

Another reason lies in the extraordinary AI investment boom. Tech giants have been funding the buildout of vast datacentres by issuing a wall of corporate debt.

Debt issuance by the “hyperscaler” AI companies is already $219bn (£160.5bn) so far this year, according to analysis by JP Morgan – potentially offering investors an alternative to treasuries and crowding out public debt.

Third, and most worrying, is the gnawing sense that despite continued robust economic growth, the US is not the rock-solid creditor it once was.

US public debt has exploded in recent years, smashing through every forecast. It lurched higher after the financial crisis and took another leg up during the Covid pandemic. It has continued to surge in Donald Trump’s second term, as tax cuts have been unmatched either by tariff revenue – some of which is now being repaid – or by spending cuts from Elon Musk’s short-lived Department of Government Efficiency.

Without radical policy change, for which there seems little appetite on Capitol Hill, the independent Congressional Budget Office expects US government debt to rise from 100% of GDP today to 175% in 30 years’ time.

Sign up to Business Today

after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, with his unwinnable war in the Middle East, capricious tariff regime and penchant for self-enrichment on an epic scale, Trump is turning the US into an increasingly unpredictable player in the global economy. Instead of the guarantor of rules-based markets and open global trade routes, the US has become a source of uncertainty and chaos.

As Adam Posen of the Peterson Institute for International Economics put it in a recent piece: “The entire world is now doing business, investing, and trying to make a living in the post-American world economy.”

The withdrawal was largely a deliberate decision by Trump’s Maga crew, who felt the US was shouldering too many of the running costs of the geopolitical order.

Yet it was partly this role as the anchor of the global economy, with treasuries the quintessential safe haven asset, that prevented the logic of runaway deficits and spiralling debt from hitting home.

By contrast, Bessent’s panicky intervention last week smacked of rising anxiety about how markets now view the US fiscal position.

Far from drawing a line under the bond rout, 30-year yields were rising again by Friday afternoon, while at the same time the dollar was sliding fast – a cursed correlation more often associated with emerging economies.

Bessent seemed to be signalling a willingness to step in again, if 30-year yields are pulled too far above 5%. As the financial commentator Stephen Innes put it: “Once traders think they have identified a policy pain threshold, they tend to come back and test whether it is real.”

Warsh will have his moment in the spotlight at the Jackson Hole central bankers’ conference this week, but the risks are clearly growing of a self-inflicted bond market crisis – with consequences that would ripple out far beyond the US.

Mateta’s Palace dispute deepens after losing appeals to end contract early

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 10:49:06 GMT

Striker wants move and said final year of deal was invalid

29-year-old took his case to tribunal and Fifa but lost

Jean-Philippe Mateta is in dispute with Crystal Palace over the final year of his contract but failed in an attempt to have it ruled invalid by an independent Premier League tribunal and Fifa. The France striker signed a four-and-a-half-year contract when he joined permanently from Mainz in January 2022 after an initial loan, in a deal that also included the option of a 12-month extension. That was activated by Palace in 2024, with Mateta’s contract now due to expire at the end of this season.

But it is understood the 29-year-old and his representatives have disputed whether that extension was valid and took the case to an independent tribunal under Premier League regulations last season. Official confirmation of the outcome has not been disclosed, although Palace insist Mateta’s contract remains binding and he played in their defeat at Everton on Saturday. Fifa also rejected his claim after ruling it did not have jurisdiction over the dispute. Mateta’s representative has been approached for comment.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

Mateta has been trying to force through a move from Selhurst Park for some time and it is understood he has interest from Aston Villa, who are considering whether to sell Ollie Watkins to the Saudi Arabian side Al-Hilal. Mateta failed a medical with Milan in January because of a knee problem after the Italian side had agreed a fee of around £30m and spent two months on the sidelines before returning to help Palace win the Conference League. Mateta was booed by some sections of supporters at first and is likely to get another frosty reception when Manchester City visit south London on Friday night in their first home match of the new campaign.

Meanwhile, Pierre Sage has insisted that Ismaïla Sarr will remain at the club despite strong interest from Galatasaray. The Senegal forward missed the 2-0 defeat at Everton due to what Sage described as a “pain in his groin” and Palace’s new manager dismissed reports that the 28-year-old had refused to travel to Merseyside because he wants to leave.

“We took the decision before the session with the doctor, the player, and me, to let him get treatment and do an individual session, and he will be back on Monday with us,” he said. “For the moment, we don’t want him to leave. He is under contract with us with three years to go and he will be with us on Monday.”

Palace are also braced for more interest this week in Adam Wharton and Daniel Muñoz, who has entered the final two years of his contract and has been linked with Everton, Nottingham Forest and Tottenham. They have already agreed a loan move for Chelsea’s Axel Disasi but may be forced into signing another centre back before the deadline if fears over Chadi Riad’s knee injury are proved correct.

The Moroccan, who was out for more than a year after suffering an anterior cruciate ligament injury on his second appearance for the club after joining in 2024, was carried off on a stretcher after attempting to block a cross in the second half against Everton. “I hope it will be better than we think,” said Sage. “We await the medical tests.”

Finland tried to end homelessness. What can we learn from its runaway success – and recent failures?

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 10:00:30 GMT

The Housing First policy led to the number of homeless people in Finland dropping by half. Those with firsthand experience explain why it worked

At 3.30am, Vello Senkel awoke to a knock on his door. Standing on his doorstep were his neighbours with an urgent request: “Do you have salt? We want to boil macaroni.” He acquiesced, but it turned out that salt wasn’t the only ingredient they were missing: “And do you also have macaroni?” His warm face, framed by jaw-length white hair, is at once charmed and outraged as he recounts the interaction while smoking a cigarette outside his apartment building the following morning.

Senkel, whose nickname is Velho (Finnish for wizard), is known for his proficiency in the kitchen. In his apartment, where he lives alongside 77 other formerly homeless people in a Helsinki suburb, he shows me his fully stocked freezer. From his neatly organised fridge he pulls out the jars of pickled cabbage and shrimp salad he has prepared to take to a friend’s house for lunch later.

When Senkel, 67, moved here three and a half years ago, he had been living on the streets of the Finnish capital for 10 days after being evicted from his home. Before that there had been a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder, and a devastating loss. His partner, whose photo is framed on his bookshelf, died after two years in a coma that started when her heart failed in her sleep.

After getting a place here, little by little, he started to build a new life. As well as cooking, he likes to play a bit of guitar every day. He brings his bass into the kitchen and becomes emotional as he plays along to an Estonian power ballad (he is originally from Estonia).

Having this apartment, he says, has “changed everything”. The housing unit, attractively set around a courtyard in converted student accommodation, follows the “Housing First” principle that has made Finland a world leader when it comes to tackling homelessness. The model focuses on housing as a fundamental human right rather than a reward. Temporary accommodation is seen not as a solution, but something to be avoided. All support is centred on ensuring that people have permanent homes, with everything else following from that – treatment, healthcare, employment. In the long run, advocates say, it is cheaper for the state for people to be permanently housed, taking pressure off other public services.

Another key component of Housing First for Senkel is the 24-hour staff support. Without it, his home would have been a “black hole” of loneliness. He feels understood by the staff here, he says. He has an agreement with the management that if they don’t see him for 72 hours they will get in touch.

In a communal living room-dining area, porridge and coffee are served every morning and there is a weekly community meeting to discuss any issues. Residents can volunteer to do small tasks such as cleaning shared spaces or picking up litter in return for a small fee that is transferred directly into their bank accounts. “You are precious,” a notice on the pinboard says. “We listen and support and together with you we build the life that is true to you. Your pathway, our shared journey.”

Marko Lahtela, who manages the unit where Senkel lives, says their tenants come to them from a range of homeless situations: some come directly from the street; others may have been evicted from their apartment or had problems paying rent. While housing is essential, it is by no means an instant fix. Many have substance-abuse issues or other long-term problems, which means building trust is vital. It is “more of a marathon than a sprint”, he says. There is no limit on how long you can live here. Some haven’t left since it opened in 2022; others move on to more independent forms of accommodation after just six months.

Tenants range in age from early 20s to 60s, but the most common demographic is men who are about 40. There are two apartments for married couples, but the rest are single-person homes. Usually people cover the rent, which starts at about €850 (£728) a month, using benefits or, for those who have one, a pension. The unit, which is run by the health and social care provider Rinnekodit, has lots of success stories, but the system is not perfect. Lahtela says there is not enough in place to stop people running into rental debt, which after two months can result in eviction – and for some, a return to the streets.

Since 2008, when the Housing First principle was introduced as the foundation of all homelessness policies in Finland, the country has achieved remarkable results. Between 2012 and 2023, homelessness rose across Europe, but in Finland, the number of homeless people dropped by more than half, from about 8,000 to about 3,400. Homelessness statistics are notoriously difficult to measure, but for context, the number of people experiencing homelessness in Spain rose by about a quarter between 2012 and 2022. In December, the charity Shelter reported that homelessness in England had risen 8% in the past year to a total of 382,618 – including a record number in temporary accommodation – and that rough sleeping had increased by 20% in just a year. Finland’s success has drawn attention from politicians from around the world – including Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham. In his first speech as PM, Burnham pledged to end rough sleeping in England, and he recently launched a £442m campaign to “get everyone in for Christmas”.

But is Finland still the model? Not long ago, the goal of the former Social Democrat prime minister Sanna Marin’s government to end homelessness by 2027 was seen as within reach, but in the last three years sweeping cuts to social services, healthcare and benefits by Finland’s rightwing government have seen the country’s success story go into reverse. The latest national survey, from last November, found that the number of homeless people had gone up for a second year in a row, to 4,579 people, a 20% rise on the previous year. Key factors cited by the government’s own report include rising housing and living costs, cuts to benefits and more cases of substance abuse and mental health problems. Homelessness has especially increased among women, under-25s and people with non-Finnish backgrounds.

As people come through the doors for breakfast at the cosy former restaurant premises of Vailla vakinaista asuntoa ry (No Fixed Abode), an NGO founded by homeless people 40 years ago, it is striking how young many of them are. After picking up food, donated by a local conference centre, and coffee, people sit down at long tables under low hanging lights. There’s a TV on in the background.

Sitting down for breakfast, Jari Häkkinen, 57, says finding a place to live is not a problem, but finding one that will be covered by his benefits is. He is determined to keep the pensioners apartment he has found, but it is €14 over his monthly limit. “I’m fighting to get that €14 a month no matter what,” says the former construction worker.

Another visitor, who asked to be named only as Leila, joins the conversation. She has been homeless for nearly 12 years and currently lives under a nearby bridge. “They are saying [Finland is a] happy country. It is not true,” she says, referring to its reputation as the world’s happiest country. “This is the reality you see.”

No Fixed Abode serves breakfast, lunch and coffee throughout the day, and in the winter, when temperatures in Helsinki can sink to -30C, they run a night cafe where a small number of people can keep safe and warm. Visitors can also pick up new clothes and speak to peer workers for support and advice. At the moment they have about 100 visitors a day, and in the colder months the number doubles.

There is no “one size, one idea, one model, one type of support service”, says Erja Morottaja, No Fixed Abode’s head of communications. “Some people might need quite light support. And then some people need quite heavy support.”

Suski Kankaanmäki, 44, is now employed there as a peer worker, but she first came as a homeless visitor after she was evicted in 2015. For six months she spent the nights on trains and in railway stations in and around Helsinki – taking the last train to somewhere, sleeping in the station then returning to the city for morning. She then spent the best part of a year in “hidden homelessness” – cooking, cleaning and dog-walking for a friend in return for a place to sleep. It was better than sleeping outside, she says, but there was an uncomfortable power imbalance.

During that time she managed to successfully apply for an apartment, but it quickly became a “drug using centre”. Having grown up in 11 different children’s institutions, it took her time to work out how to build a stable life. She got help from social workers with managing her finances but it wasn’t until a major health scare in 2021 that her life completely turned around. The feeling of not being safe is still there, says Kankaanmäki, and she never stops being on alert, but she is positive about the future and is training to be a nurse. She wants to work at a Housing First unit.

Based on what she has seen here, Kankaanmäki is pretty certain that homelessness numbers will rise further. NGOs are being gutted and new groups, such as working people on low incomes, are becoming at risk of losing their homes. There are not enough shelter places, she says, so people are sleeping in shopping centres, stations, public toilets and Helsinki airport.

Last year, homelessness in Helsinki, which has the largest homeless population of anywhere in Finland, rose by 25% – to 979 people. The increased strain is being felt at the city-run Hietaniemenkatu service centre, one of three places offering emergency short-term accommodation – intended to be for one night, although many stay longer. Staff say they are seeing more women, particularly elderly women, and more people with jobs than before. There is a sense that the country’s most vulnerable have been left to fend for themselves. “We all came to the conclusion that it is because of the current government,” says social worker Viveca, who cannot give her last name for security reasons. “There are cuts to everything. The only place they didn’t cut from is the rich.”

Its 52 emergency housing places, with multiple beds to a room, are free of charge but in high demand. From there, residents can apply for one of its 52 temporary housing places, which are individual rooms but come with a fee of up to €14.60 a day. There is a day centre with showers, washing machines and a sauna, and access to health and housing support. There is something of a revolving-door phenomenon at the centre, however, staff say, where people keep coming back because they do not have the life skills to maintain a permanent apartment alone once they have one.

Despite the recent dip in progress on reducing homelessness, there is still much for other countries to learn from Finland. Arguably, the recent problems make it an even better case study for Burnham and others.

Burnham visited Y-Säätiö (Y-Foundation), which played a central role in the creation and implementation of Housing First, in 2019. Since then, Y-Foundation, which owns more than 19,000 homes in Finland, making it the country’s largest nonprofit landlord, has twice been to the UK to support Burnham’s Manchester homelessness programme, which was inspired by the Finnish model.

Juha Kahila, Y-Foundation’s head of international affairs, is enthusiastic about what has already been achieved. For people who have been homeless, dedicated housing units with 24-hour on-site support are not the only option. The vast majority of formerly homeless people in Finland live in “scattered housing”, he says: affordable housing among different demographic groups. During a walk around Jätkäsaari, a newly developed area of Helsinki in a former container port, he is proud of how students, elderly and low income people live alongside prime real estate and green space. Often the affordable housing looks nicer than the most expensive properties.

There are about 400,000 affordable homes in Finland (in a population of 5.6 million), constituting about 30% of the overall housing stock. When he talks about affordable housing – a term often misappropriated by property developers – he is referring to the real construction costs of a property with no profit for anyone. “We have understood that the need has to be the first thing,” he says. “It is not about the quantity of the affordable homes but how you target them that makes a big difference.”

Comfort and cosiness are often cast aside as a luxury, but they are actually a key part of Finland’s successes in bringing down homelessness. If an apartment isn’t cosy, you won’t feel safe there, says Kahila, as he shows me around a building where a third of the apartments are reserved for low-income musicians. And if you don’t feel like it’s yours then it becomes a roof over your head rather than a home.

“Home is something you want to decorate, you want to spend time there. When you close the door you can … ” he pauses to take a deep breath in and out. “You can be whoever you want. It’s your safe place.”

This is how we do it: ‘Since having cancer, I’m more open – before I was straight, now I’m queer’

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 10:00:29 GMT

Following the all-clear, Kevin and Jade found a new openness in discussing sex and intimacy – and also a shared desire for exploring polyamory

How do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymously

double quotation markSince the all clear, my relationship with my sexuality has shifted a lot

I’ve been in recovery from drug addiction since I was 19, and I had cancer 10 years ago. So there have been points when sex has been important to me, and periods of abstaining and working on myself. Jade and I have been together for 11 years, and the sex was always good – not particularly kinky, just really intimate, nice sex.

I got ill after we’d been together less than a year and had to have one of my testicles removed, which put an immediate stop to any sex. Then I was in chemo, and sex wasn’t even on my mind – the whole period was incredibly traumatic. I’m eternally grateful that Jade stuck with me through it. Since then, my relationship with my sexuality has shifted a lot. I’ve become more vulnerable and open.

When Jade came back from a party and said a couple had asked her for a threesome, we were in a really good place. We were having sex multiple times a week, talking a lot, being open. We were actively looking for something fun, exciting and maybe a bit naughty to do. So when she asked how I felt about it, my reaction was, “I feel pretty good.”

We started going to parties and clubs together. The first time I saw Jade with a guy, I thought, “Oh, this is actually really nice.” We were instantly more attracted to each other. As soon as there was this little bit of spice, maybe even a threat, it gave us a boost. We found operating as a couple and seeing each other with other people easy. There was an instant uptick in the amount of sex we were having and how exciting it was.

I have scarring from the operation – all the lymph nodes were removed from one side of my groin, and there’s a big scar where they removed the testicle on the other side, so that was a massive blow in terms of confidence and self-image. But since exploring polyamory, I’m a far more confident person than I was before. I feel better than I ever have in my life. My relationship to my own sexuality, confidence and body is miles ahead of where it was. If you’d asked me three years ago, I would have said I was straight. I now identify as queer.

If you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.

Please include your country's area code if outside of the UK.

Please include your country's area code if outside of the UK.

double quotation markNow we date and have sex solo. It’s been a very mutual exploration

Kevin was diagnosed with cancer early on and that obviously shapes things. We had so many challenges that sex wasn’t at the forefront of my mind. But since then we found our feet, and have both been keen to explore new things.

We were monogamous for eight years, but decided to open things up three years ago. Some people do it to fix something in their relationship, but we were in a great space and wanted to share that and accelerate it with other people. A few years after Kevin got the all-clear, we were feeling exploratory and I had the opportunity to have a threesome at a party. I didn’t do it, but told Kevin I thought it would be fun, and he immediately said, “Right then, let’s do it.”

We started going to sex-positive parties and began playing together in group settings or with a third person. Now we date and have sex with other people solo. I sleep with men, women and everyone in between, and so does Kevin. It’s been a very mutual exploration.

I’d never really considered non‑monogamy before. There’s this assumed way of being that you accept, and then suddenly you discover all this richness available to you outside monogamy, and what it can bring to your relationship with your primary partner.

One of the main challenges is that we do things at different paces. Kevin is really open-hearted and forms quite strong, close relationships with people, which can create a bit of an imbalance. I’ve had to learn this balance between independence and togetherness between us.

For me, it feels great when both of our cups are full. We’re both getting meaningful, fun, exciting experiences independently of each other – and then also together.

Names have been changed

‘So many people say things about my appearance – it’s not normal’: Jorja Smith on burnout, body-shaming and finding freedom

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 09:00:28 GMT

Being recognised by the Brits, Grammys and Drake made the singer one of British music’s most famous names – and also left her exhausted. Now, after decompressing in her home town she returns with a record made for raving

It is a sticky, sweltering July afternoon, and I have accidentally found myself at a wake with Jorja Smith. I’m told that the pub where we have met, in the leafiest part of leafy south-west London, is usually a safe bet for an inconspicuous table. But today, sweaty black suits carrying pints drift between tables, and long queues snake round the bar.

Dressed in a simple tank top, bare-faced with her hair scraped back, Smith is waiting for me when I arrive. “I’ve been waiting for my drink for ages,” she says. “But I feel bad saying anything because, you know …”

The sombre mood doesn’t last long – in large part because Smith is effortlessly funny. When her alcohol-free sparkling wine finally arrives, she takes one sip, pauses for the waitress to disappear, then winces theatrically. “Oh,” she says. “That’s not good.” Every time we dissolve into laughter, I glance around guiltily, like we’re schoolgirls trying not to get caught talking at the back of assembly.

It’s hard to imagine a less appropriate setting in which to discuss an album made for sunburnt block parties and 2am raves. What Are the Odds, the 29-year-old’s third album, released this week, is a certified, old-fashioned ass-shaker. Made with Richard Isong – the London producer better known as P2J, whose credits include Beyoncé, Burna Boy and Tems – and featuring the likes of Wizkid and Devlin, it is a vibrant collage of Black British dance music, weaving together UK garage, funky house, 2-step and Afrobeats, into a 12-track collection that pulsates from top to bottom.

While dance music has always been threaded through Smith’s catalogue, usually in the form of a summer single – On My Mind in 2017, Little Things in 2023 – she is better known for her introspective, soulful R&B, as epitomised by her 2016 breakout single Blue Lights (which NME praised as “a fantastically introspective and clever piece of songwriting”, and had critics declaring her Amy Winehouse’s successor). This is the first time she has committed fully to the dancefloor.

“I just love dancing,” Smith shrugs. “I like going out to listen to music, a lot of my friends are DJs. It’d be nice to hear more of my stuff when I’m outside.”

The genesis of this album was different to her previous records. Her Mercury prize-nominated debut album, Lost & Found, emerged because she felt it was time to make an album. Its successor, Falling Or Flying, arrived because she felt she “needed” a second one. What Are the Odds was made almost accidentally, which is perhaps why it feels so light on its feet.

After making the effervescent club single Little Things with P2J, the pair initially planned to write a dance EP. But the songs kept coming, and the project outgrew itself. “We went through nine songs in the first two days,” Smith says, her eyes widening again at the memory. “I turned up to the studio and he’d made all this music from our conversations. I left and went straight to my label and said: ‘I think this is an album, not an EP. This is serious.’ I’m so excited about it.”

The album may be created for the dancefloor, but its emotional resonance remains unmistakably Smith. For Life mourns losing a friend to addiction; Young Heart is a love letter to Smith’s younger self; The Way It Was meditates on the end of a friendship. “If you just sang the songs with keys or piano,” she says, “they’d all probably be quite sad.”

It is tempting to read What Are the Odds as a comeback album. In the weeks before its release, various headlines have announced Smith’s “return”. When I begin to ask her about this supposed break, she cuts in incredulously. “People keep saying, ‘Oh, you’re back!’ What do you mean, back? I’ve been on tour since 2017. When people say that, I’m like … [you should] check my calendar! People are likely talking about a ‘comeback’,” she says, “because I’m back on social media. I take breaks, and I’m not always out at events and things.”

It’s an astute observation, and one that cuts to the heart of Smith’s unconventional relationship with celebrity. Since Blue Lights announced her arrival as an 18-year-old in 2016, she has become one of British music’s defining voices: a Mercury and Grammy nominee, double Brit award winner, and a featured artist capable of surfacing everywhere from Drake’s More Life to Burna Boy’s African Giant. Yet, she has never cultivated the kind of omnipresent celebrity that feels almost compulsory in the social media age, where visibility seems synonymous with existence. There are no carefully choreographed glimpses into her morning routine, no sense that her life exists to be consumed. Smith has clearly never been especially interested in that side of the bargain.

“I never wanted to be famous,” she says. “I’ve always been quite private. I just wanted to put music out as a teenager and see what happened. I feel really lucky that I’ve got such an amazing fanbase and people really show me love, but fame was never the goal.”

The tension, of course, is that success increasingly lives or dies by the algorithm. The defining British stars of recent years – PinkPantheress, Raye, Lola Young – have all been, in some part, forged in the fires of TikTok. Does Smith ever feel pressure to play that game? “Yeah definitely,” she says. “But, luckily, I’ve got a sick team, and we come up with ideas that we can do that are still me. I don’t want to be here doing trends – you’re not going to catch me doing TikTok dances or any of that stuff.”

Her inclination to privacy also stems from growing up under an unusually unforgiving spotlight. Smith first found an audience by uploading covers to YouTube, recorded from her bedroom in Walsall. Aged 15, she signed with a manager, and began making regular trips to London for songwriting sessions. After finishing her A-levels, she moved to the capital full-time, working shifts in a cafe while trying to carve out a career in music.

Blue Lights, which hauntingly paired Smith’s mellifluous voice with lyrics about police profiling and urban anxiety, landed on SoundCloud in 2016, instantly establishing her as one of the most compelling new voices in British music. The following year, Drake invited her on to his blockbuster playlist, More Life, exposing her to millions of listeners around the world.

Alongside the acclaim, though, came another kind of attention. Almost overnight, Smith became a symbol of a modern beauty ideal, often uncomfortably sexualised before she had properly entered adulthood. For years, the conversation around Jorja Smith the musician existed alongside another conversation entirely, one that Smith had no control over: that of Jorja Smith the face, Jorja Smith the body. “It’s not normal,” she says, reflecting on that time. “Growing up and having so many people having something to say about your appearance.”

The internet, as it tends to do, eventually turned. In the run-up to the release of Falling Or Flying in 2023, every online photo or video seemed to invite commentary on her weight. At one point, the phrase “Jorja Smith weight gain” trended on X for two days. It is something she brings up without prompting.

“It was difficult. I’d be reading things like: ‘What happened to her?’ Or, ‘She’s let herself go.’” She trails off. “It really knocks your confidence.”

On one occasion, she couldn’t resist replying. “Some blog page”– she waves away the name – “had put two photos side by side, like a before and after. I just commented: ‘What the hell, guys? I’m literally 18 in that picture. Why are you doing that?’” She shrugs. “People are so quick. They love you, then they hate you.”

Sign up to The Guide

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

after newsletter promotion

What made that period particularly disorientating, she says, was that the public narrative bore almost no resemblance to reality; at the very moment strangers were dissecting her body online, she felt healthier than ever.

“I’d actually started eating properly,” she says. “Before that, I’d be so busy I’d skip meals, wake up late, I was running every day, obsessively. It was the first time I actually felt healthy, and then people wanted to criticise me? It was a proper headfuck because I was thinking: Wait … can I do anything right?”

For a while, she stopped wanting to do photoshoots, or even go outside for fear of being photographed. “I sort of went into myself,” she says. “I felt like no one could really understand what I was going through.” Her coping mechanisms, she says, are to go for a walk or to the gym, though she catches herself revealing how fragile that equilibrium can still be.

Sometimes she’ll still “see comments … and start thinking: Maybe they’re right?” She stops herself mid-thought. “Oh my God,” she says, laughing in disbelief. “Even me saying that now is crazy. Because they’re just random people!

“But I have my days,” she continues. “I was talking to my mum about it the other day, and she was like: ‘At least they’re not saying you sound shit!’”

One of the ways she’s protected herself is by stepping away from those online platforms. She no longer runs her own social media – her team posts on Instagram, and she only keeps the app to message artists and friends. She hasn’t been on X in years, and never goes looking for commentary about herself.

Part of that self-reclamation meant physically removing herself, too. In 2023, after years in London, she moved back to Walsall – an unusual move for an artist at the height of their career. “I just needed a reset,” she says. “I thought: Let me move back home, touch some grass, see some trees.” London, she says, had become tangled up with the pressures of her career. This City, one of the tracks on What Are the Odds, explores her love-hate relationship with the capital. “Anything negative that happened, I kind of put London as the culprit,” she says. “I was like: ‘I hate this place. I need to get out.’” Distance has since softened London’s hard edges, and today, she divides her time between the West Midlands and the capital: “I’m feeling the buzz of what this place has to offer again, instead of feeling as if I have to wear armour all the time.”

She is fiercely protective, too, of the place she comes from. In an industry so often centred on London, she is keen to keep reminding people that remarkable artists also emerge from elsewhere. “People forget I’m not from London,” she laughs. “And I’m not from Birmingham, either!” In September, Smith will return to Walsall for a home town show at Walsall Arena, a school turned community arts space she used to visit as a girl. Part of Spotify’s Hometown Billboard campaign, the bill doubles as a showcase of local talent: childhood friend Wesley Joseph, with whom she released the single July this year, supports, alongside the Blue Lights Choir she founded to create opportunities for young people in the town. “I hope it’s a moment that inspires the next generation to believe that big things really can come from Walsall,” she says.

These days, when she isn’t working, she is trying to build a life that exists beyond music. She walks, cooks and has rediscovered running. “I’ve signed up for the London marathon next year,” she says. “I wanted a goal, and I watched everyone finishing it this year and thought: That’s such a sick thing to do.”

Despite her instinct to retreat from the spotlight, Smith is also consciously trying to step back into the world. Recently, she was on the phone with a friend back home when she mentioned turning down an invitation to a Vogue party. Her friend wouldn’t let it slide. “She was like, ‘Go! Not everyone gets invited to these things. You only live once. If you keep turning everything down, you’re going to be 70 and have zero stories of fun nights out because you never went anywhere!’” she laughs.

Outside, the heat hasn’t lifted. Mourners are still in the beer garden. As she gets up to leave, Smith pulls a cap low over her face and slides on a pair of oversized sunglasses. Until that moment, it has been surprisingly easy to forget that she is famous at all.

“It’s all about finding that balance,” she says, smiling as she stands. “But I’m feeling good. I’m starting to feel like my younger self again.”

What Are the Odds is out now on FAMM. Jorja Smith performs at Walsall Arena on 6 September.
