When I first moved to Glasgow from India, I felt welcomed and included. Now I just feel scrutinised

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 09:00:28 GMT

The city that used to be full of kind strangers is increasingly witnessing racist disorder. I hope it can find its way back to its old friendliness

Scottish people have always been known for their friendliness. “We’re not like the south of us,” they say, referring to England. The official slogan of Scotland’s largest city, “People make Glasgow”, appears everywhere – on T-shirts, buildings, bus stops and mugs. And when I first moved to Scotland from India in 2018, I was immediately welcomed by kind strangers and helpful neighbours. People showed curiosity, rather than intrusiveness. They respected queues; told me I fit right in. Music, art and cultural events were considered inclusive spaces in the city, with calls for diversity, creativity, inclusion – all the good things.

As an outsider, this was a dream come true: to be myself, to be alone, to have brotherhood and a community. It was life-changing. I could do whatever I wanted, wear whatever I wanted, walk by myself at night, even. That is a luxury, especially for a woman. But something has changed, particularly after Covid, a global recession and years of austerity. Now, I watch the steady rise of far-right, fringe violence and I feel a special scrutiny upon me.

In June, we saw disorder and racists assaults in Glasgow as hundreds of masked protesters marched through the streets. Asian business owners were harassed and people were attacked – according to the police – “because of the colour of their skin”. Later that month, a man was charged with attempted murder after allegedly attacking men leaving a mosque in Edinburgh. A video appeared to show him shouting that he was “protecting the country”. In July, a delivery driver was assaulted after anti-immigration protesters, many of them masked, some shouting racist abuse, once again “rampaged” through Glasgow. We have seen mosques defaced with “hate graffiti” – one is attacked in Britain every five days, according to new data. We’ve heard a speaker at a protest outside an asylum hotel in Falkirk calling for a crowd to “keep Britain white”. There have been activists outside the Scottish parliament staging fascist-style demonstrations. It goes to show top-down propaganda funnels to real-life incidents.

I feel this increasing hostility personally, too. Strangers point-blank question me about my nationality, accent, religion or clothes. A stranger once told me that my accent was weird. An acquaintance said immigrants were taking away jobs from locals, after I told them I was struggling to find work despite being qualified. People jump queues and are quickly confrontational. The “outsiders” that Glasgow loved and accepted have seemingly become the subject of derision and suspicion.

I find people staring at me, head to toe, for an uncomfortably long time. A customer in a Govan pub casually remarked aloud that immigrants are criminals and that we “need to go back”. An old lady on a bus interrupted me and my very white, very British husband to tell us to stop talking the way we were talking. Was it because we’re clearly an interracial couple? Is it because we categorically don’t sound like the locals? I’ll never know, but it’s gnawing now at the back of my mind when it never would have a few short years ago.

Colleagues who have been here since the 1980s and earlier tell me that racist violence has happened in Scotland before, but this time it feels different. We’re afraid to step out now. There’s a clear, marked shift in our levels of nervousness. It is certainly more imminent, more immediate – closer to home.

I blame a combination of factors for this unsettling change: the high cost of living, the worsening climate crisis and the rightwing agenda of some of the mainstream media have all increased resentment and suspicion of one’s neighbours. Then, during the Covid-19 pandemic, many people felt that they had been left alone. That the state wasn’t taking care of them as a democracy is supposed to do.

Even a global health emergency, it seemed, couldn’t make for a better world. Instead of a fairer, more equal or accessible society, we have extreme wealth inequality that is persistent and increasing. And it doesn’t help that inflammatory posts are favoured by social-media algorithms. All of this creates a tinderbox in which people of colour understandably feel afraid.

after newsletter promotion

Many places, including Leith and Glasgow, held anti-racist, pro-immigrant, pro-humanity rallies days after the racist incidents occurred. People carried signs reading: “Racism is weird, have you tried hobbies?”; “Migrants make the NHS”; “Hate has no home”. They made passionate speeches about standing up to bigotry. But is that enough? While it was heartwarming to see thousands of people come out, uniting for diversity, inclusion and multiculturalism, it won’t stop a growing hatred and fear of people like me. And so every time I’m out in public now, my stress levels go up. Am I safe alone? What is my exit strategy? Can I even afford to be angry? Others feel it, too.

I understand why many British people feel overlooked and badly done by – it’s true that Britain is unequal and unfair. But I wish that the media would not validate people’s inherent biases and misconceptions, nor politicians legitimise their worst sentiments by calling for reactions like “pure, cold rage”. It is easy to whip up hatred between neighbours, but systematic hatred and divisiveness can take decades to undo. The only individuals who benefit from scapegoating are the powerful.

We have to say “no” to this normalisation of bigotry, violence and othering. We have to focus on the living conditions and inequality we all share. We need to remember we have more in common with each other than with any billionaire. We must remember that the real blame lies with the system that wants us divided. Talk to real people who look and sound different from you. You’ll realise we’re all humans. We can do better than this.

Sanghmitra Singh is a human rights lawyer and a writer

‘The country of my birth has lost its heart’: Miriam Margolyes on how to fix broken Britain

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 05:00:24 GMT

At 85, the actor has lived through much political upheaval. But, she writes, today’s hostile times feel like ‘the worst yet’. She reflects on her journey from teenage Tory to full-throated leftist – and says there’s still time to save the nation from the bad guys

A funny thing happened on the way to 2026: I got old and the world turned nasty. It happened very quickly and it’s to do with politics (the world) and pelvic floor weakness (mine). It’s strange being this old. Sometimes when I look in the mirror, it’s a shock to see wrinkles and grey hair, because inside I am still that naughty Oxford High School girl, risking detention just for the joy of entertaining her friends. People assume that with great age comes great wisdom, but actually we remain who we have always been, only more so, and we need to make our peace with that and with each other.

The Britain I grew up in, though – that feels almost unrecognisable, and everyone I speak to says the same thing. The historian Eric Hobsbawm, whom I knew and loved, argued that people invent the past they want for their own purposes – that the real past was quite different: “Today is the great age of historical mythology.” He’s right, but that past is still the safe haven I’d like to return to. People feel adrift, they don’t understand or feel a connection to the place they thought they knew.

Now at 85, I look around at my remaining friends and at my unique relationship with a woman of different qualities but luckily the same politics. In many ways I’m having the time of my life: I’ve never been richer or more in demand. And yet my heart is heavy with foreboding …

My postwar generation lived through the rise and fall of many things: the Berlin Wall, Winston Churchill, the European Union, the NHS, the Beatles, Profumo, Elizabeth II, the Great Train Robbery, the pill, the IRA, Margaret Thatcher, the Falklands war, Black Monday and Grenfell, heart transplants, driverless cars, Brexit, the Covid-19 pandemic. But this feels the worst time yet.

The things we took for granted – free speech, the Post Office, our local bank, even the home telephone – are disappearing. The US is an enemy. Evil oligarchs and their influence stalk the world, my world, your world. In recent times, the archbishop of Canterbury resigned and north London Jews are afraid to wear a Magen David (Shield or Star of David) necklace outside their homes for fear of being attacked. You’re brave to open your mouth these days. Indeed, many have demanded I keep mine shut. But I can’t. The present has become threatening, hostile and unwelcoming to us – much as our shores must feel to asylum seekers, as they scramble for a foothold in our United Kingdom. It also feels as though the country of my birth has lost its heart. How did we get here?

Now, I’m not usually one to tell jokes. Like my farts, my humour is largely unscripted. I love making people laugh, but at heart I’m a serious person, not just a funny little wobbly thing. I’m not a fan of jokes at the expense of others, those that are trite and mean and racist. But I’ve discovered that, in terms of the relationships and tensions between our nations, sometimes jokes go straight to the jugular.

An Englishman is driving down a country road in Wales and realises he’s lost his way. He spots a local and pulls up alongside. “Dai! Dai!” he calls out in a lordly English accent, “which way is it to Cardiff ?” The Welshman eyes him up and down: “Just a minute now, how did you know my name was Dai?” The Englishman says, “I guessed, man! I guessed!” “Well, better guess your way to bloody Cardiff then, hadn’t you!”

An Irishman, a Scotsman, a Welshman and an Englishman are on a plane which is going down and there is only one parachute. The Scotsman says, “Scotland will remember me,” and jumps out to his death. The Welshman says, “Wales will remember me,” and jumps to his death. The Irishman says, “Ireland will remember me,” and pushes the Englishman out of the plane.

I don’t think the English understand why their Welsh, Scottish and Irish neighbours loathe them so much. Like the Englishman in the first joke, they’re rather baffled by the hostility, while prolonging it with their arrogant attitudes. This behaviour is, of course, not isolated to them. It turns out that we Brits are even less popular abroad than we are with each other. The history of the British Isles is full of painful moments and terrible decisions. And we need to face those. It’s much easier to look away from bad things that happened and, as with a fart, hope no one noticed. (Spoiler: everyone noticed.) Like every multinational corporation, Great Britain plc has done a lot of harm in its long life. The choice of red to represent the British empire on the global map feels entirely apt. Take these unloving nicknames that zoom in on our annoyingness, inability to wear suncream and/or stop swearing:

Brittunculi This one’s the oldest: it was found on a tablet at the Roman fort of Vindolanda on Hadrian’s Wall, a Latin term showing exasperation and meaning “wretched little Brits”.

Poms This is what the Australians and New Zealanders call us. There are various theories: the late journalist Alan Whicker said “Pom” was short for pomegranate, the bright red colour a new arrival turns in the sun down under. Others claim that Pommie is really “POME”, which stands for prisoner of mother England, and thus the British convicts who were transported to Botany Bay.

Rooinek or “redneck” The Boer nickname for the pale Brits, dangerously sunburnt again. Afrikaners of old had a ruder nickname for us, though – soutpiel (“salty penis”) – meaning that the Brits had one foot back home, the other in South Africa, so their penises were left to dangle in the salty ocean.

Limeys The American term, originating in the 1850s as “lime-juicer”, from the Royal Navy practice of adding lemon or lime juice to British sailors’ daily ration to ward off the scurvy that made all their teeth fall out.

Inselaffen Translating as “island monkeys”, this is the Germans’ contemptuous nickname, supposedly dating back to Darwin’s theories of evolution.

Les rosbifs “Roast beefs”; this French take is based on our fondness for a traditional Sunday roast. Historically they also called us “les goddams”, which originated in the hundred years war, referring to the typically potty-mouthed English soldiers. (So that’s where I got it from!) More recently, British tourists have been called “les fuckoffs”. Très charmant!

My point is, history has always been the propaganda of the victors, but it can lead you astray. So why not try listening to the other side of the story? Don’t fall for your own hype. It all seems heroic if you turn it into a monologue about why you were right all along, instead of facing the painful bits from which there’s no way you can come out well.

Our British history needs to reflect our mother tongue, which is a patchwork of words gathered from the different tribes and peoples who’ve made these islands home. There’s room for everyone: we all bring something to the table, whether invader or inhabitant. The French word for a fanlight or transom window is vasistas and comes from the seven years war, when the German soldiers were baffled by the newfangled windows they saw in French houses and kept asking “Was ist das?” The French word is a joke, a snooty echo of the German reactions, but it stuck.

People are always trying to fix language, but it remains on the move. The Normans tried to make England French; the English tried to ban the native Irish, Welsh and Scottish languages for “the greater common good” and then later to replace regional dialect and accents with received pronunciation. What idiots! Not only did they not succeed, but our shared language has ended up all the richer. If you can’t beat ’em, join ’em.

Now I know many of my opinions – particularly those on politics, Palestine and Potter (Harry) – have provoked outrage. But I can’t help it – I believe in telling the truth, even if it’s my truth. In this, again, I realise I do not fit the English stereotype. The English excel at obfuscation, you see; they are masters at avoiding the truth. It’s that rule of polite society again: one mustn’t rock the boat, ruffle feathers or put anyone’s nose out of joint. How absurd. Facts are facts.

My advice? If you believe someone is a liar, stay away from them. All around us, our politicians, news outlets and the media – the very people we are supposed to trust – are caught up in a relentless and divisive campaign of fearmongering and misinformation. Now it feels more crucial than ever to think for ourselves, debunk the deceits and sort the sheep from the goats.

Mummy used to say “speak as you find”, and I think that’s an excellent way of sorting out decent folk from the vile. What unites us is far greater than what divides. Don’t be afraid to learn from everything wrong in our past – and there is a lot wrong in our past – let’s just do it better in the future.

I bet you didn’t know I was once a Tory candidate. But unlike most of the former Conservatives who have swelled the ranks of the current Deform party, I have grown into maturity and swung left. My campaign was in May 1955: I was 14 and in the upper fourth at Oxford High School. A general election was being held in the country, and we decided to hold one at school. Of course I was a Conservative: my parents had always been Tories – it was all I knew. They both worshipped Winston Churchill and credited him with having saved the United Kingdom from the Nazis. For Mummy, being Tory was a key part of her upwardly mobile climb, and so it was for my father, who, despite being a passionate supporter of the newly created NHS, could not imagine following Labour. They were delighted to hear I was the Tory candidate. We don’t remember who dared to stand against me in our form, or what my policies and promises were at the hustings – I was an old-school Tory and definitely pro capital punishment, so I dread to think – but I carried the day.

after newsletter promotion

Lawrence Turner, the Tory who won the Oxford constituency when I won the upper fourth, went on to vote in favour of the Suez invasion, spend more than he earned and finally go bankrupt. Rather sweetly, one of his last parliamentary activities was presenting a petition to preserve the copyright of the words of WS Gilbert, one half of the prolific theatrical partnership Gilbert and Sullivan who created the comic operas that were the ironic soundtrack to the burgeoning British empire. Turner proved ineffectual again: he was not “the very model of a modern major-general” or even of a modern member of parliament, and copyright expired in 1961.

Right seemed self-evidently right until I was assailed on two respectable fronts. After my election success, the father of my best chum from those days, Biddy Peppin, insisted I was invited to tea. He was that unusual thing, a leftwing bank manager, and his chosen task was to turn my path into a socialist future. And then another friend, Liz Hodgkin, also invited me for dinner. The Hodgkins were academic royalty – Liz’s mother Dorothy was later to win a Nobel prize – but they were committed socialists, too. You know how sometimes you can fall in love with a whole family? Well, I did. Their dinner guests were all communists and convinced Marxists (oh, that I had the courage to be a Marxist now, but that Putin, he puts me right off) and were winsome, hugely entertaining and great storytellers. Previously I had thought of communists as grim and humourless but boy, was I wrong. And so, eventually, this lady was for turning. I made a U-turn in the direction of sanity and humanity, and have never looked back. My parents were surprised and shocked by my new politics. But had they lived to experience the full horror of the last 14 years of Conservative reign under Cameron, May, Johnson, Truss and finally Sunak, I hope they, too, would have seen the light and embraced the left.

The rise of the far right in Britain today can be traced back to a daft dyke. It depresses me to share that one of my fellow lesbians could be so silly, but the truth must be faced, and in 1923, Rotha Lintorn-Orman founded the first British fascist movement. In 1895 she was born in Kensington (where else?!) into enormous wealth. Obviously liking uniforms and women – and women in uniforms – she and a close chum originally wanted to join the Boy Scouts, but the Scouts wouldn’t have them. When the first world war broke out, she served as an ambulance driver, and was decorated for valour.

After the war, Lintorn-Orman, a passionate admirer of Mussolini, formed the British Fascisti. But other, more extreme fascist societies proliferated and soon Lintorn-Orman and her cronies were outflanked. She descended into alcoholism and drug addiction, indulging in “drunken orgies and undesirable practices”, and her organisation died. But fascism would live on – from Oswald Mosley and his Blackshirts right through to Tommy Robinson.

Now I’m old, I understand that older people like things “the way they were”. Me, too: I hate upgrades – be it in computers, in phones, in style, in my neighbours. I want what I had. And so, change (which the politicians tell us we want), I actively don’t want. Change makes me feel powerless and then I get angry and look for someone to blame. At least I know enough not to blame immigrants and asylum seekers. The mess the country’s in has got nothing to do with them, but too many of us have been bamboozled into thinking it has.

I grew up knowing I’d receive a fine education and would get a job when I left university (which was free in 1963). Fascism had had its day, we thought. More than 70 million people had died to secure our freedom. But now racism was impossible to ignore, as one by one the last vestiges of the Empire started claiming their independence. The Windrush generation came to Britain – at the government of the time’s invitation – to staff our new welfare state, believing they were wanted and would be appreciated for leaving their homes and families, but finding the promised motherland felt harsh, hostile and unwelcoming.

Taking advantage of this highly charged political climate, a new British fascist party – the National Front – was born in early 1967. The next year Enoch Powell, Conservative MP for Wolverhampton South West, made his “Rivers of Blood” speech. He posed as a brave visionary; perhaps he even believed that he was giving voice to the displaced white community of the Midlands who felt crowded out by Black and Asian immigrants.

I knew straight away what Powell wanted to achieve with the speech: to fan the flames of public dissent. His Oxford education, classical training and powers of oratory served him well. He saw the race card as the way to obtain power. It still is.

Today, a nasty little turd is floating about in our polluted waters. It has many names; one sticks out more than the others. A public schoolboy, posing as “one of the lads”; someone who thought it was funny to hiss at Jewish boys just after the second world war; someone who was given £5m to keep himself safe; someone who got German citizenship legally for his sons (his ex-wife is German) so Brexit disadvantages don’t inconvenience those close to him. There is a widespread fear that Farage (AKA the Odious Niggle) could succeed to the leadership; the kingdom is teetering on the brink of annihilation. But it’s not too late. After all, it is not the lie that passeth through the mind but the lie that sinketh in and settleth in it that doth the hurt. (Thanks, Francis Bacon.) While the bad guys seem to be winning everywhere, I’m not giving up – and neither should you.

Exhausted by but addicted to doomscrolling, sliding from one terrifying headline to another, it’s easy to forget we are all in the same unsteady boat, north or south, young or old, lower, middle and even upper class, ignoring the culprits hiding in plain sight. It’s not the foreigners, legal or illegal, who are pissing on us; it’s the billionaires who own the media and the internet and can pay the debts of the political parties they want to control, and fuck the rest of us. Well, I’m not putting up with it any longer. And neither need you. Let’s have a laugh. It’s the antidote (and all the ammunition) we need to those arseholes who forget that Britain was great before they were born – we can see right through them.

Never forget that laughter is a good medicine, ridicule and satire can change minds, and there’s always sex. Mind you, it’s a while since I enjoyed the full-throated variety, but I know it’s out there.

I refuse to be cut off from the wealth of possibilities that Britain and Ireland offer. Let’s live, have fun, learn new tastes, new words, new mastications. Build bridges, cross chasms. And before we go to the moon again, let’s reap the benefits strangers in our midst offer. It’s not their fault that things are tough. It’s ours. This is my middle finger to naysayers, Nigel Farage and everyone who says “whatever”. It’s time to be Great Britain again – or at least Better Britain. Steady the Buffs and onwards!

This is an edited extract from Miriam’s Full English by Miriam Margolyes, published by John Murray on 3 September at £25. To support the Guardian, order your copy from guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Drill, Burnham, drill? The oil basin that is a totem for Trump – and a headache for Britain’s new PM

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 05:00:23 GMT

North Sea oil, once the driving force of the UK economy, may be dwindling but it remains a symbol of prestige and a rich resource for political debate

When oil was first discovered off the north-east coast of Scotland in September 1969, industry folklore has it that the duty superintendent on the rig carefully poured it into a pickle jar commandeered from the canteen and took it back to Amoco’s Great Yarmouth office in Norfolk. There, it was emptied into an ash tray, sniffed and then set alight.

From that modest start, North Sea oil – as the huge basin of oil and gas reserves quickly became known – emerged as a driving force of the British economy and a symbol of national power and renewal as the UK emerged from the Opec oil crisis.

By 1977, the then Labour prime minister, Jim Callaghan, declared: “God has given Britain her best opportunity for 100 years in the shape of North Sea oil.” A subsequent white paper said it offered “a unique opportunity for Britain to improve her economic performance, raise her living standards, move forward to full employment, and develop a socially just society”.

A decade later, the basin became a central part of Margaret Thatcher’s political project , with its revenues approaching 10% of the UK’s total tax take at times, supporting a programme of tax cuts and privatisation.

Output peaked at the turn of the century, when the basin produced a staggering 4.4m barrels of oil equivalent a day. Aberdeen, chosen over Dundee by the fossil fuel corporations for their onshore headquarters because it had fewer links to bothersome trade unions, was booming, with offshore jobs plentiful and well paid.

Ewan Gibbs, a specialist in the history of energy in the UK at the University of Glasgow, said that as the oil began to flow, it was seized upon by politicians and the public as a symbol of British imperial might.

“At its peak, oil was associated not only with immense wealth but also with power and international prestige,” said Gibbs. “It came to embody a sense of national renewal.”

Now, those boom years are firmly in the past. The amount of economically viable oil and gas has declined rapidly in the past two decades and by 2030 the basin will produce just 15% of its peak output.

Many of the biggest oil and gas corporations have left as stocks dwindle – BP was the latest, announcing this summer an end to six decades in the basin. And the jobs are going too. During the boom years, North Sea oil directly employed about 120,000 people and supported hundreds of thousands more jobs indirectly. Data from the Office for National Statistics suggests that figure has now dropped to about 27,000 direct employees.

However, although its economic significance has waned, the idea of North Sea oil has retained a disproportionate grip on the national psyche, and – as culture wars over the climate crisis continue to be stoked by politicians and media on the right – it remains a useful symbol of sovereignty and power for some.

“Even as it declines, there is still a strong sense for many people that this is Britain’s oil, that it is bountiful and belongs to the country, and that if we don’t exploit it we are turning our back on something important,” said Gibbs.

“It is this emotional attachment, this idea that this is our oil that means, even as the area becomes less economically significant, it retains an outsized importance in the country’s imagination.”

In the run-up to the 2024 general election, the Labour party announced there would be no new exploratory licences for oil and gas in the North Sea.

It was a significant moment in the fight against climate breakdown. In 2021, the International Energy Agency had said there could be “no new investments in oil, gas and coal” if the world was to avoid the worst impacts of the climate crisis. Now, the government of one of the richest countries in the world was making it clear it was moving away from fossil fuels to focus on renewable energy.

It was also a victory for the then energy secretary, Ed Miliband. He had been making the case within Labour that a rapid transition to a cleaner energy systems would not only help tackle the climate crisis but had the potential to make the UK a “clean energy superpower” and unshackle it from the increasingly volatile fossil fuel market, creating jobs and lowering bills.

Miliband argued that the transition to a renewable future could also offer a lifeline to communities in north-east Scotland that had seen jobs and wealth disappear as the flow of oil dried up, despite hundreds of new drilling licences being awarded.

“In the 20th century through North Sea oil, Britain exported to the world,” Miliband told a speech to the Labour party conference before the 2024 general election. “In the 21st century … Britain will be an energy superpower once again, exporting clean power to the world and controlling our economic destiny. British families and businesses will never again be held to ransom by [the Russian president, Vladimir] Putin.”

But fast forward two years, and despite wars in Iran and Ukraine again highlighting the perils of dependence on a volatile fossil fuel market and an escalating climate crisis, those plans are once more at the centre of a political storm.

The leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, and the Conservative party leader, Kemi Badenoch, have called for a massive expansion of drilling in the North Sea, claiming they would reverse the ban on new licences if elected.

In a speech this year, Farage declared that the UK should be “self-sufficient in gas”. Badenoch followed with the promise of a growing UK oil and gas industry that would “ensure our energy security for generations to come”. .

Donald Trump is also a fan of a UK version of “drill, baby, drill” in the North Sea. In one of several interventions on the subject, he claimed the basin was “one of the greatest reserves anywhere in the world … with 500 years of oil and gas reserves left”.

Such statements have left climate experts, geologists and energy specialists scratching their heads.

Steve Pye, a professor of energy systems and the deputy director of the Energy Institute at University College London, said: “The North Sea basin has been in decline since 2000. There are no credible prospects of reversing this.”

But in the midst of a cost of living crisis, others are making the case for any intervention, however small, that might ease the burden on households and boost Treasury coffers. Some trade unions and parts of the Labour party are in favour of exploiting the North Sea’s existing licences, arguing they provide some jobs and bring in at least some tax revenue.

Experts, however, point out that energy prices are set globally and there is not enough oil or gas in the North Sea to have any impact, so there would be no reduction in UK bills whatever the country did.

Also, the vast majority of what is left in the North Sea is oil that overwhelmingly goes abroad to be refined and then sold on the international markets, meaning it has no impact on the UK’s energy security.

More of the gas produced in the North Sea goes to UK homes and businesses but there is less of that left, certainly not enough to make any meaningful impact on our reliance on imports. A recent study by Carbon Brief found that even if the government allowed new licences it would only make a fractional difference: gas extraction from the North Sea is forecast to drop 99% by 2050 without new licences, compared with 97% if new licences were awarded.

Conversely, the study found that the continued expansion of renewables and low-carbon technologies in the North Sea would reduce reliance on volatile gas imports much faster than allowing new drilling, with energy from new wind and solar from the latest government auction expected to produce six times more electricity by 2030 than new drilling licences would.

On employment, the campaign group Uplift points out that the number of jobs supported by the oil and gas industry has more than halved in the last decade – from 441,000 to 214,000 today – despite previous governments issuing hundreds of new licences in six separate licensing rounds.

And on tax, critics have questioned the scale of the benefit once you take into account state subsidies to oil and gas companies, which globally run into the hundreds of billions of pounds.

Others question the public appetite for fattening the profit margins of fossil fuel companies, which made a record $93bn in profit in the three months to June, while fossil fuel-driven climate disasters, including wildfires and droughts, hit Europe, the UK experienced five heatwaves this summer, and energy costs continued to rise.

In June last year, when he was still the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham backed the fossil fuel treaty, a proposed international pact on phasing out coal, oil and gas – calling it a “lifeline” that “all governments” should join.

In recent weeks, Burnham, now prime minister, has spooked many who want to see this commitment transferred to national government when he said he would take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas drilling in the North Sea and that the government could not ignore the potential resources it holds.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, who replaced Miliband as energy secretary, has expressed similar views since taking office, although previously she has spoken out about the realities of the climate crisis. With consultations on the Jackdaw and Rosebank field projects now closed, a decision from the government could come at any time.

Tessa Khan, the director at Uplift, said it was “a dangerous fantasy” to talk up the potential of North Sea oil as a fix for Britain’s problems.

“We have seen that, time and again, the arguments put forward by the fossil fuel lobby and their supporters in favour of more drilling have fallen away upon making contact with reality – from falsehoods about lowering bills to exaggerations about improving energy security. After 50 years of drilling, the fact is the UK has burned through most of its gas reserves, while most of what remains is oil that is largely exported.

“Politicians know this. Pretending otherwise for political gain, on an issue as serious as energy security, is unedifying and a betrayal of UK energy workers who urgently need a coherent plan to deliver long-term, secure jobs – which will only now come from renewables and other industries – not some pipe dream.”

At its core, Khan said, the ongoing debate was the result of an extensive lobbying campaign by the oil and gas industry for lower taxes and greater profits for shareholders and executives.

“We shouldn’t fall for it. The lesson of the past five years is clear: the best protection against global energy shocks is accelerating renewables and helping households and businesses switch to clean electricity. This is just common sense in today’s world.”

In October last year, the UK government unveiled plans for an extra 400,000 jobs in the burgeoning green economy over the next five years.

Making the announcement at the Siemens turbine factory in Hull, Miliband said the government planned to double the number of people working in green industries by 2030, with a particular focus on training those coming from fossil fuel jobs, school leavers, the unemployed, veterans and ex-offenders.

The national plan was given a cautious welcome by unions, from Unite to the GMB, which have long been pushing for a more detailed plan for how people will switch from fossil fuel to clean energy jobs.

The green economy is certainly becoming an increasingly significant part of the UK’s future. A recent report from the Confederation of British Industry found it already supported a million jobs and higher wages, with nearly half a trillion pounds of further investment in the pipeline.

This rapid growth is visible in the North Sea itself, with huge windfarms springing up across the basin. The electricity they generate accounts for about 18% of the UK’s total. Overall, in 2025, renewables provided 50.4% of the UK’s electricity, compared with 31.8% from fossil fuels.

Despite this rapid growth, there are growing concerns that any benefits from these developments are bypassing the workers and communities that need them most.

Unite and GMB, the unions representing oil and gas workers, say the transition to renewable energy is not delivering the secure long-term jobs that were promised and – to the dismay of climate activists and others within the union movement – they have been vocal about their support for more drilling in the North Sea.

Others fear the renewables sector is experiencing a repeat of mistakes made during the oil boom, when a big slice of the profits and benefits were taken by private oil companies.

Connor Watt, of Platform, which works with current and former oil workers, unions, community groups and climate activists across Scotland, said: “The three main wins from the transition to renewables should be jobs, cheaper energy and income from electricity generation that can be used to bolster public finances, to help local communities. But at the moment, despite huge renewable projects going ahead, none of those three things have materialised and people are beginning to wonder why.”

Oil and gas workers, unions and community energy groups have organised a campaign to rethink how the government is conducting the “just transition”. They are calling for a greater role for community ownership and nationalisation to stop the profits and benefits bypassing local workers and communities. They are also calling for the government to set up a community wealth fund to ensure the benefits are felt across the country.

Watt said North Sea oil had brought some local wealth and jobs but after a decades-long boom there was “no real legacy to speak of.”

Many campaigners look to Norway, where the government set up a sovereign wealth fund when it discovered oil and gas in the North Sea. It is used to safeguard the economy and fund future public spending and is now worth more than $2tn – the biggest fund of its kind in the world. Analysts say that if the UK had taken a similar approach, a UK sovereign wealth fund could be worth about £850bn now.

Watt said: “If you compare what has happened here with what Norway did with its sovereign wealth fund, which has had huge benefits for the people of that country, we did something totally different – a market-led approach which has seen the vast majority of the benefit flow into the profits of global corporations rather than local communities.

“Once again we are seeing a market-led approach [in the renewables industry], where the vast majority of benefits are simply not going to local communities. People are increasingly disillusioned after decades of economic decline. Life is getting harder and the likes of Reform are exploiting that frustration to deepen division and line the pockets of their industry backers.”

The debate about North Sea oil and gas extraction looks set to rumble on, even as its economic significance dwindles.

But for many whose lives and livelihoods are entangled with what happens there, it is a distraction from the decisions that will actually shape their future.

Watt said: “The real question policymakers and local communities must grapple with now is: can the UK capitalise on the renewable energy revolution? And if it does, will it be the workers and communities across the UK who benefit, or corporate profit margins?”

Is a French Sunday the secret to a healthier, happier life?

The Guardian Sun, 23 Aug 2026 04:00:21 GMT

The idea of being deliberately unproductive is certainly tempting. The only concern is that you might enjoy it too much ...

They know what they’re doing when it comes to kissing, toast and horns, so get ready for a French Sunday. A new theory suggests that embracing this intriguing-sounding strategy might just be the secret to life, and, more importantly, to dreading Monday less.

Apparently in France the Sabbath really is a complete day of rest; not for the French any running of errands, cleaning or batch cooking. Rather than trying to do everything, they do nothing. And the hypothesis is that the French Sunday – or le dimanche français, as nobody is calling it – is transformative, and stamps out the Sunday Scaries for good.

The idea of being deliberately unproductive is certainly tempting. It feels bold and controversial because it’s the antithesis of the modern way of life, where we cram as much as we can into every single second, all aiming to become the most efficient, effective, prolific versions of ourselves. Sacré bleu, exhausting! No wonder we’re not looking forward to climbing back on the hamster wheel on Monday; we haven’t given ourselves a break, in either sense.

A French Sunday is not a waste of a day, you’re not being slothful, you are staving off burnout and recharging. Instead of running yourself ragged trying to wring the most out of the weekend, you’re sleeping in, vegging out, relaxing, lolling, pottering, while thinking chic thoughts, or whatever. Perhaps reading a bit, although holding a book takes a lot of energy, so caution is advised.

The only potential pitfall with the French Sunday is enjoying it too much, climbing too enthusiastically on board and trying to extend it. Can’t imagine many bosses would approve a proposal to introduce a company-wide French Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday, but, you know, God loves a trier. Bonne chance with that.

Polly Hudson is a freelance writer

Infantino angers Concacaf nations by hijacking meeting in Caribbean

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 18:02:04 GMT

Gianni Infantino used opportunity to lobby for support

Fifa president was asked to stay away from CFU meeting

Gianni Infantino has risked alienating numerous Concacaf nations, whose support he is seeking in his re-election campaign, by hijacking a meeting of the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) to announce Fifa-funded development projects for the region with millions of dollars that had been delayed for months.

Multiple sources attending the CFU meeting in the Dominican Republic said many of the Concacaf members were infuriated by Infantino’s behaviour, particularly as he had been asked to stay away by their president, Victor Montagliani.

The Concacaf position echoes previous complaints about Fifa’s operations from the Jordan FA, whose president, Prince Ali bin al-Hussein, accused Infantino of bribery this month when he claimed they have not received prize money from last year’s Arab Cup due to the country’s failure to endorse the president.

Infantino appears to have seen the CFU meeting as an opportunity to lobby for election votes among Caribbean countries in the hope of causing a split within Concacaf, who have aligned with Uefa and the Asian Football Confederation in demanding his resignation after the World Cup sell-off debacle.

In a letter addressed to Infantino on Friday, Montagliani had asked the Fifa president “in the name of football to reconsider your attendance”, pointing out his presence would take the spotlight away from a regional under-14 tournament being held alongside the meeting.

Despite that entreaty, Infantino is understand to have turned up at the resort of Punta Cana with a large Fifa entourage including the secretary general, Mattias Grafström, and Elkhan Mammadov, a staunch ally who is responsible for maintaining good relations with the 211 members in his role as director of member associations.

Before making funding pledges in the CFU meeting, Infantino’s team are understood to have approached individual member associations lobbying for support. Mammadov has played a central role in attempts to keep them onside since the Fifa Forward Enterprise scandal broke and his insistent approach has caused disquiet in some quarters.

One source said the official Fifa party had attempted to portray their governance crisis as a private dispute between Infantino and Montagliani. The Canadian businessman has not commented since news of the proposed Fifa Forward Enterprise emerged, but has been widely touted in Europe as a possible contender to replace Infantino.

The pair met briefly and shook hands before the CFU meeting in an exchange captured by Infantino’s personal camera crew.

While Mexico, Grenada and St Kitts and Nevis have all broken with Concacaf and declared their support for Infantino, the majority of their 41 members are understood to back the alliance with Uefa advocated by Montagliani.

The Uefa/Concacaf pact extends beyond attempts to unseat Infantino, with the two confederations in talks about setting up a joint Nations League in 2028 that could develop further into a new global competition.

Fifa’s official website published an article 24 hours after the meeting in which Infantino claimed to have received a warm welcome, although he conceded that alternative options were expressed.

“I received a very, very warm welcome here in the Dominican Republic,” Infantino said. “It’s important to engage, to have a dialogue, to express views and opinions – a lot [has] been happening in the last few weeks and it’s important that you hear, you listen and you’re able to, also, express what your feelings are.”

I’m known as The Black Farmer because there are so few of us in the UK. It’s one of the ways farming must change

The Guardian Sat, 22 Aug 2026 08:00:57 GMT

Running a farm is tough – TV’s Clarkson’s Farm shows that – but I know many minorities would love the chance. And we would all benefit

Who’d be a farmer? Clarkson’s Farm on Amazon is great entertainment but it also gives some indication of the stresses and challenges behind the farm gate. Would anyone who lacked the significant alternative income that Clarkson is lucky to have want that? Well, actually, yes.

I’m an entrepreneur who owns a farm, as opposed to hands-on running the small one I bought 25 years ago, but as I look around the industry, I’m struck by a significant fact: the very reason I can be known as the Black Farmer is because I am such a rarity that it makes me readily identifiable.

Because of what I do, people – many of them British minorities – often ask me how they can be farmers, how they can secure some land and set up for themselves. Don’t be surprised at that: among Britain’s minorities, millions have rural origins in lands abroad. It is a mistake to see people of colour as intrinsically urban – my own origins are in rural Jamaica. But when they ask me, I can’t really help them. There is no obvious route for them to follow, and there is precious little land they could possibly farm. This is the reality. In 2025, when Defra completed its most recent survey of principal farmers and holders in England, it found 99.7% of those who responded self-described as white.

I’m aware of the pitfall here. I know the danger these days of wanting to talk about diversity and being dismissed as woke. I’m hardly woke: in 2010 I fought a rural seat for the Conservatives. But in any other industry, that figure, 99.7%, would prompt some questions.

Here are the problems. If you are black or Asian or a kid from another minority in London, or Manchester, or Birmingham or Newcastle, where do you start? Your parents don’t own even an acre of land. You don’t have the network, or the knowledge that comes from growing up within or adjacent to a farming family and a farming community.

There is the ongoing and emotive debate about inheritance tax and whether farms should so easily be passed down from generation to generation. I’m among those who celebrate the families that have worked the same land year after year, decade after decade. That brings a knowledge and continuity essential to rural communities and our food supply. But as well as inheritance, we have to think about entry. People cannot resolve to make that commitment if they cannot see a way in.

How could that be different? Think about who owns the land. The National Trust, for example, is the country’s largest farm-owner, with more than 1,300 tenant farmers. Think about the Duchy of Cornwall, the crown estate, the Church of England. Universities and local authorities also control large tracts of land. There are people and institutions that could administer properly controlled programmes to allow those from non-traditional farming backgrounds to have a go. They could create starter farms and offer affordable tenancies. They could provide mentoring, pairing experienced farmers with ambitious newcomers, and give access to equipment. Maybe there could be targeted apprenticeships, allowing people to learn the ropes on someone else’s farm – a process that may lead to them owning their own farm. One might cite 28-year-old Kaleb Cooper on Clarkson’s farm, although in that case it is clearly the younger man teaching the older how it is done.

The supermarkets could play a role, as they wield enormous influence over British food and how it is produced. Why can’t they create routes for a new generation of growers, providing a sure path for produce to reach the public? That would be a move towards diversity with a clear economic purpose. Farming could do with new blood: people who question the traditions, people who know about different foods, cultures and business models – people who look at a field and can envision things that previous generations couldn’t.

I think back. I grew up in Birmingham and my first experience with the land was helping my father on his allotment. My route was defiantly non-traditional. I struggled with undiagnosed dyslexia, joined the Parachute regiment and got kicked out, flipped burgers, worked as a chef and then produced cookery programmes for the BBC, which allowed me to buy a farm in Devon. Locals dubbed me “the Black Farmer”. I wish there were many more of us.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

I would never want to denigrate those who work so hard, and who may have toiled for generations to run their farms, produce the food we need and sometimes – if they are lucky, if the weather permits, if the stars align – make a profit. But I also want to be just as excited by the prospect of another black kid from Birmingham getting an opportunity, or a minority kid from a council estate in Manchester becoming the first farmer in the family.

Farming is key to the future, and the climate crisis is forcing us to think fast and hard about crops, water, soil and what we do with them. Old timers, new thinkers – we need both.

Wilfred Emmanuel-Jones is a businessman and founder of The Black Farmer food company

Five Great Reads: Secret filming, secret surgery and 30 years of Pokémon

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 22:33:37 GMT

Guardian Australia’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend. You’re looking well, some might say “refreshed”. Is it the diet, the exercise, a relaxing holiday? You’d tell me if you’d had something “done”, right? According to the experts, and some thrilling anecdotes, cosmetic procedures are more popular than ever, but admitting to them certainly isn’t. And secrets – from those kept by the Botox brigade to the mysteries revealed by devastating drought – appear to play a theme this week.

They have been branded “pervert or predator” glasses, a portent that a dystopian age of surveillance is upon us. Wherever you look, someone has an opinion (not always negative) on Meta Glasses, the clunky-ish but somehow sought-after offering from the tech gods. Now people are also reporting they have been secretly filmed in their own homes, at concerts and at work – and there’s a whole line of business helping it along.

‘We don’t have privacy any more’: Meta’s smartglasses are supposed to let you know the wearer is recording by the presence of a flashing LED light. But there are hundreds of vendors, easily discoverable online, who specialise in disabling it. One of those tells Maggie Harrison Dupré: “In public, I don’t think we have privacy any more, period. My argument is if you’re really worried about your privacy, don’t go outside.”

And it gets worse: Covert recordings may just be the first step in a more sophisticated surveillance apparatus integrated with another deeply controversial technology: facial recognition.

How long will it take to read: Just under nine minutes.

Further reading: ‘I’ve definitely lost followers’: influencers face backlash over Meta ‘pervert glasses’ content.

The heatwave scorching Europe and much of the northern hemisphere has turned once verdant landscapes dry and desolate. One of the starkest examples has been on the shores of the EU’s longest river. The Guardian travelled 100 miles along the Danube, where some residents are struggling to secure drinking water.

Hunger stones: In the Hungarian capital, Budapest, there is a rock that for centuries has served as a warning. It was named Ínség-szikla – the Rock of Starvation. When it began to emerge from the Danube, it meant the river had fallen so low that floating mills could no longer operate, crops were probably failing, and hunger would almost certainly follow. Today, amid record-low water levels on the river, the rock has surfaced almost in its entirety, along with the sandy riverbed on which it rests, astonishing geologists and government scientists sent to examine it.

Notable quote: “It’s gone. Everything has dried up. Since I started farming this land after the end of communist rule, I’ve never seen a catastrophe like this.”

How long will it take to read: Three and a quarter minutes.

Further reading: The threatening thaw: climate professor on heatwave risks to tipping point of permafrost, and, for something hopeful: ‘Success story’ hailed as bluefin tunas caught off Yorkshire for first time since 1960s.

James Ford went from tearing up 00s dancefloors as one half of Simian Mobile Disco – musicians and DJs who elevated the electro-rave era of the decade – to becoming the most sought-after ear in music, collaborating with the Arctic Monkeys, Pet Shop Boys and Pulp. But when he was at the height of his powers, leukaemia struck. ***

“The obvious thing that has come out of all of this is that it does make you recognise what and who the important things in your life are and that life is exceptionally fragile.” James Ford

‘I’ve had a good innings’: When he was diagnosed, Ford, who had just turned 46, could admit his life had been a good one. A great one, even. “I’ve had some great times, I’ve got a lot of good memories and I’ve made some things I’m really proud of. I think I’ve been a generally good person in the world. And so I was almost at the point where I was like, if I die, I’ve had a good innings. I wouldn’t be that scared of it.”

But that didn’t stop him: During his second, brutal, round of chemotherapy, Ford undertook another remarkable chapter of his life, and began, while still in hospital, making music. Nurses got used to administering their daily medical care while Ford messed with drumbeats and sang, creating his new album.

How long will it take to read: A life-affirming four minutes

Further reading: ‘We never apologised for our rage or revenge-seeking’: riot grrrl legends Heavens to Betsy reunite; ‘I love provocative stories’: producer Christine Vachon on fighting for her ‘offensive’ movies.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

If you want to feel old, consider this: Pokémon turned 30 this year. In Japan, where it was created by zinester turned game designer Satoshi Tajiri as a sort of swan song for the ageing Game Boy, it rapidly transformed from a schoolyard phenomenon to a national one. And then the rest of the world followed suit.

A classic tale of scaremongering: The news reports in Australia, back in 1999, warned “The most popular toy this Christmas could be turning our children to witchcraft and violence”. Pokémon was seen as something between a vice, an addiction and even a past-time that could lead to animal abuse and dogfighting. There were old wives’ tales of kids jumping off buildings because they thought they’d evolved into Pidgeotto.

But it turns out that Pokémania was not an affliction but a shared, communal experience that linked you to people all over the globe. Millions of kids around the world knew what a Cubone was and, as a result, felt a little less isolated.

How long will it take to read: Two and a quarter minutes.

Further reading: How Pokémon Go encouraged me to find wonder in the world

Laura got away with it for two years before she was rumbled. It was at dinner, with her partner, when he looked at her and said: “Why aren’t you scowling at me? Frown!” Laura tried to frown, and he was like: “No, you’ve had Botox.” Turns out, lots of people are spending thousands to alter their appearance – but also hope that no one notices. Why?

A ‘noticeable shift’: “I am definitely seeing more patients who prefer not to tell friends, family, or even colleagues that they’ve had aesthetic treatments,” says one doctor.

Notable quote: “Really, it bears no real relevance to our relationship. It’s a bit like: ‘What he doesn’t know, can’t hurt.’”

But things don’t always go to plan: One woman, who had fillers in her lips, thought she’d be able to get away with it. “I didn’t tell anyone as I guess I was a bit embarrassed to admit to it as I was approaching my 40s … but about 24 hours later my lips blew up.”

How long will it take to read: Just over six minutes

Further reading: Do you have to be hot at work? Eight people on how looks influence their jobs

The Premier League returns, F1’s Dutch Grand Prix and The Greatest Rivalry – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 21 Aug 2026 16:03:02 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

Blink and it’s back – just 34 days after a captivating World Cup came to a close, the Premier League returned on Friday night as the champions Arsenal took on newly promoted Coventry – and Saturday sees five more fixtures. There’s no better way to launch your football weekend with our compelling rolling blog, with Cameron Ponsonby and Barry Glendenning keeping pace with all the day’s breaking news and vibes from around the grounds. In Scotland, Rangers and Celtic are in action, and there’s a full-fat programme in the Championship. Why not join the conversation: send your thoughts to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

Tanya Aldred checks in from Derby where Ben Stokes’ Division Two frontrunners Durham are in action. Elsewhere, Surrey are taking on County Championship leaders Nottinghamshire at the Oval, title-challenging Somerset face Essex at Taunton, where New Zealand batter Henry Nicholls has been impressing on debut. At the Utilita Bowl, Yorkshire have been huffing and puffing against Hampshire, while at Grace Road rock-bottom Leicestershire are taking on Glamorgan. Then there’s Sussex against Warwickshire and the former England opener Zak Crawley has been in fine form for promotion hopefuls Kent against Middlesex at Merchant Taylors’ School. The other fixtures are Worcestershire against Gloucestershire and, at Old Trafford, Northamptonshire battling Lancashire.

Saturday’s Premier League action begins in Hull, where Manchester United ‌will start to discover whether last season’s resurgence under Michael Carrick can survive the burden of expectation. Hull’s return to the top flight guarantees a raucous atmosphere, while United, who reinforced their midfield with the close-season signing of Belgium international Youri Tielemans, will be ​eager to show that last season’s promising campaign was no one-off. Tim de Lisle helms our live blog, with Will Unwin reporting from the MKM Stadium.

With the ink drying on a fresh contract at Red Bull, Max Verstappen can give his home Dutch Grand Prix a fitting sendoff this weekend by becoming Formula One’s sixth different winner in ⁠six races. The old-school seaside circuit ⁠is slipping off the calendar after ​this year’s race and victory on Sunday would be a bittersweet occasion for Red Bull’s four-time world champion and his throngs of orange-shirted supporters. Verstappen has come close to winning this season, with two second places including Hungary ⁠before the August break that ended this week, and the 28-year-old has always been on the podium – three wins and two second places – since the track returned to the championship in 2021. Philip Cornwall will be keeping tans on the Dutchman’s fortunes in the sprint race and qualifying at the helm of our lap-by-lap blog. Giles Richards reports.

Barry Glendenning is back at post, with two key Premier League fixtures fully on his radar. Everton host Crystal Palace eager to lay down an early season marker having lost their opening game in each of the past four seasons. Pierre Sage arrives from Lens as the visitors’ new manager with a similar stuttering-start hoodoo to shrug off: of the 16 previous Palace managers to oversee a Premier League match, just two have won their first. Another new manager, Oliver Glasner, will be eager to show Nottingham Forest can cope without Elliot Anderson against Leeds. The England international was sold to Manchester City for £116m during the World Cup. The Austrian has an enviable record on debut, however: he has won his first league game in charge with four of his five previous clubs.

Billed as the Greatest Rivalry, the All Blacks are in South Africa for a four-Test series to see, one can only assume, which international team can be deemed the best around. Having beaten New Zealand in the Rugby World Cup final in 2023 the Springboks are the current world champions and, on home soil, many would fancy them to live up to that title. But never underestimate the All Blacks. The scene is set for a cracker. Daniel Gallan will have minute-by-minute updates from the first Test in Johannesburg.

Big-spending Spurs travel to Brentford, hoping to make last season’s pitiful 17th-place finish a distant memory. Roberto De Zerbi arrived late last season but kept a divided, flagging Spurs up and the club have backed the Italian in the transfer market, with the Manchester ⁠City winger ⁠Savinho arriving on Friday for a cool £75m, but a consistent goalscorer is possibly the missing element to propel them into the front rank of contenders: Dominic Solanke, Dejan Kulusevski, Mohammed Kudus, Xavi Simons and Wilson Odobert are all injured. Brentford have again made a canny foray into the summer transfer market. In Mamadou Sangare, the £39m club record signing from Lens promises to become one of the season’s breakout players. Scott Murray hosts the MBM, with Jacob Steinberg reporting.

Emillia Hawkins and Yara el-Shaboury pick up the baton to preview the day’s action with breaking news and much more as we settle down for another engaging set of Premier League fixtures, with three games on offer. Email matchday. live@theguardian. com with your notions and queries.

Emillia Hawkins pops up again for the first of the day’s match blogs as Manchester City begin a new post-Pep Guardiola era at home to Bournemouth. A new manager is in the dugout in Enzo Maresca, key players Rodri, Bernardo Silva and John Stones have departed and, for the first time in years, there are genuine questions about what City will look like. The challenge is no longer staying ahead of the pack, but perhaps keeping up with it. A debut too for Marco Rose in the Cherries’ corner. The German head coach has a tough act to follow after Andoni Iraola left the south coast club for Anfield. Jamie Jackson reports.

While the season started a new era with dominant Mercedes winning six races in a row, one for George Russell and five for championship leader Kimi Antonelli, the past five have told another story with a different winner every weekend. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, Russell, Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, Antonelli and McLaren’s Lando Norris have been the winners and now Max Verstappen and McLaren’s Oscar Piastri look most likely to keep the sequence running as the second half ‌of the season kicks off at Zandvoort. Champions McLaren have won the last two Dutch Grands ​Prix, current champion Norris in 2024 and Piastri in 2025, and will be going for a hat-trick with the team bringing the second part of an upgrade package introduced in Hungary. Mercedes, with Antonelli now 50 points clear of closest rival Hamilton, have not won at Zandvoort since Juan Manuel Fangio in 1955 and intend to rectify that at what will be the fifth of six sprint weekends this season. Yara el-Shaboury steers our lap-by-lap coverage.

Liverpool begin life after Mohamed Salah and with a new ​manager in Andoni Iraola when they travel to Newcastle, whose summer has been defined by sweeping change. Newcastle embark on a new chapter with Matthias Jaissle replacing Eddie Howe as manager ​and the likes of Guimaraes, Sandro Tonali ‌and Anthony Gordon having departed. Jaissle’s first competitive fixture is sure to be an emotional one as Newcastle and Liverpool come together to celebrate the life of Kevin Keegan, a man who meant so much to both clubs, before kick-off before resuming a rivalry which has sparked some classic encounters in the Premier League era. Michael Butler hosts the live blog, with Louise Taylor and Sam Dalling reporting from St James’ Park.

The Data Center Backlash Bursts Into the Midterms

The New York Times August 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

With opposition to the centers mounting, many Democrats and a growing number of Republicans are campaigning against them.

By Shane Goldmacher

Shane Goldmacher is a national political correspondent. He reviewed television and digital ads airing in races across the country about data centers for this piece.

The fight over data centers is suddenly at the epicenter of the midterm elections.

One new ad in Texas begins with someone typing into a chatbot, “Why is my electric bill going up?” Another in Ohio blames one of the state’s Republican senators for a proliferation of data centers, calling them “a total scam.” And in top House battlegrounds in Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, the Democratic challengers are all running ads against the server warehouses powering the artificial intelligence boom.

Data centers have become unlikely fault-lines in the broader fight over an A. I. revolution that is remaking the global economy and threatening to disrupt the job market. Now politicians are racing to tap into the backlash — or inoculate themselves — as political strategists in both parties described the issue as an unusually fast-moving force that is already reshaping races for the House, the Senate and governor’s mansions.

“It’s very much a bottom up, organic movement,” said Anna Greenberg, a veteran Democratic pollster, who said that while people’s views on data centers were largely tied to how close they live to them, the facilities were also becoming symbols of the excesses of Silicon Valley.

“Data centers are a physical manifestation,” she said. “Billionaires are building them, and it feeds into all of the big tech skepticism that is there. It’s very symbolic of everybody’s issues with A. I.”

There are signs that the emerging data center debate is scrambling the usual partisan divisions.

So far, Democrats have chiefly been the ones racing to harness voter anger about data centers over rising electricity prices, water use and mistrust of the tech sector. They aim to punish Republicans for cozying up to industry by approving many of these projects.

But in recent weeks, a growing number of Republican candidates have scrambled to shield themselves from any fallout. They have voiced skepticism about data centers, despite President Trump’s full-throated cheerleading for the A. I. industry and fears among party leaders in Washington that blocking construction of the centers could slow the economy and make the United States less competitive against China.

Some Republicans are now using “data center” as an epithet, and casting themselves as the real opponents of corporate tax breaks and unfettered construction. Last week, Mike Rogers, the Republican running for Senate in the key swing state of Michigan, said that he supports a one-year moratorium on data center construction.

Polls show a revolt brewing against data centers. A Gallup poll conducted in March showed 71 percent opposed local construction of the centers, and a summer survey from the Annenberg Public Policy Center of the University of Pennsylvania showed that the number of people opposing new data centers in their areas had risen by 12 percentage points since February and March.

The fallout has been so swift that in some races, including the governor’s contests in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Florida, both Democrats and Republicans are airing television ads about data centers.

On Wednesday, a remarkable memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that data center politics was endangering Senator Jon Husted of Ohio, a Republican. His challenger, Sherrod Brown, the state’s former Democratic senator, has aired millions of dollars of ads, calling Mr. Husted “the face of data centers in Ohio.”

“More than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” the memo said.

NRSC memo on Ohio data centers.

The one-page document, which was earlier reported by Axios, amounted to a desperate plea for the well-heeled industry to finance an advertising campaign — lest a Husted loss serve as “a cautionary lesson” for politicians elsewhere.

Zac McCrary, a Democratic pollster, said that opposing data centers offered Democrats a rare chance to make inroads in rural areas and small towns that are resisting the developments.

“It absolutely shakes up the snow globe on the partisan coalitions in a part of the world where Republicans have been dominant,” he said. “It’s one of the few issues today that does not immediately code as red or blue, left or right.”

In Florida, Representative Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for governor, spent more than $2 million on one ad in his primary, vowing to “protect” the state from data centers that “jack up utility rates.” In the ad, he tried to cast that position as standing with Mr. Trump, whose administration sought to blunt some of the opposition earlier this year by proposing a “ratepayer protection pledge,” in which data centers promise not to drive up electricity costs.

His Democratic opponent in the fall, David Jolly, said that “we don’t want crime or data centers in our neighborhoods” in one of his first ads of the general election.

In a sign of how top-of-mind data centers have become, Mr. Donalds brought up the topic unprompted at an event last week in Naples, Fla. “Listen, I know people have concerns,” he said. “I’ve seen the polling. But leadership isn’t just looking at polling.”

He then tried to thread the needle between selling the importance of artificial intelligence for the United States’ competitive future and addressing boiling anger at local data centers. “I don’t want it near your home, just like I don’t want it near my home,” Mr. Donalds said.

Mr. Jolly’s position is less complicated. In an interview on Thursday, he said Florida should impose a moratorium on data center construction until the full impacts could be studied.

The fierceness of the mounting opposition has startled some in the tech sector.

“This is a powder keg,” warned Chamath Palihapitiya, a public-facing venture capital investor, in a post on X this week, responding to the dire warning in the N. R. S. C. memo. He wrote that the A. I. industry had “failed miserably in doing the basics” of selling itself.

Political strategists and pollsters in both parties said that voters have linked the facilities to concerns over higher electricity prices, water use, the fate of farmlands and general fears about the advent of artificial intelligence and big tech.

“They didn’t do a good enough job explaining anything,” Ryan James Girdusky, a Republican political strategist and podcaster, said of the industry.

In Texas, the Democratic candidate for Senate, James Talarico, and for governor, Gina Hinojosa, have held recent events about data centers, accusing their Republican rivals of pocketing data center donations while backing expansions.

“Texans are mad,” Ms. Hinojosa said in an interview. “It is hard to convey what feels like an invasion by data centers with no rules, no laws to protect Texas. They’re popping up everywhere.”

It was her advertisement that featured a chatbot being asked about the cause of rising electricity prices. The answer it provides? Blaming Gov. Greg Abbott and data centers.

Even before that ad, Mr. Abbott, a Republican, had been shifting his stance on data centers. Less than a year ago, Mr. Abbott bragged that Google’s $40 billion investment made Texas “the epicenter of A. I. development,” bringing both construction jobs and tax revenues.

But this summer he announced new standards for data centers on water use and electricity and called to end some tax incentives. Earlier this month he directed the state’s utility commission to audit all data centers seeking permits before they could move forward.

“Data center growth cannot come at the expense of Texans’ livelihoods,” said Catherine Frazier, a spokeswoman for Mr. Abbott.

Mr. Abbott is hardly the only politician pivoting.

Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, a potential Democratic candidate for president in 2028, had been a booster of A. I. investments. In June 2025, Mr. Shapiro said he was “proud” of Amazon’s $20 billion data center investment, bragging it would be the largest private sector investment in the state’s history.

On Tuesday, Mr. Shapiro signed an executive order imposing what he called the “strictest guardrails in the nation” to stop “predatory developers.”

“I’ve heard loud and clear from the people of Pennsylvania,” said Mr. Shapiro, who is up for re-election this year.

Now Mr. Shapiro has started airing a television ad attacking his Republican challenger, Stacy Garrity, as the “number one fan of data centers.” Ms. Garrity has her own ad hitting Mr. Shapiro for “data centers in our backyards,” but her campaign can afford only a small fraction of the airtime.

Another Republican candidate for governor running on data center politics is Representative Tom Tiffany of Wisconsin, who has attacked his Democratic rival as “Data Center David Crowley.” Mr. Crowley narrowly won the nomination over a democratic socialist, Francesca Hong, who had demanded a data center moratorium.

Neither Mr. Crowley nor Mr. Tiffany has called for a moratorium.

Mr. Crowley has preferred to let local communities decide, with a number of guardrails and restrictions. Mr. Tiffany, who called data centers “exciting new technology” just a few months ago, is now calling for a repeal of tax incentives.

In Michigan, William Lawrence, a progressive activist, rode an anti-data center message to win the Democratic nomination in a key Michigan House seat this month and then immediately made a general election ad targeting Representative Tom Barrett, the Republican incumbent, on the issue.

Mr. Barrett campaigned on Tuesday with Speaker Mike Johnson in Michigan, who warned that, while “community concerns” needed to be accounted for, “a broad moratorium against data centers is kind of a dangerous prospect right now.”

The next day Mr. Barrett began airing a new data center ad of his own, in which he claimed that “I stood up to my own party and voted against giving your tax dollars to data centers.”

In an interview, Mr. Lawrence, who supports a moratorium, called the ad “outrageous” and said voters would not be satisfied with half measures. Data center opposition, he said, was “number one in terms of intensity” in the district.

“It’s bringing together three-time Trump voters, anti-vaxxers, environmentalists, independents, nonvoters, people who are in our cities, people who are in the rural areas,” Mr. Lawrence said. “And it’s bringing together all these people because none of us trust big tech to do right by our communities.”

Patricia Mazzei and Ruth Igielnik contributed reporting.

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.
